The state of the art in 2026 is a system that takes organs from donors dead two ways, repairs them on machines, accepts them infected and cures the infection, borrows them from pigs for months at a time, and transplants the bladder, the uterus, the hand, and the face—and still ends every year with a waiting list longer than the one it started with, because the demand it serves grows as fast as the art. That is the whole of the state of the art, and it is why the queue of Sections 5 and 6, and not the laboratory, remains the system’s contested ground.

17. The Cocked Hat: Where the Record Does Not Agree With Itself

Three bearings give a triangle, not a point, and this report’s triangle is printed here as the paper prints its own position: honestly inside it. The desk files, in one place, the disagreements the sections carried. Twelve people die each day waiting, on the federal government’s current page; seventeen was the same government’s figure through 2025, and the hard counts by organ sit beneath both. The waiting list is 109,817 on one dated snapshot and 108,790 on another, and the transplant total for 2025 is 49,064 in the network’s release and 49,065 in the Medicare agency’s rule. Whether MELD 3.0 repaired the sex gap is disputed between studies that measured transplant probability and studies that measured survival. Whether America lacks transplant surgeons is disputed between a match table showing filled positions recovered and a literature of falling applications and burnout, while the shortage in transplant medicine stands uncontradicted. Whether presumed consent raises donation is disputed between the cross-country associations and the best-adjusted null result, with Spain’s own architects testifying against the popular version. Whether the crackdown on out-of-sequence allocation removed an abuse or cost transplants is disputed in the system’s own before-and-after numbers. Whether the federal safety findings against the Kentucky procurement organization are sustained is disputed by the organization, with its appeal pending. What fraction of the world’s kidney transplants are bought is unknown on any current measurement; the only number is from 2007. What China’s transplant volume truly is, is contested between official statistics, an independently published finding that the reform-era data fit a formula too precisely to be counts, and estimates the official record cannot house. And whether the predictive software at the edge of the match is artificial intelligence is, on the documents, a dispute about a label.

The desk’s summary, then, in the plain terms the record supports. Organ donation in America in 2026 is a national, public, formula-ranked system wrapped in private gates: a financial clearance before the list, a center’s discretion at the offer, a review board’s exception inside the score, a second listing for those who can pay for one, and an insurer’s network deciding at which hospital the formula’s answer is carried out. The law forbids the sale of organs absolutely and polices the queue instead; the courts guard the rules of that queue and have never handed out an organ; the judges’ single intervention for a named patient suspended a rule for two children for a few days and is remembered, thirteen years later, precisely because it stands alone. The shortage is real and arithmetical—109,817 waiting, 49,064 transplanted in the best year in history, twelve dead a day on the current count—and a documented share of it is manufactured at the acceptance desk, where 29.3 percent of recovered kidneys are refused into discard. Abroad, the forbidden market persists on a scale nobody has measured since 2007, the one legal paid system’s own vendors say it should end, and the China file stands graded and unresolved. Over it all, the art itself has been transformed in a generation: two roads to death, machines that repair organs in transit, donors once refused now routine, a pig kidney that kept a man alive long enough to receive a human one. A television drama asked, on Sunday night, whether a computer or a rich man can move a name up the list. The record’s answer, filed in full above, is that the computer does not exist, the rich man’s lawful instruments are the duplicate evaluation and the second listing, the hands that move the list belong to centers and boards and are documented to the percentage point—and that the list itself, its length, its arithmetic, and its dead, is the story the drama was standing in front of.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty items.

Subjective
Vulture—recap of Cupertino, “Harper” (Season 1, Episode 6), CBS, aired November 8, 2026

The occasion, as recapped: the 27-year-old next in line for a liver, the wealthy venture capitalist moved ahead of her, the hospital’s blame laid on its AI-generated list, and the testimony that the list had chosen her and a physician’s hand had not. Rated four stars. Filed as the generator of this report, and for nothing else.

Subjective
National Organ Transplant Act, 42 U.S.C. §274e, and the Act’s compilation (govinfo.gov)

The prohibition in its own words, the $50,000 and five-year penalty, the organ definition, the payment exceptions, and the 2007 paired-donation carve-out. The statute the whole report stands on.

Subjective
Health Resources and Services Administration—organ donation statistics and the OPTN modernization updates, 2024–2026 (organdonor.gov; hrsa.gov)

The federal ledger: 109,817 on the list at July 30, 2026, twelve deaths a day in the current framing, the modernization’s contracts and board election, and the December 2025 contract that left the matching system with its builder and took the safety work away.

Subjective
U.S. Government Accountability Office—Organ Transplantation: HHS Action Needed, GAO-26-107434, January 2026

The overseer’s verdict: contracts let to assess the network’s weaknesses, no detailed plan for the next phase, evaluations of the contractor begun retroactively in March 2025 after years of none, and three recommendations with the Department’s concurrence.

Subjective
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services—press releases of July 21 and September 18, 2025, and August 5, 2026

The enforcement record in the government’s voice: the Kentucky investigation’s 351 cases and 103 with concerning features, the first mid-cycle decertification of a procurement organization at Miami, and the decertification begun against Network for Hope, which disputes the findings and has appealed.

Subjective
Ariane Lewis—“The Quest to Revise the UDDA,” Neurocritical Care (2024); Cambridge, Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics (2025)

The death-definition file: the drafting committee’s indefinite pause of September 2023, the draft’s contested five points, the neuroendocrine gap between the statute’s words and the clinic’s practice, and the state variations from New Jersey’s exemption to New York’s accommodation.

Subjective
OPTN Ethics Committee—ethical analysis of normothermic regional perfusion (2024); American College of Physicians, statement of concern (2021)

The perfusion dispute from its two poles: the college’s call for a pause and its characterization of the procedure, and the committee’s findings on the dead donor rule, consent, and protocol—filed as an analysis, expressly not a policy.

Subjective
Rafael Matesanz and colleagues—“Opt-out legislations: the mysterious viability of the false narrative,” Kidney International (2019); Arshad, Anderson and Sharif, Kidney International (2019); Gardiner and colleagues, Transplant International (2026)

The consent file: the Spanish architects’ verdict that their law is a theoretical presumed consent of insignificant effect, the thirty-five-country null result, and the five-year account of England’s fall in family consent after its switch. The cocked hat of Section 4 in three papers.

Subjective
Global Observatory on Donation and Transplantation—2024 report (WHO/ONT collaborative, Transplantation, 2026); Library of Parliament, HillStudy 2026-06-E

The world table: 47,180 deceased donors worldwide in 2024, Spain first by rate at 53.9 per million, the United States first by count and second by rate at 49.7—with the Belgian and Czech ordering differing between reproductions, as the report states.

Subjective
OPTN/SRTR 2024 Annual Data Report—Overview, Kidney, and Deceased Donation chapters (srtr.hrsa.gov)

The registry’s own arithmetic: 70,600 added to the lists in 2024, 3,743 kidney deaths and 4,901 removals for deterioration, organs recovered per donor up at 3.35 and organs transplanted per donor down at 2.66. The supply paradox in the source’s own tables.

Subjective
UNOS—“U.S. Surpasses 49,000 Organ Transplants While Deceased Organ Donations Dip,” January 28, 2026; HRSA—“Organ Transplants Exceeded 48,000 in 2024,” January 15, 2025

The record years: 48,149 transplants in 2024 and 49,064 in 2025, the fifth consecutive record, with living donors at 7,237 and deceased donors down for the first time in a decade. The Medicare agency’s one-count-higher printing of the 2025 total is filed with them.

Subjective
JAMA Internal Medicine—out-of-sequence kidney allocation, 2020–2023; The New York Times, February 2025

The departure from the run: 342 kidneys placed out of sequence in 2020, 2,927 in 2023, the newspaper’s nearly-one-in-five accounting, and the post-memorandum fall in both the practice and the daily transplant count. The dispute is filed unresolved.

Subjective
The MELD 3.0 literature—preliminary UNOS-era study, Transplantation (2024); multicentre study (2025); Hepatology (2025); Di Napoli and colleagues, Frontiers in Transplantation (2026)

The sex-gap file in four instruments: the pre-fix ratios of 0.88 and 1.39, the post-fix non-significance, the narrowing ninety-day gap, the attenuation by height, and the flat contradiction on survival. Printed as a disagreement because it is one.

Subjective
Khazanchi and colleagues—JAMA Internal Medicine (2026); National Kidney Foundation, CKD-EPI 2021 implementation guidance

The repair file: the 1.159 multiplier and what it delayed, the race-free equation’s adoption dates, 21,119 candidates with a median 1.7 years restored, the 5.3-per-thousand rise in Black transplant rates—and one center’s 39.8 percent delivery of its own eligible corrections.

Subjective
Murnaghan v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, No. 13-3083, E.D. Pa.—temporary restraining order of June 5, 2013 and supplemental memorandum of June 7, 2013; Halpern, Annals of Internal Medicine (2013), with Harvey’s reply

The one judicial touch on an individual’s ranking, in the judge’s own limiting words, with the ethicist’s “troubling precedent” and the family’s counsel’s answer filed beside it. The fullest single document in this report’s court file.

Subjective
Callahan v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, No. 1:19-CV-1783-AT, N.D. Ga., opinion of January 16, 2020; Adventist Health System v. HHS, No. 21-1589, 8th Cir. (2021); the OPTN Final Rule, 42 C.F.R. §121.8

The policy-litigation file: the doctrine stated by the court itself, the denied injunctions, the one-day life of the liver policy in May 2019, and the regulatory text every case construes—including its preservation of the right to decline an organ.

Subjective
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services—OPO conditions-for-coverage final rule, CMS-3409-F, October 30, 2026; Part B-ID application, Form CMS-10798; Cigna Coverage Policy 0560 (2026)

The payer-and-ratings file: fourteen lowest-tier and twenty-one middle-tier service areas opened to competition on 2024 data, the immunosuppressive-drug benefit’s narrow terms, and a current coverage policy classing composite-tissue transplants experimental. The front door and the back wall of the system, in the agencies’ and carriers’ own documents.

Subjective
Declaration of Istanbul on Organ Trafficking and Transplant Tourism (2008, revised 2018); Zargooshi, follow-up of Iranian kidney vendors (2001); the Ekweremadu judgment, Old Bailey (2023)

The forbidden market’s documents: the definitions the world uses, the only legal paid system judged by its own sellers—seventy-six percent for a ban—and the first trafficking conviction under the United Kingdom’s Modern Slavery Act.

Subjective
Robertson, Hinde and Lavee—BMC Medical Ethics (2019); Robertson and Lavee—American Journal of Transplantation (2022); the China Tribunal judgment (2019); United Nations experts’ statement, June 14, 2021; the position of the People’s Republic of China (2022)

The China file, each instrument at its own grade: the formula-fitting donation data, the seventy-one papers, the people’s tribunal’s finding and its own stated limit, the experts’ alarm, and the official denial. Filed together because the report’s method requires the whole shelf, not a selection.

Subjective
The New England Journal of Medicine—Moers machine-perfusion trial (2009), DCD heart trial (2023), DONATE HCV (2019), HOPE Act kidney trial (2024); Nature (2018) and Nature Medicine (2025); The Lancet on the Andrews bridge case, September 3, 2026

The invention file: the pump’s vindication, the restarted hearts, the cured infections, the HIV-positive donors made standard, and the pig kidney that carried a man 271 days to a human one. Every first in Section 16 traces to a document on this shelf.

item.title: The Kraków Suspect Dies in Hospital, the Mediator Comes to Washington, and Asia Buys Back Friday
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The overnight file for Monday, November 9, 2026: Małopolska police said the 24-year-old Kraków suspect died early Monday in hospital as Poland began its second day of national mourning and prosecutors pursued the terrorism investigation without the man who could have answered it, Dana Gas said it was assessing damage at Khor Mor after dousing the fire with no staff injured, Qatar's prime minister was scheduled at noon in the Oval Office in the Iran mediation while Tehran waited for an answer to its two-day proposal, and Asian markets bought back part of Friday's rout while the Senate count stayed frozen. Collected at 0400.
item.content:encoded:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Kraków Suspect Dies in Hospital, the Mediator Comes to Washington, and Asia Buys Back Friday

The night file, while Washington slept: the one man who could have answered the Kraków questions will not answer them, and Poland’s second day of mourning opened with the investigation turned from a questioning to a reconstruction. The region’s other fire acquired an operator’s statement: the Khor Mor fire is doused, the damage is being assessed, and no restart is promised. The Iran mediation acquired a room and an hour: the Oval Office at noon, closed, with Qatar’s prime minister inside it and Tehran’s foreign minister on the record waiting for an answer. Asia’s markets, handed the same weekend, bought back part of Friday. The Senate count did not move for a third day. Monday holds the meetings; Tuesday still holds the talks and the deadlines.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 23, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the fourth tanker claimed in Hormuz, the halt at Khor Mor, and the count frozen at Friday’s figures. The reports filed here are the night’s reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Sunday’s facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

The night closed one file by death, priced another by the barrel and the index, and moved no count, no coalition and no tanker claim from claim to confirmation. In Kraków, Małopolska police announced early Monday that the suspect, a 24-year-old man wounded in the shootout with police on Saturday, died in hospital, in the Guardian account and the second police account filed below. The dead of the case therefore stand at ten on the accounts that count him with his victims: six in the Main Market Square, three at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and the man himself. Prosecutors pursue the terrorism investigation on the sequence, the weapons and the emblems on his clothing; no motive has been established, and the man who held it is dead. In Iraqi Kurdistan, the operator Dana Gas said Monday it was assessing damage at Khor Mor after dousing the fire, with no injuries to staff, in the operator’s statement filed below; production stands halted and 2,800 megawatts stand off the grid. In Washington, the day’s schedule is the news: Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff’s office, and at noon the president meets Qatar’s prime minister behind closed doors on the Iran file, the vice president meeting him separately, in the schedule account filed below. In Paris the G7 foreign ministers meet Monday and Tuesday. In Tokyo the Nikkei closed its morning up 3.44 percent. The desk files the night in that order.

Kraków at 0400: The Suspect Is Dead, and the Questions Stay With the Living

Poland’s second day of national mourning began with an announcement from the police who shot the man. “We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Małopolska police wrote on X, in the accounts filed below. The man, 24, named in Polish media as Michał O., had been in critical condition since Saturday, when officers shot him within minutes of the first shots in the Main Market Square. He had not been formally arrested and had not been questioned; prosecutors had said both waited on his medical condition. That waiting is now permanent. The investigation the national prosecutor’s office opened as a terrorist offence covers two acts, the killing of six people in the square with the attempted killing of many others including police officers, and the killing of the three at the home; with the suspect dead, its work is the work the overnight accounts list: the full sequence, the source of the weapons, the meaning of the emblems, and whether anyone else took part in planning.

The morning’s new evidence is clothing and guns, and both arrive attributed and unfinished. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka told TOK FM radio on Monday that the man’s clothes carried many different emblems, partly examined and interpreted, the patches associated with various motifs that specialists are still analysing; she would not say more while the investigation runs. The minister’s Saturday reading stands where it stood: fascination with far-right ideology and very radical, ultra-nationalistic views, in the interior minister’s words, and a reading is what it remains. On the weapons, one Monday account counts 11 firearms recovered in all, four from the man or his car in Kraków and seven from the family home, in the victims and firearms account filed below; Polish media report he held a firearms permit and may have obtained guns from the home, and police have not confirmed that account. The wounded stand at 17 injured in the prosecutors’ count carried in the morning accounts, against 15 and 16 in the weekend’s files, with the two officers’ conditions divided in the accounts between regained consciousness in the evening file and one officer in a coma in the Monday account; both are printed in the Cocked Hat. The six of the square stand as the midnight edition named them by age and nationality, and the three at home stand at father 53, mother 52 and sister 21 in the Sunday confirmation the morning accounts repeat. Kraków’s own mourning runs through November 11; the national mourning ends Monday night.

Khor Mor at 0400: The Fire Is Doused, the Assessment Begins, and No Hand Is Claimed

The gas field’s operator has spoken, and its statement is the night’s firmest new document in the region. Dana Gas, joint operator of Khor Mor, said in a Monday statement that production was halted on Sunday following a suspected drone attack, that it was assessing the damage after dousing a fire sparked by the attack, and that there were no injuries to staff. The statement confirms the halt from the party that runs the field; it gives no restart date and no damage figure. The rest of the file stands as Sunday left it: a single drone struck a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank, in the electricity ministry sources’ account; employees were evacuated to shelters; gas supply stands suspended to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok; the loss stands at 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts, with more than 70 percent of the region without power in the regional accounts, in the Al Jazeera account and the Press TV account filed below. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s joint investigative committee is ordered; an initial assessment found no casualties. No group has claimed the attack, and no authority has named a hand. The field was shut once before this year, in July, on security threats, and restarted later that month; that history is in the operator’s account, and it is a history, not a forecast.

Hormuz at 0400: The Claims Restated, the Lane Near Oman, and Still No Confirmation

No tanker fire of the weekend acquired an independent confirmation in the night, and the morning files are restatements with one new sentence about a lane. The Guards’ Navy’s position stands in its fuller morning form: three oil tankers struck mines and caught fire extensively in a prohibited lane on Sunday, in the Antara account filed below, beside the Iranian Navy’s fourth tanker in the eastern strait, in the IANS account filed below; the two services’ counts differ by one ship, as the midnight edition printed them. One morning summary states the limit plainly: the reports do not establish that a fourth tanker incident occurred on November 9, and no flag or destination has been given for any of them, in the summary account filed below. The weekend’s maritime record that rests on incident reports rather than claims also stands: two tankers hit within an hour on Saturday evening in the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reports, one burning eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab with its crew evacuated, open-source analysts tentatively naming it the Navig8 Messi, and the American disabling of the bulk carrier Huda in the Gulf of Oman, in the maritime account filed below. The new sentence is Iraq’s: Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Iraq reached an understanding with the United States on Sunday to facilitate crude exports through the strait using a shipping lane near Oman, in the market accounts filed below. A lane agreed is not a lane used; no sailing under it is in the file at 0400.

Washington at 0400: A New Chief of Staff, a Mediator at Noon, and an Answer Owed

Monday in Washington is a handover and a meeting, and both were set before the weekend. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, takes the chief of staff’s office today, succeeding Susie Wiles, who moves to the Trump Political Operation; the president’s announcement of Friday stands as the record of the change, and the opposition’s answers stand as the midnight edition filed them, Senator Schumer’s and, on Sunday, Representative Jeffries’s statement on ABC that his party will not work with Mr. Miller, in the Sunday account filed below. At noon Eastern the president meets Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar’s prime minister and foreign minister, in the Oval Office in a session the White House schedule marks closed press; Vice President Vance is due to meet him separately, an American official told Reuters, in the schedule account above. Mr. Al Thani is the principal channel between Washington and Tehran; the vice president has spent roughly a fortnight in near-daily contact with him on the indirect Iran channel, in the backchannel account filed below.

What the mediator carries into the room is a sequence, and what he carries out of it is not yet in any file. The proposal described by the mediation sources runs in two days: on day one the United States lifts its naval blockade and releases some frozen Iranian funds while Tehran invites International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to the bombed nuclear sites; on day two the strait reopens and nuclear talks resume on Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on X on Sunday that Tehran was still waiting for Washington’s answer to that proposal. Against the sequence stand two American sentences from Sunday: the president’s, to CNN, that fresh attacks are highly unlikely if talks produce a strong agreement, with further targets mapped if fighting resumes; and Secretary of State Rubio’s, before the G7 talks in Paris, that he would not call the negotiations close to a breakthrough and that Iranian demands are in part unacceptable. No readout of any Monday meeting exists at 0400, because the meetings have not happened. The desk files the schedule, the proposal as its sources describe it, and the two sentences, and nothing beyond them.

Paris and Abu Dhabi at 0400: The Ministers Sit Monday, the Table Sits Tuesday

The G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday, and the Abu Dhabi round opens Tuesday, and the connection between the two rooms is Europe’s seat. The Paris gathering, among the last major events of France’s G7 presidency, takes up air defence and energy support for Ukraine ahead of winter, in the Paris account filed below; Secretary Rubio is expected on both days. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot’s Sunday statement stands: Europeans will be well represented in Abu Dhabi and France will take part, he told RTL radio, and he cannot yet say who will represent France, in the Reuters account filed below. Russia has said there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says they will participate; both statements stand, as the midnight edition printed them. The delegations stand as reported and not as settled: Russia’s led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky in the accounts, Ukraine’s named differently among the files, the Americans Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side. In Ukraine the file did not move in the night: the Komyshuvakha toll stands at at least 55 dead, the missing at 45 in the regional administration’s Sunday figure and about 50 in the intelligence agency’s, the search continuing in intervals under drone threat, in the toll account filed below; and President Zelenskyy’s reading of Friday night’s barrage, pressure ahead of the talks, stands as his reading.

Jerusalem at 0400: The Mandate’s First Working Day

Mr. Eisenkot’s 28 days began Sunday at the President’s Residence, and Monday is the first working day inside them. The mandate’s facts stand as the weekend filed them: 48 seats in his four-party bloc, 61 required, 67 recommendations to 46, four conditions published for joining his government, and no coalition. The expected meetings are the day’s file: Mr. Bennett on Sunday evening, its outcome not taken in by midnight and not supplied in the night’s accounts, and Mr. Liberman on Monday. The contest underneath stands in the positions the accounts carry: Mr. Liberman prepared for painful compromises, including on conscription, to build 61 without the Arab-led parties, and ruling out a minority government resting on their abstention, in the compromise account filed below; the arithmetic that account prints is the only road to 61 yet drawn on paper, 48 plus United Torah Judaism’s 7 and Shas’s 6, and it runs through the draft law his bloc campaigned on. On Tuesday the new Knesset is scheduled to convene. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the negotiations run. Nothing in the night’s file adds a seat, removes a condition, or names an agreement.

Al-Ayyat and Riyadh at 0400: Two Files That Did Not Move, and One That Moved Sideways

Egypt’s railway file rests where Sunday’s late count left it, and the morning accounts are the Sunday accounts carried forward. Seven dead in every later account; the injured at 112 in the Health Ministry’s count, 114 in the prosecutors’ provisional estimate, and at least 125 in the chief prosecutor’s late Sunday statement; the Giza-to-Fayoum train against the stationary Cairo-to-Aswan train between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa; President al-Sisi’s order for an urgent investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent; and no cause stated by the railway authority, the prosecutors or the ministry, in the wire account and the ministry account filed below. The dead have not been named. The investigation owns the cause, and it has not spoken.

Riyadh’s file moved sideways in the night: the damage, not the event, is now the disputed item. The Saudi Energy Ministry’s account stands, debris from an intercepted attack, minor damage to an Aramco administrative building in the financial district, no casualties. Against it stands a later filing reporting footage verified by BBC Verify in which one floor of the building is severely damaged and window glass is broken across several floors, in the intercepts account filed below. The coalition’s interception count stands at three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles destroyed, with two ballistic launchers in Saada destroyed in answer; the Houthi spokesman’s operations stand at four in one account and six in another, in the daily brief filed below; and the Sanaa toll stands unmoved at 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, in the Houthi-run health ministry’s count, which Saudi Arabia’s communications center said it was investigating. Every figure keeps its owner. The desk prints the ministry’s word and the verified footage’s picture side by side, and reconciles neither.

The Count at 0400: A Third Day Without Figures

Neither Senate race was called in the night, and no new figure was published for either, for the third day running. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on the tally stamped Friday evening; Alaska stands at Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes on a count posted Wednesday, in the count guide and the delay account filed below. Monday is the first day on which either count is scheduled to move: Alaska’s next update is due Monday or Tuesday, November 9 or 10, and is expected to carry early votes and a large batch of absentees. Tuesday remains the heavier date in both states: Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by 5 p.m. Tuesday and its affidavit voters must cure identification by then, counties certify by November 13, and Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no candidate reaches 50 percent. The estimates of Mississippi’s remainder still run from about 3,139 mail ballots to the state Republican chairman’s 23,000 to 25,000, with a tracker’s roughly 30,498 in its own model. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

Asunción and Shizuoka at 0400: A Detention’s Second Night, a Count Settled

Paraguay’s file carried one long explanatory account in the night and no new ruling. Former President Santiago Peña spent a second night in pretrial detention at the Presidential Escort Regiment, former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo in detention beside him, 27 people charged in the Ueno case in all, the repayments at $160 million to nearly 1.2 million savers in the central bank’s reporting and $153.5 million on the same savers in the guarantee fund’s second accounting, in the collapse account and the detention account filed below. Mr. Peña’s plea stands at not guilty through his attorney, Ricardo Preda; he declined to testify; no court has ruled on the substance of any charge, and he is presumed innocent. President Pedro Alliana is naming the cabinet that serves through 2028. Ueno froze the accounts of nearly three million customers in a country of 6.5 million; how much of the roughly $850 million in public money it administered can be recovered is not established.

Central Japan’s file is settled at the figures the midnight edition closed with, and Monday is its assessment day. The injured stand at 22 in the prefectures’ division, 19 in Aichi with one serious and three minor in Shizuoka, against 21 in the updated Jiji Press count and 24 in a local papers’ tally no official account carried forward, in the correction file filed below. The earthquake stands at magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency and 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, 1:04 a.m. Sunday beneath western Shizuoka, upper 5 in Chita, no tsunami, no deaths. The agency’s guidance stands for about a week, the risk highest in the next two to three days, its landslide thresholds lowered for the hardest-shaken municipalities, and its further investigation of the quake set for a meeting on Monday in the television accounts. No overnight aftershock of consequence is in the file.

The Markets at 0400: Oil Down, Asia Up, and the Two Readings of One Weekend

Asia’s markets opened the week by buying back Friday, and oil opened it by selling the weekend’s claims, and the desk files both prices without choosing between their readings. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 closed its morning at 59,411, up 1,976 points or 3.44 percent, recovering just over half of Friday’s fall, with Taiwan’s index up between 5.3 and 5.9 percent across the morning accounts, South Korea’s Kospi up between 1.4 and 1.8 percent, and the regional index outside Japan up 0.8 percent after a 4.6 percent fall last week, in the Reuters market account and the recap account filed below; the chipmakers led, and the accounts carry an inquiry at Nvidia over its chief executive as the sentiment item the rebound shrugged off. Oil’s prints moved through the morning rather than settling: Brent at $97.48, down 84 cents, at 0138 GMT, $97.67 in the later Perth print the midnight edition filed, $96.91 down 1.5 percent at 0629 GMT in one account, and $98.35, up 3 cents, at 0427 GMT in another, in the Reuters oil account filed below. The prints are an hour-by-hour movement under two opposing weights, the president’s sentence that fresh attacks are highly unlikely while talks progress, and a strait in which four tanker fires are claimed and none confirmed. Brent fell 17 percent last week, its steepest weekly drop since 2020 on the LSEG figures in the accounts. What New York does with the same file on Monday is not yet in the record.

Monday Opens: Handovers, Meetings, and a Second Day of Mourning

The day the night hands over is a working day built of other days’ appointments. In Poland it is the second and last day of national mourning, with Kraków’s mourning running to November 11 and the terrorism investigation now running without its suspect. In Washington Mr. Miller takes his office and the Qatari prime minister is in the Oval Office at noon. In Paris the G7 ministers sit, with the Abu Dhabi table set for Tuesday and Wednesday. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot meets Mr. Liberman inside a 28-day clock that started Sunday. In Iraqi Kurdistan the assessment at Khor Mor begins with the field dark. In Alaska the count may move today or tomorrow; in Mississippi nothing moves until Tuesday’s deadlines. Everything the week left open with a date still carries Tuesday’s date in the main: the talks, the American inflation report, the mail and cure deadlines, and the president’s larger Iran decision, which has no date at all. The log proceeds to Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s wounded, the counts run 15, 16 and now 17 injured in the prosecutors’ morning count, counting different sets at different hours; on its two officers, regained consciousness in Sunday’s evening account and one in a coma in Monday’s account, the desk prints both and resolves neither. On the three at the home, the ages now agree at 53, 52 and 21 in the repeated confirmation, against the two other sets the weekend’s files carried. On Hormuz, the Guards count three tankers and the Navy counts a fourth, no party that did not claim a fire has confirmed one, one name is offered tentatively by analysts, and a morning summary states that no fourth incident on November 9 is established. On Khor Mor, the halt and the 2,800 megawatts are confirmed by the ministries that lost them and now by the operator that runs the field, and the hand is claimed by no one. On Riyadh’s tower, minor damage in the ministry’s word and a severely damaged floor in verified footage. On oil, four prints between $96.91 and $98.35 in one morning, a movement and not a level. On Asia, Taiwan up 5.3 or 5.9 and the Kospi up 1.4 or 1.8 by the hour of the print. Against the triangle, the night’s single-valued facts are these: the Kraków suspect is dead, announced by the police who shot him, and the investigation continues without him; the Khor Mor fire is doused and its damage is being assessed by its operator, with no staff injured and no restart promised; the Qatari prime minister is scheduled at noon in the Oval Office and Tehran waits for an answer; the G7 sits in Paris and the Abu Dhabi table sits Tuesday; no Senate race was called and no figure moved; and Asia bought back part of Friday while oil moved both ways under it. The log proceeds to Monday.

Subjective
CoinEdition — Asia market recap: Asian stocks recover from the midterm-driven tech rout while the Nvidia inquiry weighs on sentiment

Asian equities rose on Monday as a bounce on Wall Street helped the region recover part of last week’s heavy losses, although an inquiry at Nvidia kept investors wary. Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 3.45 percent and the broader Topix opened 2.82 percent higher. Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 5.33 percent, South Korea’s Kospi added 1.68 percent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.19 percent, and MSCI’s index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.8 percent, recovering part of last week’s 4.6 percent drop. The rebound follows a Friday in which the Kospi tumbled about 9 percent, the Nikkei lost roughly 6 percent and the Hang Seng fell more than 1 percent. Nvidia’s board launched an independent probe into its chief executive, the account reports.

item.title: A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The midnight file for Monday, November 9, 2026: what Sunday settled and what it left open. At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven and the chief prosecutor's late count put the injured at 125, with no cause stated. In Kraków the six of the square were named by age and nationality, the square reopened, and the joining of the square to the house remained a spokesman's 'highly likely.' In Hormuz an Iranian Navy statement raised the day's claimed tanker fires to four, a maritime account tentatively named one vessel, and Reuters could confirm none of them; a drone halted Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no claim of responsibility. Gadi Eisenkot published four conditions and no coalition exists; the Senate count stayed frozen at Friday's figures, Mississippi at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637; and oil fell at Monday's open after the president said fresh attacks on Iran were highly unlikely while talks progress. Collected at 0000.
item.content:encoded:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

A Fourth Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, Khor Mor Goes Dark, and the Count Still Waits

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Sunday settled the toll at Al-Ayyat at seven dead, settled the hurt in central Japan at 22 in the prefectures’ own division, named the six of the Kraków square and reopened it, and put a price on Monday—oil down at the open. It left open everything with a deadline: a fourth tanker claimed in Hormuz and none confirmed, a gas field dark in Iraqi Kurdistan with no one claiming the drone, a mandate in Jerusalem exercised in conditions and not yet in a coalition, a Senate count frozen since Friday, and the Abu Dhabi table, enlarged on Sunday, still two days from sitting.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 9, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 22, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, and in Sunday’s earlier editions, Nos. 19 and 21, and its special reports. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled counts, names and a price, and it left causes, claims and coalitions open, and the desk files the day in that order. At Al-Ayyat the dead settled at seven in every later account, and the injured reached their last Sunday figure late in the day, when the chief prosecutor’s office put them at at least 125, in the updated running account filed below; no authority has stated a cause. In Kraków the six killed in the Main Market Square stand named by age and nationality, the square reopened late Sunday, and the joining of the square to the three dead at the suspect’s home stands at a prosecutor’s spokesman’s “highly likely,” in Reuters’ evening account filed below. In the Strait of Hormuz the claims grew after the evening edition closed: an Iranian Navy statement raised the day’s tally of tankers said to have struck mines to four, in the Navy’s account filed below, and no tanker fire of Sunday has been confirmed by a party that did not claim it. In Iraq a drone halted the Khor Mor gas field and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdistan grid, with no casualties in the first assessment and no claim of responsibility. In Jerusalem Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate produced four conditions and the week’s meetings, and no coalition. In the United States the Senate count posted nothing new for a second day. And at Monday’s open in Perth, oil fell, in Reuters’ market file filed below. Monday holds the handovers and the meetings; Tuesday holds the talks and the deadlines. That is the day whole, as it stands at midnight.

Al-Ayyat at Midnight: Seven Dead, 125 Injured in the Late Count, and No Cause

The railway file closed Sunday with its numbers at their highest and its central question unanswered. The Health Ministry’s staircase ran four dead and 88 injured, then seven dead and 112 injured, and late Sunday the chief prosecutor’s office put the injured at at least 125, with more than 70 of them discharged after treatment, in the Associated Press account filed below. Prosecutors who inspected the site said the Giza-to-Fayoum train, No. 134, hit the last carriage of the Cairo-to-Aswan train, No. 2010, which was stationary on the same track between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations; a conductor was among the dead, and the dead have not been named. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a prompt investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent. No cause has been stated by the railway authority, the prosecutors or the ministry. Settled: the place, the two trains, the seven dead. Open: the 125 against the 112 and 114 also printed under official names during the day, and the cause, which the investigation now owns.

Kraków at Midnight: The Square Reopened, the Six Named, the Joining Still a Spokesman’s Word

Poland’s second day of mourning is Monday, and Sunday ended with the case in its legal shape and its human shape both on the record. The six of the square are counted by age and nationality: a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50. Prosecutors have opened the investigation as a terrorist offence covering two acts, the six murders in the square and the three murders at the home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and are preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine. The spokesman Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the same person carried out both; highly likely remains an assessment, not a finding, and the suspect, in critical condition and not yet formally arrested or questioned, has answered nothing. The wounded stand at 16 in Reuters’ evening count, including the two officers and the gunman, and at 15 in other accounts; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief and at 53, 52 and 20 in the prosecutors’ account, and the desk prints both triangles. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński declined on Sunday to withdraw his Saturday reading of the attacker’s views, and the opposition’s demand that he produce its basis stands unanswered. The square reopened late Sunday. National mourning runs through Monday.

Hormuz at Midnight: A Fourth Tanker Claimed, One Tentative Name, and Qeshm Unsettled

The strait’s tally grew by one after the evening edition closed, and its confirmation count did not grow at all. The Iranian Navy said a further tanker struck a mine in the eastern strait before noon on Sunday, its identification systems off in a prohibited area, and called it the fourth tanker to hit mines on Sunday; the Guards’ Navy’s own statement of the day counts three, exploded and on fire along an unauthorized route. The two statements are both Iranian, they differ by one ship, and the desk prints both. Against the claims stand the day’s firmer items, none joined to the tally by any authority: the Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, and the American disabling of the M/V Huda on Saturday, explained by Central Command. One name has been offered for one ship, and it is offered as tentative: open-source analysts identify the tanker that caught fire off Khasab, its crew evacuated and firefighting tugs alongside, as the Navig8 Messi, in the maritime account filed below. No owner, flag authority or coast guard has confirmed that identification. On Qeshm the record also disagrees with itself: the Tasnim agency reported two missiles struck the island, Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes and suggested the explosions might be related to Iranian military activity, and Reuters, in its Sunday file filed below, said it was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. Three projectiles reported launched from Sirik toward vessels stand likewise unconfirmed, with no hit established.

Khor Mor at Midnight: 2,800 Megawatts Gone, and No Claim

The evening’s one confirmed interruption became, by midnight, the region’s largest measured fact. A single drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday night; production halted, the fire was still raging in the first reports, and crews were ordered into shelters. The Kurdistan electricity ministry put the generation lost at 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts, gas supply was suspended to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, and accounts put more than 70 percent of the region without power, with hospitals and water stations given priority and hydroelectric stations called on. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties, and Baghdad directed a joint investigative committee, in the accounts filed below. The region’s ministries called the attack a terrorist attack in a joint statement. No group has claimed it, one reporter at the scene could not say whether the projectile was a drone or a rocket, and a security source’s claim about its launch place is unconfirmed. Settled: the field is stopped and the megawatts are counted. Open: the hand, the damage, and the restart.

Riyadh and Sanaa at Midnight: The Launchers Destroyed, the Toll Standing at 33

The Saudi–Yemen ledger did not move in its figures on Sunday night, and its two sides stand as far apart at midnight as at noon. The coalition said it destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Saada that it said were used in Sunday’s attack on Riyadh, after intercepting three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles. The Energy Ministry’s account of the Aramco Tower stands: damage from falling debris, no casualties. The Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree’s claims stand against it: the financial district and King Khalid International Airport targeted, in operations the movement counts at four in one account and six in another, and a tally of coalition attacks over 24 hours that stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. The Sanaa figure did not move: at least 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, in the Houthi-run health ministry’s count for Saturday’s strikes on homes at al-Shariyah, east of the capital, which Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication said it was investigating. Every figure in this paragraph has its owner attached; none has been verified by a party that did not issue it.

Komyshuvakha at Midnight: 55 Dead, and the Missing at 45 or About 50

Ukraine’s file closed Sunday on a disagreement of five names. The toll of Monday’s bombing of the former school and the shelter at Komyshuvakha stands at at least 55 dead in every Sunday account, and Sunday’s drone strike on the rescue crews there injured no one and damaged specialized equipment, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The missing do not agree: the military intelligence agency HUR lists around 50 people still missing, and the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin, put the figure at 45 on Sunday afternoon, in the Associated Press account filed below. Many bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis continues. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members it says took part in the first strike; Russia’s differing account of its operations around Komyshuvakha stands in the earlier files, and no Russian statement on Sunday’s drone strike was taken in. The accounts of both attacks rest on Ukrainian officials and the Associated Press’s reporting; no party that did not issue them has verified the toll.

Jerusalem at Midnight: Four Conditions Published, the Meetings Set, No Coalition

The mandate’s first day ended where it began: 48 seats in hand, 61 required, 28 days running. Mr. Eisenkot’s four conditions for joining his government stand as he published them: acceptance of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence upheld, universal military, national or civilian service supported, and Hamas recognised as a terrorist organisation. His challenge to Likud and Religious Zionism, to back a government under him if they stand by their calls for unity, drew no answer taken in on Sunday. The contest underneath the arithmetic is the conscription question, and its positions are all on the record: Mr. Liberman prepared to make painful compromises, including on the conscription law, to build 61 without the Arab lists; the commentator Amit Segal’s assessment that the price of such an arrangement is that the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted; the Democrats’ chairman Yair Golan’s position that the ultra-Orthodox must be drafted; and Mr. Bennett’s party’s statement that its silence is not consent. Mr. Eisenkot was expected to meet Mr. Bennett on Sunday evening and Mr. Liberman on Monday; no outcome of the Bennett meeting was taken in by midnight. The Joint List said it was willing to help end Mr. Netanyahu’s tenure without demanding a place in the government, and had not yet been asked to commit its votes. On Tuesday the new Knesset is scheduled to convene.

Abu Dhabi at Midnight: Europe’s Chairs Claimed, the G7 in Paris on Monday, the Table on Tuesday

The talks have not begun, and everything about them that changed on Sunday was shape, not substance. France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans will be well represented in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday and that France will take part, that he will not personally sit at the table, and that Paris has not yet named its representative, in Reuters’ Paris file filed below. Russia’s delegation is reported led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky; the accounts of Ukraine’s delegation differ among themselves in the files taken in, and the desk prints no lead name as settled. Russia has suggested there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says this time they will participate; both statements stand. The G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday, with air defence and energy support for Ukraine on the agenda in the accounts taken in. The American president predicted a “very big” deal extending beyond Ukraine; Mr. Barrot said he did not know what the president had in mind. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side.

Washington at Midnight: Miller Takes the Office on Monday, and the Answers Are In

The handover announced Friday takes effect at the start of the new day, and Sunday supplied the last of the considered answers to it. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, becomes chief of staff on Monday, November 9; Susie Wiles, whose resignation the president received Thursday night and whose last day was Friday, moves to the Trump Political Operation. The president’s words stand in the record: “Stephen’s been with me since the beginning. He gets it.” The opposition’s answers now stand in two voices: Senator Chuck Schumer’s, that the president “has learned nothing from his historic defeat,” and, on Sunday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s, on ABC’s “This Week,” that his party will not work with Mr. Miller, in the Sunday account filed below. From the president’s own party, Representative Marlin Stutzman’s dissent stands as filed at evening. The Federal Register published nothing on Saturday or Sunday. Settled: the sequence and the date. Open: what the new chief of staff does with the office, which no statement yet describes.

Asunción at Midnight: 27 Charged, the Repayments Counted Two Ways, and No Ruling

Paraguay’s file ended its first weekend with the detention standing, the charges widened, and the money counted in two currencies of account. At least 27 people face charges in the Ueno case, including the bank’s lead shareholder Miguel Vazquez; former President Santiago Peña and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo are held in pretrial detention, Mr. Peña at the Presidential Escort Regiment, each of his two charges carrying up to ten years on the prosecutor’s statement. He declined to testify Saturday, maintains a plea of not guilty through his lawyer Ricardo Preda, and is presumed innocent; no court has ruled on any part of the case. On the repayments, the figures differ in their basis and the desk prints both: the central bank’s reporting, carried in the accounts filed below, puts about $160 million paid to nearly 1.2 million savers, while a second accounting of the guarantee fund puts the same 1.2 million savers at 994.6 billion guaraníes, equivalent to $153.5 million, as of November 6. Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including state pension funds; how much of it can be recovered is not established. President Pedro Alliana is naming a new cabinet to serve through 2028.

The Count at Midnight: Frozen at Friday’s Figures, and the Estimates Still Apart

For a second day the count posted nothing, and midnight is the hour to say plainly what that means: the last votes counted in either Senate race were counted by Friday evening. Mississippi stands at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on 953,314 counted, the tally stamped 5:02 p.m. Friday. Alaska stands at Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes, 48.2 percent to 47.9, on a count posted Wednesday. The estimates of what remains in Mississippi run from about 3,139 mail ballots outstanding on Friday’s count to the state Republican chairman’s 23,000 to 25,000 affidavit or mail ballots, with a tracker’s roughly 30,498 ballots left in its own model; the desk prints the three with their owners. The calendar is the settled part: in Mississippi, mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive, and affidavit voters must cure missing identification, by 5 p.m. Tuesday, November 10; counties certify by November 13; state law provides no recount for this race, and a plurality wins. In Alaska the next count is expected Monday or Tuesday, absentee ballots arrive through November 18, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for that day if no candidate clears 50 percent. The Associated Press ledgers stand at 54 Democrats to 44 Republicans in the Senate and 252 to 161 in the House, with 22 House races uncalled, Colorado’s 4th among them. Neither Senate race has been called, on the sixth day after the election.

Shizuoka at Midnight: The Hurt Settled at 22, and the Agency Meets on Monday

Central Japan’s file is the day’s one clean settling. The afternoon official division stood at midnight: 19 injured in Aichi Prefecture, one of them serious, and three minor injuries in Shizuoka, 22 in all, between a morning figure of 15 and a printed 24 that no later official account carried forward. The earthquake stands as filed: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency and 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time Sunday beneath western Shizuoka at about 40 kilometres’ depth, upper 5 on the Japanese scale in Chita, no tsunami threat and no deaths. One later account gives 21 injured in an updated Jiji Press count against the Associated Press’s 22, and the desk notes it without moving its figure, in the correction file filed below. The agency lowered its landslide-warning thresholds for the hardest-shaken municipalities of Aichi, kept its guidance of caution for about a week with the risk highest in the next two to three days, and is to investigate the quake further at a meeting on Monday, the television accounts report. A separate magnitude 4.3 tremor in the Kumamoto area on Sunday produced no reports of serious damage.

The Markets’ Reading: Oil Fell at Monday’s Open

The weekend’s claims met their first price in the small hours, and the price went down. Oil fell at Monday’s open in Perth after the president said fresh American attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely” if negotiations continued to advance, Reuters reported: Brent down 64 cents, or 0.64 percent, to $97.67 a barrel, briefly down more than a dollar, and West Texas Intermediate down 35 cents to $90.51, against Friday’s settlements of $98.32 and $90.83. An earlier print in the same opening, at 0138 GMT, carried Brent at $97.48, down 84 cents; the two prints are an hour’s movement, not a disagreement. Asian shares opened higher in the early accounts, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 up about 3 percent in the first Monday trading after its 5.96 percent fall on Friday. The reading the desk files is narrow: at the first price after a weekend of claimed tanker fires, a halted gas field and debris in Riyadh, the market paid more weight to a president’s sentence about talks than to any claim out of the strait. What the American and European sessions do with the same file on Monday is not yet in the record.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point, and Sunday’s triangles are these. On Al-Ayyat, the dead agree at seven and the injured stand at 125 in the prosecutor’s late count against 112 and 114 printed under official names during the day; the cause is stated by no one. On Kraków, the wounded stand at 15 or 16, the three at home at two sets of ages, the joining of the two scenes at a spokesman’s “highly likely,” and the minister’s reading as a hypothesis defended and challenged, with the man who could answer it silent in hospital. On Hormuz, the Guards count three burning tankers and the Navy counts a fourth, Reuters confirms none, one name is offered tentatively by analysts and by no authority, and Qeshm is a missile strike in one Iranian account and unconfirmed military activity in another. On Khor Mor, the halt and the megawatts are confirmed by the ministries that lost them, and the hand is claimed by no one. On the missing at Komyshuvakha, the agencies of the same government stand at 45 and about 50. On Jerusalem, a mandate has conditions and meetings and no coalition. On Asunción, the repayments are $160 million in one accounting and $153.5 million in another, on the same 1.2 million savers. On the count, the margins are Friday’s and Wednesday’s, and the estimates of what remains run tenfold apart. The log turns with Monday’s handovers in Washington and meetings in Jerusalem and Paris, and Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi and deadlines in Mississippi and Alaska. The desk files the day settled where it settled, and open where it stands open.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 30 items.

Subjective
The Orbit Post — two trains collide south of Cairo, killing seven and injuring at least 125

The running account, updated at 20:57 UTC on Sunday: the chief prosecutor’s office said late Sunday that seven people were killed and at least 125 injured, the toll given by the Health Ministry; its earlier updates carried seven killed and 114 injured, and before that four killed and 88 injured. Investigators at the site found the Giza-to-Fayoum train had hit the last carriage of the Cairo-to-Aswan train, stationary on the same track. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered a swift investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent. No cause was given on Sunday.

Subjective
Gazette Herald, carrying the Associated Press — seven killed and more than 125 injured in the train collision in Egypt

Seven people were killed and at least 125 others injured when two trains collided in the Al-Ayyat district of Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, the chief prosecutor’s office said in a statement late Sunday. The Health Ministry said more than 70 of the injured had been discharged after treatment. The crash occurred when a train travelling to Fayoum crashed into the rear of a train heading to Aswan; an inspection indicated the Aswan train’s last carriage was stationary on the same track. The president ordered a prompt investigation.

Subjective
AfroNews — Egypt: seven killed in the train collision

Egypt’s Health Ministry said seven people died and 112 were injured in Sunday’s train collision at Al-Ayyat in Giza governorate, and 45 of the injured had been discharged. Prosecutors later gave a provisional estimate of seven dead and 114 injured, saying the count continued. After inspecting the site and hearing witnesses, prosecutors said the front of the Giza-to-Fayoum train hit the rear of the Cairo-to-Aswan service, which had stopped on the tracks; both trains were travelling in the same direction. President al-Sisi ordered an urgent inquiry and accountability, and Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir visited. The cause remained unestablished.

Subjective
Reuters — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting as security fears grow

KRAKOW, Nov 8: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in the southern city’s historic main square. Sixteen people were wounded in addition to those killed, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital. One of the dead was a British citizen and another Austrian; five foreign nationals, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that the three bodies at the home had gunshot wounds, with firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition recovered. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s Saturday reading drew a demand from PiS deputy head Przemysław Czarnek for explanations; on Sunday the minister told TVN24 he was not retracting his statements. The square and surrounding streets reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s was suspended for twelve hours, the first time since 1939, PAP reported; and the two wounded officers have regained consciousness.

Subjective
Le Monde — Poland in shock after the Kraków mass shooting

Poland woke up on Sunday, November 8: on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Kraków a man opened fire with an automatic weapon from his car, killing six people and wounding 15 others around the market square in the historic centre, and was arrested a few streets away after a shootout of about 20 minutes. Police identified him as Michał O., a 24-year-old Polish national with no criminal record, from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; that evening police found the bodies of his parents and sister in the family apartment. Initial findings did not clarify his motives but revealed a young man with radical ideas, in Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s account; on Sunday morning prosecutors announced an investigation into an act of terrorism; two days of national mourning, Sunday and Monday, run with flags at half-staff.

Subjective
European Interest — the prosecutor’s office launches its investigation into the Kraków attack

Spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption announced the start of an investigation into the Kraków attack, classified under terrorist offences and covering two acts: the murder of six people with a firearm in the square, with attempted murder of others including police officers, and the murder of the three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. The bodies at home are given as a father aged 53, a mother aged 52 and a sister aged 20. Both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment. The suspect has not yet been formally arrested because of his medical condition, though he remains under constant surveillance, and preliminary findings indicate he possessed a firearms permit.

Subjective
Press TV — the Guards’ Navy: three oil tankers engulfed in flames in the Strait of Hormuz

The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Navy says three oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran’s regulations on maritime traffic, in incidents starting in the early hours of Sunday along an unauthorized shipping route, with the tankers’ navigation and identification systems switched off. The statement attributes the burning to the “mischief” of the American army. Less than a day earlier the Guards’ Navy said two tankers attempting the strait via unauthorized routes had struck naval mines and caught fire, one east of the waterway and one within it. Southern routes near Omani waters are declared unauthorized and mined; safe passage is confined to designated northern corridors requiring prior authorization.

Subjective
Press TV — the Iranian Navy: another tanker set ablaze after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz

The Iranian Navy says a tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the eastern Strait of Hormuz before noon on Sunday, having switched off its identification systems and sailed through a prohibited area. It was, the statement says, the fourth oil tanker to hit mines in the waterway on Sunday. In a separate statement the Guards’ Navy reported three tankers struck by mines and on fire on Sunday. The Navy warned the strait would remain closed to vessels violating Iranian regulations until all threats had been removed.

Subjective
The Maritime Executive — a tanker burns after a strike in the Strait of Hormuz

On Saturday at least two tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, including one that caught fire about eight nautical miles off Khasab, on Oman’s Musandam Peninsula; its crew was evacuated, no injuries were reported, and at least two firefighting tugs were working the blaze. Open-source analysts have tentatively identified that vessel as the Navig8 Messi, a products tanker chartered to ADNOC L&S, hit once previously in August and since repaired. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency received a second report of a tanker hit by a projectile during an outbound transit, its crew safe and no environmental impact reported. On Saturday American forces also targeted and disabled the vessel Huda.

Subjective
Reuters — Iran suggests the blasts are not American attacks as both sides report ships hit

Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than American strikes, while both sides reported shipping hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island; the Tasnim agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm, with no official information on possible damage. The United States said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday evening. Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire. Reuters was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. The Saudi Energy Ministry said an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities.

Subjective
Reuters — production suspended at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field after the drone attack

Nov 8: production was halted on Sunday at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, one of the largest in the Kurdistan region, after a drone attack hit the field. Two sources in the region’s electricity ministry said production was suspended after a single drone strike hit the LPG storage tank, causing a fire that was still raging. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the attack did not result in casualties, based on an initial assessment. A joint statement by the region’s natural resources and electricity ministries described the attack as a “terrorist attack.” Some 2.8 gigawatts of power generation in the Kurdistan region was lost, the electricity ministry said. There was no claim of responsibility.

Subjective
Al Jazeera, as carried by the Jamaica Inquirer — the drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield

A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials, and the Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power. Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in Sulaimaniyah governorate. Electricity Ministry spokesperson Omid Ahmed said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of generation off the grid. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties, based on an initial assessment.

Subjective
The Insight International — the drone attack halts gas production at the Khor Mor field in Sulaimani

An attack on the Khor Mor gas field in Chamchamal district late on Sunday started a large fire and halted production at the Kurdistan Region’s biggest source of power plant fuel, local officials and security sources said. Reuters quoted two security sources as saying a drone was used; an engineer at the field said a gas storage facility was hit and all crew were ordered into shelters. Kurdistan24 reported the strike hit the “Old Field” section, which produces liquefied petroleum gas. A reporter at the scene could not say whether the projectile was a drone or a rocket, and a security source’s claim that it was launched from Tuz Khurmatu has not been independently confirmed. The electricity ministry said generation would drop by between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts, with priority given to hospitals and water stations. No group has claimed responsibility.

Subjective
Pollar — the Houthi attack damages the Aramco tower in Riyadh as the Houthis report 33 dead in Saudi strikes

Debris from an intercepted missile damaged an Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district on Sunday; the Saudi Energy Ministry called the damage minor and said no one was killed or injured. The Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the group had launched four operations using ballistic, cruise and drone missiles, presented as a response to coalition bombing that killed 33 civilians east of Sanaa on Saturday. The coalition spokesman Turki al Maliki said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles and three ballistic missiles over Riyadh and southern regions, and later reported destroying two ballistic missile launchers in Saada used in the attack on Riyadh. The Houthi-run health ministry says coalition strikes hit al-Shariyah, a village east of Sanaa, on Saturday; its spokesman reported 33 dead and 39 injured as near-final figures. Every casualty figure in the account comes from the Houthi side, with no independent count offered.

Subjective
Military.com, carrying the Associated Press — Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine

ZAPORIZHZHIA, Nov 8: a Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter earlier blasted by multiple guided bombs as residents waited for humanitarian aid. No one was injured in Sunday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Ukraine said the earlier attack killed at least 55 people. As of Sunday afternoon, 45 people were listed as missing, according to the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin; many bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing. Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 164 drones across Ukraine overnight into Sunday, 137 of them shot down. The same file carries France’s foreign minister saying Europeans will participate in the Abu Dhabi talks, and the American president predicting a “very big” deal with Russia.

Subjective
NewsCubby — Ukraine reports a drone attack on rescue crews; the aid-centre toll reaches at least 55

Updated November 8: a Russian drone damaged specialized rescue equipment at the Komyshuvakha aid-centre site on Sunday, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said; no injuries to its personnel were reported. Ukrainian authorities report at least 55 deaths from the November 2 bombing of a school used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter, with the military intelligence agency HUR still listing around 50 people as missing. The briefing reconstructs the first attack: at least nine FAB-3000 guided bombs in the regional administration’s account, a second strike on the shelter after the first, the two rescuers killed named as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksii Sushchevskyi, both 44, and 167 more people evacuated from threatened areas of southern Kherson on Sunday. The toll and the account of the attack come from Ukrainian officials and have not been independently verified, the briefing states.

Subjective
Israel Realtime — Eisenkot to receive the mandate; rival coalition plans take shape

Published November 8 at 3:59 p.m. Israel time: President Isaac Herzog invited Gadi Eisenkot to receive the mandate to form a government on Sunday at 5 p.m. Factions representing 67 Knesset members recommended Eisenkot, 46 recommended Benjamin Netanyahu, and a faction representing seven declined to recommend anyone. Avigdor Liberman announced he was willing to compromise on conscription legislation and form a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties, demanding a government backed by 61 members without the Arab parties and with every member of United Torah Judaism and Shas included. Eisenkot’s proposed alternative is a minority government of parties holding 48 seats, supported externally by the Arab parties, potentially with United Torah Judaism abstaining. Negotiating teams met minutes after Liberman’s announcement, and Eisenkot and Liberman are expected to meet despite their rivalry.

Subjective
Marc Schulman, Substack — November 8, 2026: Eisenkot gets the mandate, as Liberman’s push for a Haredi alliance complicates coalition talks

This afternoon President Herzog officially gave Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government; he has 28 days, plus 14 more if he requests them and Herzog grants the extension, and if he fails the mandate will go to Prime Minister Netanyahu. Eisenkot is quoted: an absolute majority of Knesset members support change and support him as prime minister, and he intends to send a formal appeal to all factions to become partners in forming the government. Liberman is described as willing to give up his promise on the draft and reach agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties because a deal cannot be made with the Arab parties, and as positioning himself in the contest over leadership and pace. On Tuesday the Knesset is scheduled to convene, with rumors some will try to disrupt the session; Likud has filed a lawsuit against the election results.

Subjective
The Business Standard, carrying Reuters — Europeans will join the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the French foreign minister says

PARIS, Nov 8: Europeans will participate in talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday. “The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions,” Barrot told RTL radio; he could not yet say who will represent France. American envoy Steve Witkoff said Washington would bring delegations from Ukraine and Russia together in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11 to discuss ending the war, post-war security agreements and de-escalation. The round had until Sunday been presented as trilateral.

Subjective
Euronews — Europeans to join the Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, says Foreign Minister Barrot

European countries, including France, will be involved in the talks between Russians and Ukrainians due to open on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi under American mediation, the French foreign minister announced on RTL and Public Sénat. Barrot said he would not personally be at the negotiating table and that he could not yet tell who would represent France, but that France would definitely be there. He said he did not know what the American president had in mind in predicting a larger deal. Until now the talks scheduled for November 10 and 11 had been presented as trilateral negotiations among Ukrainian, Russian and American officials.

Subjective
The Levant Files — the Sunday live file, closed: Iran talks remain open as the drone attack halts Iraqi gas production

The live file for Sunday, November 8, closed with its headline standing: Iran talks remain open as the drone attack halts Iraqi gas production. In its closing entries: a drone attack halted production at the Khor Mor gas field, cutting gas supplies to five power stations, and Iraq’s prime minister said an initial assessment found no casualties; Baghdad said it was discussing an American request to close all but two crossings with Iran.
