At 1800 on the fifth day after the election, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1800: The Count of the Hurt Settles at 22

Central Japan’s correction file, which at midday ran from 15 to 24 injured, settled in the afternoon reports. The afternoon official reports list 19 injured in Aichi Prefecture—one serious injury and 18 minor—and three minor injuries in Shizuoka, 22 in all, in the afternoon account filed below; the television count carried in the second file below gives the same division, 19 in Aichi including one serious case and three in Shizuoka, where an 80-year-old woman fell in Hamamatsu’s Hamana Ward. The morning’s lower figure, 15, was the count of an assessment in its first hours; the 24 carried by some accounts remains in the record as the highest figure printed, and the afternoon official division is the one the desk carries forward. The earthquake itself stands as filed: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka at about 40 kilometres’ depth, upper 5 on the Japanese scale in Chita, Aichi, no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The agency’s Sunday acts are also in the file: having regard to loosened ground, it lowered the thresholds for issuing landslide warnings for the municipalities of Aichi that shook hardest, and its standing guidance—caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that this quake’s pattern is unlikely to lead to the Nankai Trough megaquake—stands unrevised. A second, separate tremor, magnitude 4.3 in the Kumamoto area at 10:53 a.m., produced no reports of serious damage or injury. Particulars of the hurt are in the accounts: in Tokoname a woman in her fifties was taken to hospital with a fractured ankle; in Toyota a man in his forties and a woman in her eighties fell and struck their heads and were conscious in hospital. The sleeper train Sunrise Izumo made a temporary stop; none of its approximately 290 passengers was reported hurt.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Board, and a Monday That Must Reprice the Weekend

There was no American or European session on Sunday, so the desk prints the board the weekend leaves and the questions Monday must answer. Friday’s close stands as the Sunday situation report carries it: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.31 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.425, up 1.09 percent; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; and the VIX at 25.64, down 9.01 percent. The ten-year Treasury yielded 4.859 percent; gold’s last print was $4,079.50. Oil’s settlements stand where the midday edition printed them—Brent at $98.32 a barrel, West Texas Intermediate at $90.83—on a week that took about 13 percent off the barrel on the desk’s baseline and about 17 percent on the Sunday newsletter’s, the disagreement filed at midday and unrevised here. The one Sunday session in the file, India’s seventy-minute Diwali Muhurat sitting, closed up 400 points on the Sensex. What Monday holds is a list, not a forecast: the first full session since three tanker fires were claimed in the strait and a drone halted a gas field that feeds five power stations; a chief of staff taking office in Washington; coalition meetings in Jerusalem; and, on Tuesday, the Abu Dhabi talks and the counting deadlines in two American states. The steepest Friday move in the file is Tokyo’s: the Nikkei 225 fell 5.96 percent on Friday, the evening brief notes. Monday’s open is the first price the weekend’s claims will meet.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Al-Ayyat, the dead agree at seven in every later account and the injured stand at 112 in the ministry’s later count and 125 in another account of the ministry’s figures; the desk carries the seven and prints both injured figures. On Kraków, the wounded stand at 15 or 16 by the hour and the source; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief, at 53, 52 and 21 in the police statement, and the sister at 20 in the prosecutors’; the joining of the two crime scenes stands at a spokesman’s “highly likely”; and the minister’s reading stands as a hypothesis its author declines to withdraw and its critics demand he document. On Hormuz, three tanker fires are claimed by the force that polices the route, one projectile report on Qeshm is attributed by one agency to the United States and confirmed by no one, three projectiles from Sirik are reported by a state broadcaster with no hit established, and the one confirmed interruption of the evening is a gas field in Iraq stopped by a drone nobody has claimed. On Riyadh, the damage is debris in the ministry’s account and torn facade in the witnesses’, and the Houthis’ own tally of the coalition’s attacks stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. On the count, the margins are Friday’s and the outstanding-ballot estimates run from about three thousand to twenty-five thousand depending on who is counting what. On Shizuoka, the hurt settled at 22 in the afternoon official division, between a morning 15 and a printed 24. On Jerusalem, a mandate has been exercised in words—four conditions, published on its first evening—and no government exists. On Asunción, the detention is a fact, the charges are allegations carrying stated penalties, the repayments are a central bank’s figures, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at 1800 with everything of consequence in this file falling on the same two days: Monday’s handovers and meetings, and Tuesday’s talks and deadlines.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-eight items.

Subjective
Reuters — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting as security fears grow

KRAKOW, Nov 8: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in the southern city’s historic main square, an attack the government said was likely inspired by far-right ideology, following a string of October school stabbings officials linked to extremist content online. Sixteen people were wounded in addition to those killed, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital. One of the dead was a British citizen and another Austrian; five foreign nationals, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that the three bodies at the home had gunshot wounds, with firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition recovered from the property. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s Saturday reading drew a demand from PiS deputy head Przemysław Czarnek for explanations and the information behind it; on Sunday the minister told TVN24 he was not retracting his statements and that the motive investigation was ongoing. The square and surrounding streets reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s was suspended for twelve hours, the first time since 1939, PAP reported; police tightened security in Warsaw and other cities; and the two wounded officers have regained consciousness.

Subjective
Pollar — Evening Brief, 8 November: Kraków mourns, Miller prepares, trains collide, Peña detained

The evening brief, compiled from Der Tagesspiegel, TVP Info, Polsat News, ANSA and others: officials counted Kraków’s six dead as a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50; reports put the wounded at 15 or 16; prosecutors said the two wounded officers had been woken from drug-induced comas after surgery while the suspect remained critical under guard; police found his 52-year-old father, 51-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister shot dead in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; and Italian students who sheltered in a cafe left by bus for Italy. On Washington: Donald Trump named Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff from November 9, and Representative Marlin Stutzman called the promotion a mistake. On Egypt: a Giza-to-Fayoum train ran into the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan train at Al-Ayyat; the toll rose through the afternoon from 64 injured and no confirmed deaths to at least seven dead and 112 injured, with 52 to 72 ambulances reported and President al-Sisi ordering an investigation. On Paraguay: prosecutors say Ueno Bank held about 3.6 trillion guaraníes in public and social-security funds in September 2026, including $163.8 million of Itaipú funds; by November 8 the central bank said 1.2 million customers had received partial or full reimbursement, small depositors first up to 10 million guaraníes; Petropar filed a complaint; and President Alliana began naming a new cabinet.

Subjective
AAP — Poland in mourning after the Kraków mass shooting

Poland has begun two days of national mourning after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into the busy central square in Kraków and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him; the defence minister described the attack as an “act of terror.” By Saturday evening mourners had left candles, the square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as the investigation continued, and St Mary’s Trumpet Call was paused overnight in tribute. Authorities found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; flags were lowered to half-mast; prosecutors have opened an investigation into murder and attempted murder, including of police officers, as an act constituting a terrorist offence; and four women and two men were killed in the square shooting.

Subjective
Relish Wire News — seven killed, 112 injured as a train rams another in Egypt’s Al-Ayyat

Seven people were killed and 125 injured on Sunday when a Fayoum-bound train struck the rear of a Cairo–Aswan train in Al-Ayyat, Giza Governorate, causing carriages to leave the track; the collision involved Train No. 134, Giza to Fayoum, and Train No. 2010, Cairo to Aswan, between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations, according to the National Authority for Egyptian Railways. Egypt’s Health Ministry’s figure, reported by Al Jazeera, is seven dead and 112 injured; Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar had previously reported four dead and 88 injured; the most recent figure in the account raises the injured to 125, with hospitals receiving 132 cases in total including the seven deaths, 71 injured discharged and 43 still hospitalised—23 at Al-Ayyat, 13 at Al-Wasta and 7 at Atfih—after 72 ambulances took part; injuries range from bruises and abrasions to fractures, head and face lacerations and chest injuries.

Subjective
The Orbit Post — two trains collide south of Cairo, killing seven and injuring 114

A train from Giza to Fayoum hit the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan service in the Al-Ayyat district on Sunday, derailing several carriages. The account tracks the toll in steps: the earlier Health Ministry count, reported by Reuters and the Associated Press, was four killed and 88 injured; the ministry later raised the toll to seven killed and 114 injured, Sky News reported, with Al Jazeera reporting seven killed and more than 112 injured, also citing the Health Ministry, and reports citing Ahram Online putting the injured at 112 with 45 discharged after treatment. The crash happened between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations; the railway authority said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum hit the rear of another heading from Cairo to Aswan; authorities did not name the people who died or say how many passengers were aboard.

Subjective
Crosswire News — two trains collide south of Cairo, killing at least seven and injuring over 100

Two trains collided on Sunday in the Al-Ayyat district of Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, killing at least seven people and injuring more than 100, according to later official counts. The Transportation Ministry said a train heading to Fayoum crashed into the rear of a train bound for Aswan and that one train derailed. An early Health Ministry count listed four dead and 88 injured, and state media reported 120 wounded. The chief prosecutor’s office said a train conductor was among the dead and that an inspection found the Giza–Fayoum train hit the last carriage of the Cairo–Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi ordered medical care, a prompt investigation and accountability for anyone found negligent.

Subjective
Associated Press, via Bytes Europe — Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine

ZAPORIZHZHIA: a Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter earlier blasted by multiple Russian guided bombs as residents waited for humanitarian aid. Ukraine said Monday’s attack killed at least 55 people in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region; no one was injured in Sunday’s strike, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service; around 50 people were still listed as missing, the military intelligence agency HUR said, with many bodies unidentified and DNA analysis ongoing. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members involved in the “double tap” strike. The account also carries Saturday’s farewell ceremony in Zaporizhzhia for six police officers killed in the strikes, and residents still searching for the missing, among them a 72-year-old man whose wife went to collect humanitarian aid and did not come home.

Subjective
NewsCubby — Ukraine reports a drone attack on rescue crews; the aid-centre toll reaches at least 55

Updated November 8: a Russian drone damaged specialized rescue equipment at the Komyshuvakha aid-centre site on Sunday, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said; the service reported no injuries to its personnel. Ukrainian authorities now report at least 55 deaths from the November 2 bombing of a school used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter in the Zaporizhzhia region, with HUR still listing around 50 people as missing. The briefing reconstructs the first attack from the Ukrainian accounts: at least nine FAB-3000 guided bombs in the regional administration’s account, a second strike on the shelter after the first, early tolls of 18 and then 24 dead rising as the search continued, the two rescuers killed named as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksii Sushchevskyi, both 44, and 167 more people evacuated from threatened areas of southern Kherson on Sunday, including 22 children. The toll and the account of the attack come from Ukrainian officials and have not been independently verified, the briefing states.

Subjective
Military.com, carrying the Associated Press — Russia targets emergency crews; Barrot on Abu Dhabi

Published November 8 at 2:59 p.m. EST: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Sunday that France and other European representatives would participate in the American-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11. “France will be there and will ensure that Europe’s voice is heard,” Barrot told RTL radio; he did not specify who would represent France or whether European officials would participate directly in negotiations. The talks were previously presented as a trilateral meeting between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, with President Donald Trump predicting a “very big” deal with Russia extending beyond Ukraine to “all of Europe.” The same file carries the Associated Press account of Sunday’s drone strike on the rescue crews at Komyshuvakha.

Subjective
Euronews — Europeans to join the Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, says French minister Barrot

European countries, including France, will be involved in the talks between Russians and Ukrainians due to open on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi under American mediation, the French foreign minister announced on RTL and Public Sénat. “The Europeans will be well represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these talks,” Jean-Noël Barrot said, specifying that he would not personally be at the negotiating table and that he could not yet say who would represent France. Barrot said he did not know what the American president had in mind. Until now, the talks scheduled for November 10 and 11 had been presented as trilateral negotiations bringing together Ukrainian, Russian and American officials. Published November 8, updated at 17:32 UTC.

Subjective
StockBiz — Europe confirms participation in the Russia–US–Ukraine talks

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed that European countries, including France, will send representatives to the trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, expected to focus on ending the conflict, post-conflict security agreements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues, on the agenda American envoy Steve Witkoff announced. Ahead of the meeting, American negotiators were also expected to meet representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union and NATO in Brussels to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s future security framework and support for reconstruction. According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi will be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky.

Subjective
Press TV — IRGC Navy: three oil tankers engulfed in flames in the Strait of Hormuz after maritime violations

November 8, 11:04 GMT: the IRGC Navy says three oil tankers have exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran’s regulations on maritime traffic; the incidents occurred starting in the early hours of the day along an unauthorized shipping route, with thick smoke spreading across the strait; the tankers had switched off their navigation and identification systems and were burning due to the “mischief” of the US “smuggling and aggressor army”; and vessels defying Iranian regulations would face similar consequences. The statement came less than a day after two oil tankers attempting transit via unauthorized routes struck naval mines and caught fire, one east of the waterway and one within the strait itself, after deactivating their navigation and positioning systems to slip through an unauthorized southern corridor. Iranian forces maintain full control over transit, the statement says, requiring prior authorization and confining safe passage to designated northern corridors; southern routes near Omani waters have been declared unauthorized and mined.

Subjective
Israel.com — Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say three tankers caught fire in Hormuz

Iran’s Guards said three tankers they called noncompliant burned in the Strait of Hormuz, as a British maritime agency reported a tanker fire off Oman, in an account drawn from The Times of Israel. The Guards described the vessels as “noncompliant” and said they had exploded and burned while using what Tehran calls an illegal channel; the statement did not name the ships or say which countries they belonged to. UKMTO reported a tanker on fire in the strait off Khasab, Oman, its crew evacuated, dated to the previous day rather than Sunday. The account states plainly what the Guards’ wording does not do: it does not say who caused the explosions, does not claim the Guards struck the ships, and does not attribute the fires to anyone else. An Israeli outlet’s report, citing the British agency, said an oil tanker had been attacked and that reports indicated the Guards had fired a missile that hit the vessel; that claim is attributed to unnamed reports and has not been confirmed in the Guards’ statement or the UKMTO account. None of the reports names the tankers, their owners, their flags or their cargo, and no casualty figures have been given.

Subjective
All Israel News — following reported explosions on three ships in Hormuz, the IRGC threatens vessels operating outside the Iranian route

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced Sunday morning that explosions occurred on three oil tankers “traveling along unauthorized routes in the Strait of Hormuz,” in a statement on the Islamic Republic News Agency: “three offending oil tankers—traveling along unauthorized routes in the Strait of Hormuz—have suffered explosions and intense fires.” The Guards did not take direct responsibility for the explosions, despite previously firing on vessels attempting to transit outside the approved route and having deployed sea mines in the strait; the statement said Iranian regulations have been repeatedly communicated to all vessels and warned that any vessel attempting transit outside the Iranian-approved route could expect a similar fate. The explosions came after United States Central Command conducted additional strikes on Qeshm Island and announced it had disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman which “attempted to violate the naval blockade”: CENTCOM forces disabled the vessel on November 7 after its crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the blockade multiple times.

Subjective
The Levant Files — the Sunday live file: Qeshm impacts reported, Khor Mor halted, and the mandate’s first evening

The live file for Sunday, November 8, in updates through 23:57 Cyprus time: a drone attack on Sunday night halted production at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province—the drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank and set it alight, two sources in the regional electricity ministry told Reuters; Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi reported no casualties in the initial assessment; the Kurdistan electricity ministry said gas supplies to five power stations were cut and generation would fall by an estimated 2,500–2,800 megawatts; no claim of responsibility. At 22:44 Cyprus time Al Jazeera Arabic cited Tasnim as reporting projectiles it attributed to the United States had come down on Qeshm Island, following IRNA’s report of explosions and possible targeting; American involvement, damage and separateness from Saturday’s blasts remain unverified. Iranian state television reported three projectiles launched from Sirik toward vessels said to be violating navigation restrictions, with no hit established. President Trump said Task Force Iron Gate was operating at full capacity and told CNN fresh strikes were “highly unlikely” if negotiations advanced, with 38 bridges identified as potential targets if action resumed; Foreign Minister Araghchi said Tehran’s two-day proposal remained on the table with conditions including an end to the war on all fronts. The American Treasury has asked Baghdad to close all but two crossings with Iran; Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said talks were continuing and warned of economic harm. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Saada used in Sunday’s Riyadh attack; Houthi spokesman Saree claimed hits on the financial district and the airport, which Saudi authorities did not confirm; the Energy Ministry attributed the Aramco Tower damage to falling debris with no casualties. Three officials told the Associated Press Syria was preparing to send fighters, an initial contingent of about 600, for a possible deployment on the Saudi side of the Yemen border; a Syrian source had said Saturday there were no plans to send troops into Yemen. In Gaza, five people were killed when a sandbank collapsed in heavy rain, and health officials at Nasser Hospital said an Israeli strike killed a man and a woman in al-Mawasi, which Israel’s military said targeted a Hamas member. After the mandate ceremony, Eisenkot set four conditions for joining his government and was expected to meet Bennett on Sunday evening and Liberman on Monday; the Joint List told N12 it was willing to help end Netanyahu’s tenure without demanding a place in government and had not yet been asked to commit its votes.

Subjective
Daily Inference — 33 killed in Sanaa strikes as missiles fly over Riyadh

Saudi officials said debris damaged an administrative building in the capital’s financial district without causing casualties. In Yemen, the Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi strikes near Sanaa killed at least 33 people and wounded 39 on November 7, in Bani Hushaysh district, most of them women and children on the ministry’s account; Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication said it was investigating the reported deaths; Reuters could not independently verify the casualty account, and the missiles’ origin and the source of the debris have not been independently established. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh on Sunday, and its spokesman also reported two cruise missiles intercepted in the Riyadh and southern regions. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the movement had carried out six operations against Saudi sites, including King Khalid International Airport, oil facilities and an Aramco distillation tower in Riyadh, and alleged the coalition had conducted 105 airstrikes and missile attacks against Yemen over 24 hours. The account notes the renewed fighting has broken the truce reached in 2022 and that the International Organization for Migration said in October more than 200,000 people had been displaced since the latest round began.

Subjective
Trend Arab — Saudi Arabia thwarts Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh and the Eastern Province

Saudi Arabia’s air defence systems intercepted three ballistic missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthis, targeting the capital, Riyadh, and the Eastern Province, coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki announced on Sunday. The escalation coincides with intensified fighting inside Yemen, where government forces have launched the ‘Dawn of Yemen’ operation to reclaim Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa. The Houthi-run Health Ministry reported that 33 people, including children and women, were killed in coalition air attacks on the village of al-Shariyah near Sanaa on Saturday, with at least 39 wounded in strikes that reportedly hit homes, roads and emergency teams; the coalition has not yet commented on these reported strikes and they could not be independently verified. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed the coalition conducted 105 air and missile strikes across Sanaa and seven other governorates in 24 hours, bringing the total to 4,369 since the conflict escalated, and asserted the Houthis executed six operations targeting Aramco facilities, Riyadh airport and military positions along the border.

Subjective
Israel Realtime — Eisenkot to receive the mandate; rival coalition plans take shape

Published November 8 at 3:59 p.m. Israel time: President Isaac Herzog invited Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence to formally receive the mandate to form a government on Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. Israel time, the announcement issued Saturday evening following Thursday’s consultations and weekend discussions with leaders including Prime Minister Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Factions representing 67 Knesset members recommended Eisenkot, 46 recommended Netanyahu, and a faction representing seven declined to recommend anyone; the recommendations are separate from competing proposals for a government’s composition. Once assigned, Eisenkot has 28 days, with presidential extensions totalling up to 14 more. Under the Basic Law, if he presents a government and the Knesset rejects its request for confidence, the decision on the next stage returns to the president; the mandate also determines which faction supplies the chair of the Knesset’s Arrangements Committee. Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman announced he was willing to compromise on conscription legislation and form a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties; Eisenkot’s proposed alternative, in this account, is a minority government of 48 seats supported externally by the Arab parties, potentially with United Torah Judaism abstaining.

Subjective
Israel Realtime — conscription: Segal’s assessment, Bennett’s party and Golan

Published November 8 at 5:16 p.m. Israel time: the commentator Amit Segal argued that Liberman’s rejection of reliance on the Arab parties had undermined Eisenkot’s minority-government plan before Eisenkot formally received the mandate, and that the promise to draft the ultra-Orthodox had vanished from the opening positions, the price of an arrangement involving Liberman, Eisenkot, Bennett and the ultra-Orthodox parties already established—the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted—which he portrayed as a victory for Rabbi Landau; that assessment differs from Liberman’s stated position that he has not abandoned conscription. Segal also reported Liberman was giving up on appointing Yair Lapid as Knesset speaker, leaving Eisenkot or Bennett as the alternatives. Bruria Naim Arman, chief executive of Bennett’s Together party, told activists that silence does not imply consent and restated the goal of a Zionist government of reform that would implement a revolution in military service; Segal questioned whether a government formed with Arab-party votes would meet the former condition and said Bennett had not agreed to Liberman’s proposed arrangement and was not expected to. Democrats chairman Yair Golan wrote that his party wants a partnership with the ultra-Orthodox community, but a genuine partnership requires mutual responsibility, and that ultra-Orthodox Jews must be drafted into the military.

Subjective
All Israel News — paving the way to a surprise coalition? Liberman announces support for a government with an ultra-Orthodox party and the Eisenkot bloc

Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman publicly announced his support on Friday for forming a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism, soon receiving backing from The Democrats and UTJ, though it remains unclear whether the other Change Bloc members who campaigned on a strict new draft law will agree. For the bloc to reach 61 seats it would need to add both UTJ’s seven and Shas’s six to its own 48; UTJ has publicly broken with the prime minister, while Shas supported Netanyahu. Liberman appeared to backtrack on his longstanding demand for harsh penalties for draft dodgers, arguing a government is needed quickly to “prevent the destruction” of the Jewish state; he criticised Eisenkot for past decisions, ruled out a rotation agreement for the premiership, and declared himself prepared for “painful compromises” on three conditions—ending the “Netanyahu era,” preventing new elections, and ruling out a minority government relying on the abstention of the Joint List and Ra’am—adding: “On all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise… this includes the issue of the conscription law. This pains me, and I know it pains many others as well.” Eisenkot had reportedly been more interested in a minority government relying on outside Arab-party support; his party said Thursday it planned to form “a national emergency government… immediately.” Updated November 8.

Subjective
NationWire — Paraguay’s ex-president Peña jailed in the bank probe

Published November 8 at 15:39 ET: Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at the Presidential Escort Regiment after prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain; Peña, 47, was questioned for about three hours on Saturday and declined to testify at the hearing, his lawyer Ricardo Preda maintaining the plea of not guilty: “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” Each charge could carry up to ten years, prosecutor Nancy Salomón said. At least 27 people face charges, including Ueno’s lead shareholder Miguel Vazquez; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, and headed the lender until 2023 before becoming its regulator. Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including roughly $355 million in state pension funds; the central bank began liquidation on November 2 after the solvency ratio fell below half the required minimum and intervened on November 3. The Chamber of Deputies voted 78–0 to impeach and the Senate removed Peña 44–0 with one absent; removal stripped him of the lifetime Senate seat and immunity of a former president; he is only the second Paraguayan president removed by impeachment, after Fernando Lugo in 2012. The central bank said Saturday that $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme. Prosecutors are weighing requests to freeze assets.

Subjective
Hong Kong Business Wire, carrying AFP — impeached Paraguay leader charged over the bank implosion

Paraguayan prosecutors charged ex-president Santiago Peña and took him into custody on Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests. Peña, Paraguay’s youngest-ever president, was removed by the Senate on Friday, three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links, and was brought before prosecutors and charged with “breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain” after about three hours of questioning over his links to Ueno Bank, a digital-first company with which nearly half of Paraguay’s population of 6.5 million have accounts. An indictment states that “between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities” and “was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank’s economic group in an irregular manner.” Peña spent Friday night in custody after being arrested within an hour of his impeachment trial; protesters gathered outside his home to demand he be locked up in a regular prison. He was replaced by former vice president Pedro Alliana, who promised not to abandon the almost three million depositors, including pensioners, affected by Ueno’s demise; thousands had taken to the streets demanding their money back after the central bank took control of Ueno, citing fears for its solvency.

Subjective
USA Today — Trump names Stephen Miller the new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said top aide Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, a dramatic staff shake-up days after Republicans suffered historic losses in the midterm election, and the most significant White House personnel move of his second term. The 41-year-old Miller, a deputy chief of staff, will begin as chief of staff on November 9, while Wiles moves to the president’s political operation. The overhaul comes after Wiles became a target of Steve Bannon and other MAGA allies after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate; Wiles, 69, previously worked on Trump’s three campaigns before being tapped as chief of staff. The account carries the opposition’s reading in its section heading: “Schumer: ‘Trump has learned nothing from his historic defeat.’”

Subjective
Daily Caller — Trump taps top immigration adviser as new chief of staff

President Donald Trump has tapped top immigration adviser Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, his announcement coming three days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms. In a post on Truth Social on Friday, the president announced that Miller will fill the position starting Monday and thanked the current chief of staff: “I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff—She has done a great job.” Following the announcement, Wiles confirmed in a statement on X that Friday would be her final day, and the Caller confirms that Wiles gave the president her resignation on Thursday night. Miller has served as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser since January 2025, and posted on X on Friday: “It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.”

Subjective
Huffman Writes — SITREP: November 8, 2026

The Sunday situation report: in Mississippi the count did not move at all—the tally stood at 2,574 votes on 953,314 counted, stamped 5:02 p.m. on Friday, with mailed and affidavit ballots due or curable by 5 p.m. on Tuesday; the results page updated at 3:16 a.m. ET on November 8 shows the same totals, so no votes have been posted since Friday evening; the state Republican chairman, Mike Hurst, told CNN that between 23,000 and 25,000 affidavit or mail-in ballots were outstanding. The congressional ledgers did not move over the weekend: the Associated Press ledger read 252 Democrats to 161 Republicans in the House with 22 races uncalled, and 54 to 44 in the Senate with two uncalled. Polymarket priced Colom at 99.0 percent and Peltola at 98.6—the venue’s prices, not the report’s view. The Federal Register published nothing on November 7 or 8; the Supreme Court and the D.C. Circuit filed no opinions in the window. The board is Friday’s close: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.31 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.425, up 1.09 percent; the Dow at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; the VIX at 25.64, down 9.01 percent; the ten-year Treasury at 4.859 percent; gold’s last print $4,079.50. On Israel, the report notes the mandate went to the man with fewer seats—Netanyahu’s camp 53, the opposition bloc 48, Likud the largest single party at 27—and that the Arab parties won a record 19 between them.

Subjective
Senate Watch, on YouTube — Senate update, November 8: what changed in Mississippi, Alaska and the leadership fights

The Sunday roundup, one chapter per story, its figures as of the dates shown on screen and campaign claims labelled as claims: Mississippi—Democrat Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,574 votes, 49.1 percent to 48.8, with about 97 percent counted on the Associated Press count posted Friday evening, his lead grown from 1,138 on Thursday morning; about 3,139 mail ballots were outstanding as of Friday and count if they arrive by Tuesday, November 10; affidavit ballots are still being reviewed and estimates of how many remain vary; counties must certify by November 13 and Mississippi has no recount process. Alaska—Democrat Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes with about 74 percent counted, on a count posted Wednesday; the next count is expected November 9 or 10 and a ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no one tops 50 percent. The Associated Press has Democrats at 54 seats and Republicans at 44, so Democrats take control on January 3; the two open races decide whether the majority is 54, 55 or 56.

Subjective
The Gold Standard — the Japan quake injures people in Aichi and Shizuoka

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake shook central Japan early on Sunday, injuring people in Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures. Afternoon official reports list one serious injury and 18 minor injuries in Aichi, and three minor injuries in Shizuoka—22 in all. Japan’s weather agency said no tsunami was expected and warned of more strong shaking over the week after the quake. Published Sunday, November 8, 2026, at 8:48 p.m. Adelaide time.

Subjective
TV Asahi News, on YouTube — a large tremor before dawn: maximum intensity upper 5 in the Tokai region, 22 injured

An earthquake with a maximum intensity of upper 5 struck the Tokai region in the early hours of November 8, injuring 22 people in various locations, including those who fell. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency the earthquake occurred at about 1:04 a.m. with its epicentre in western Shizuoka Prefecture, registering upper 5 in Chita City, Aichi Prefecture. In Aichi Prefecture 19 injuries have been confirmed, including one serious case; in Shizuoka Prefecture three people were injured, including an 80-year-old woman who fell, in Hamana Ward, Hamamatsu City, where an intensity of lower 5 was observed. The Sunrise Izumo sleeper train made a temporary stop, but none of its approximately 290 passengers was reported unwell or injured.

item.title: Prosecutors Open the Kraków Case as a Terrorist Offence, a Third Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, and the Mandate Is Handed Over in Jerusalem
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The midday file for Sunday, November 8, 2026: Polish prosecutors opened a formal investigation into Saturday's Kraków shooting and classified it as a terrorist offence, preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine, while the wounded count stood at 15 in some accounts and 16 in others; Iran's Revolutionary Guards raised their Hormuz tally from two burning tankers to three, still without names, and answered the new American Task Force Iron Gate as wordplay; President Herzog handed Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form Israel's government at the 5 p.m. Jerusalem ceremony; France said Europeans will join Tuesday's Abu Dhabi talks; the Senate count did not move, Mississippi at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637; and the markets' Sunday reading rested on Friday's settlements, Brent at $98.32 and West Texas Intermediate at $90.83, with India's Diwali Muhurat session up 400 points. Collected at 1200.
item.content:encoded:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Prosecutors Open the Kraków Case as a Terrorist Offence, a Third Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, and the Mandate Is Handed Over in Jerusalem

The news at midday on a mourning Sunday: the Kraków case acquired its legal shape in the morning—an investigation opened, a terrorist-offence classification, six murder charges in preparation and possibly nine—while its human counts still disagreed by one in three places. In the Gulf, the Guards’ tanker tally grew from two to three without a single ship being named, and Tehran answered Washington’s new land-routes task force in one word. In Jerusalem the mandate changed hands at 5 p.m. as scheduled. In Paris the Abu Dhabi table acquired European chairs. The count did not move. The markets, closed in America and Europe, read the weekend off Friday’s settlements and one festive hour in Mumbai.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 19, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Special Report No. 4, filed at 0910 today. Where the midday figures differ from the morning’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Sunday at noon is a file of openings and standings, and the desk files it in that order. In Kraków, on the first day of Poland’s national mourning, prosecutors opened the formal investigation the overnight edition left unopened: the Saturday attack is classified as a terrorist offence, the investigation covers two acts—the murder of six people in the Main Market Square and the murder of three people at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski—and prosecutors are preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine if the same hand is established for the three at home, in the prosecutors’ Sunday statement filed below. The suspect has not been formally arrested, because his condition in hospital does not allow it; he is under constant surveillance, and no motive has been established. In Jerusalem, the mandate the night announced was handed over: President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot the task of forming Israel’s next government at the ceremony set for 5 p.m. local time, 1000 ET, on the strength of 67 recommendations against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; Mr. Eisenkot has 28 days, and no coalition exists. In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards raised their own tally in the morning from two tankers burning to three, still naming none of them, and their spokesman dismissed the American Task Force Iron Gate, announced Saturday, as wordplay. In Paris, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans will be represented at Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi, which had been presented until Sunday as a trilateral table. The Senate count did not move: Mississippi stands at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637 in the Sunday-morning tallies, and both counts speak next on Tuesday. The markets are closed in the United States and Europe; the Sunday reading is Friday’s settlements—Brent at $98.32, West Texas Intermediate at $90.83—and India’s one-hour Diwali session, which closed up. That is the whole of the midday record: a case opened, a mandate handed over, a tally raised without names, a table enlarged, a count standing, and a week waiting on Tuesday.

Kraków at 1200: Prosecutors Open the Case

The morning’s completed act in Poland is a legal one. A prosecutor of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption has commenced an investigation into Saturday’s attack, classified under terrorist offences, spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk announced, in the statement carried by the Polish news agency and filed below. The investigation covers two distinct acts: the murder of six people with a firearm in the square, with the attempted murder of others including police officers on duty, and the murder of the three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek noted that the division handles cases related to terrorist crimes and that both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment. Mr. Waszczuk told ABC News that prosecutors are preparing six murder charges, potentially rising to nine if investigators establish that the gunman was also responsible for the deaths of his parents and sister, in the second account filed below. The three at home were found with bullet wounds, the police spokesman said, so it is likely they died of gunshot wounds; likely is the word in the record, and no finding has been made. The suspect himself has not yet been formally arrested, because his medical condition required hospital transport; he remains under constant surveillance and cannot yet be questioned, and prosecutors say that may not be possible for hours or days. One fact of care arrived with the legal file: both injured police officers have regained consciousness, the spokesman confirmed.

The corrections the midday watch exists to print are in this case, and the desk prints them as disagreements, not as choices. The wounded count does not agree across the Sunday files: the prosecutors’ statement carries 16 injured, including the two officers; the morning accounts from the square carry 15. The overnight edition carried both figures in its own files and printed the disagreement; at noon it stands unresolved. The suspect’s age does not agree either: the prosecutors and the police give 24, as this paper has filed him, while several Sunday accounts give 25, and one gives a birth year, 2002, that supports neither cleanly. The age of the sister found dead at home does not agree: the accounts the overnight edition relied on gave 21, following the police confirmation; the prosecutors’ account filed this morning gives 20, for a father of 53 and a mother of 52 on whom all accounts agree. The desk does not round a disputed fact into print; it publishes the triangle. What is settled at noon is the shape of the case: nine dead in one investigation, six in a public square and three in a private house, a terrorist-offence classification, an interior minister’s reading of radical, ultra-nationalist views that remains a reading, and a country in the first of two days of national mourning, with a Mass for the victims set for 4 p.m. local time at St. Mary’s Basilica and Kraków’s own mourning running through November 11. No motive has been established by any investigator, and no charge has yet been laid against a man who cannot be questioned.

Jerusalem at 1200: The Mandate Is Handed Over

The ceremony the night announced took place on its schedule. President Herzog was to hand the mandate to Mr. Eisenkot at 5 p.m. Sunday at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem—1000 ET, two hours before this edition collected—and the live file filed below heads its 5:07 p.m. Cyprus-time entry, 1007 ET, with the handover itself: Herzog hands Eisenkot the mandate to form Israel’s next government. The arithmetic under the ceremony stands as the overnight edition filed it. Factions representing 67 of the Knesset’s 120 members recommended Mr. Eisenkot, against 46 for Mr. Netanyahu, with United Torah Judaism’s seven recommending neither; the 67 are not a coalition—they are 48 members of Mr. Eisenkot’s four-party change bloc and 19 from the Arab-led parties, whose support as formal partners Mr. Eisenkot has ruled out, in the account filed below. The October 27 election gave Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats and the change bloc 48, neither at the 61 required. Mr. Eisenkot’s own statement, posted Saturday evening, is on the record: “Now is the time for the formation of a national emergency government,” and, “I will do everything to make us worthy.” Mr. Netanyahu’s answer, in a video statement the same evening, urged the change-bloc parties to form a national unity government that must include his previous coalition allies—a prospect the accounts describe as unlikely. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the formation proceeds. The clock is now the fact: 28 days from today, with a presidential extension of up to 14 days possible, and no agreement of any kind announced by noon.

Hormuz at 1200: Two Tankers Become Three, and Iron Gate Is Answered

The Guards’ tally grew in the morning, and nothing else about it changed. The Revolutionary Guards Navy announced on Sunday that three oil tankers had exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after travelling on a route it declares off-limits, raising the tally it gave in the night—two tankers, struck on mines, one east of the strait and one within it—by one, in the live file and in the Guards’ own outlet’s account, both filed below. The third fire’s cause is not separately stated; no tanker is named, no flag is given, and no crew is accounted for, by the Guards or by anyone else. The neighbouring facts stand unjoined, as the desk filed them at 0400: the United Arab Emirates National Guard rescued all 22 crew, all Arab nationals and all stable, from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman that it did not name; the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a tanker on fire Saturday about eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, its crew evacuated; and United States Central Command identified the ship its aircraft disabled in the same waters on Saturday as the St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda, struck in the stern with precision munitions after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to run the naval blockade, in the morning account filed below. No authority has linked any of these three reports to any other, and the desk does not link them. Three fires claimed, one rescue confirmed, one disabling explained, zero tanker names published: that is the strait at noon.

The war of statements supplied the rest of the Gulf file. Central Command announced on Saturday a new unit, Task Force Iron Gate—about 20 civilian and military personnel in Tampa, Florida, directed by Admiral Brad Cooper to monitor, detect, and disrupt the movement of advanced weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, in the task force account filed below. On Sunday the Guards’ spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, answered it to the Fars agency: “The Iron Gate plan is just wordplay. The Americans cannot achieve their goal of imposing severe economic pressure and causing Iran’s economy to collapse this way.” He added that Washington can never achieve the economic blockade it seeks, whatever form it takes, and warned of a harsher response if the United States attacks Iranian vessels. In the second Gulf theatre, the Saudi-led coalition’s Sunday-morning tally stood at five interceptions—two ballistic missiles toward Riyadh, one toward the Eastern Province, and two cruise missiles in the Riyadh and southern regions—with the Energy Ministry reporting limited debris damage to an Aramco office building in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District and no casualties, in the live file filed below. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry condemned the Houthi attacks in the strongest terms on Sunday, citing the two ballistic missiles toward Riyadh, and called for an immediate halt, in the QNA statement filed below; Bahrain and Syria condemned the attacks as well in the accounts taken in. The other side of that ledger also moved: the authorities in Sanaa raised their toll for Saturday’s strikes on homes in Bani Hushaysh district, near the capital, from 27 killed and 36 wounded to at least 33 killed and 39 wounded. Each figure is printed with its owner; none has been verified by a party that did not issue it.

Abu Dhabi at 1200: Europe Joins the Table

The talks acquired participants on Sunday, two days before they open. Europeans will participate in the talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday, in Reuters’ Paris file filed below: “The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions. I can’t tell you yet who will be representing France on this occasion, but France will certainly be there.” Mr. Barrot added that no one will speak in Europe’s name without Europe in the room. Until Sunday the meeting had been presented, by the American envoy who announced it and by every capital, as trilateral—Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, the first direct round in months, on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, and humanitarian questions. Ukraine’s position going in stands as its president stated it Saturday: Russia is intensifying its attacks—36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones in his count of Friday night’s barrage—to lay the groundwork for pressure on Ukraine’s position and its partners’ at the talks, and Russia perceives diplomacy as a form of aggression, in the Arab News account filed below. Mr. Zelenskyy has also said he hopes the round opens the way to a meeting of leaders. No Russian statement taken in by noon answers either the pressure charge or the European chairs. What changed at midday is the table’s shape, not its agenda: no agenda, draft, or text has been published by any side.

Asunción at 1200: The Detention’s Second Day

Paraguay’s file did not move on Sunday, and the desk files it standing, with its papers in order. The detention order of Saturday stands through its second day: Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility—the Presidential Escort Regiment in the local accounts—and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in a detention centre, on charges of breach of trust and administration for personal gain in the investigation of the digital lender Ueno, whose collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts, in the Reuters account filed below. The judge said detention was necessary to ensure Mr. Peña remained in the country while the case proceeded. Mr. Peña’s attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists he is pleading not guilty. Prosecutors are reported to be seeking a freeze of the former president’s assets, a request no ruling taken in by noon has answered. The sequence stands as filed: the central bank resolved Ueno on Tuesday, November 3; the Senate removed Mr. Peña on Friday; Vice President Pedro Alliana holds the presidency for the term through August 2028; the charges were laid and the detention ordered on Saturday. The charges are charges. Mr. Peña is presumed innocent of them, and no court has ruled on any part of the case.

The Count at 1200: The Margins Stand, the Snapshots Are Dated

Neither Senate race moved on Sunday morning, and the correction this watch owes is about dates, not digits. The Sunday-morning tracker, updated at 8:16 a.m. Central, carries Mississippi exactly where the week left it: Scott Colom, the Democrat, at 467,930 votes to Cindy Hyde-Smith’s, the Republican incumbent’s, 465,356—a margin of 2,574 votes, 49.1 percent to 48.8, with about 97 percent of the expected vote counted and roughly 30,498 ballots estimated left, in the two-races account filed below. Alaska stands where it has stood since Wednesday: Mary Peltola, the Democrat, at 102,962 first-choice votes to Dan Sullivan’s, the Republican incumbent’s, 102,325—a margin of 637, with about 74 percent counted and the second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. holding 3,600 votes, more than five times the margin. Against those standings, the desk notes a figure in circulation this morning: an explainer on the delays, republished Sunday, carries Mississippi’s margin as 1,138 votes—which was Wednesday night’s margin, in the explainer filed below. Both figures are true of their hours; only one is true of this one. A count is a dated instrument, and the desk dates it. The calendar around the standings is unchanged and triple-headed: on Tuesday, November 10, Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and its boards of commissioners complete the provisional count, and Alaska publishes its next update; Mississippi counties certify by November 13; Alaska’s absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set, no candidate having cleared 50 percent. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with the two Senate races, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead by 3,172 votes in Friday’s figures, no newer figure taken in by noon. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. At noon on the fifth day, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1200: The Count of the Hurt Settles Into a Range

Central Japan’s morning produced the day’s other correction file: not a new event, but a settling count. The earthquake itself stands as the overnight edition filed it: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka Prefecture at a depth of about 40 kilometres, upper 5 on the Japanese intensity scale in Chita, Aichi—the strongest shaking in western Shizuoka in 107 years and in Aichi since 1997—with no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The injured count rose through the morning and the accounts do not land on one figure. The Seoul account, drawing on the meteorological agency and NHK, counts 15 injured—12 in Aichi, hurt in falls and by blows to the head, and three in Shizuoka, in the morning file filed below. The wire account carried in India counts at least 22 injured, with shattered storefront windows and disrupted trains, in the second file below; local papers and broadcasters in the region have carried 24. The desk publishes the range, 15 to 24, and notes that the counts were taken at different hours of an assessment still under way. The agency’s standing guidance is the settled part: caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that the quake’s pattern differs from, and is unlikely to lead to, the Nankai Trough megaquake.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Settlements, One Festive Hour, and a Monday

There is no American or European session to report on a Sunday, so the desk reports the readings the weekend published. On the settlements, the Sunday accounts agree to the cent: Brent crude closed Friday at $98.32 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $90.83, in the Saudi Sunday-morning snapshot and in the Sunday markets newsletter, both filed below, the snapshot noting that Saudi markets open their week on Sunday with those Friday figures as the last confirmed settlements. On the week’s size, the accounts do not agree, and the disagreement is a matter of baselines: the newsletter measures Brent down about 17 percent from $117.64 at the end of the week before; this paper’s Saturday file measured the same barrel down 13.3 percent on the week from its own baseline, and a Sunday market table prints 12.7 percent for Brent and 11.9 for West Texas Intermediate. The settlements are the point; the percentages are the triangle, and the desk prints both. Underneath every measure sits the same fact the newsletter states plainly: expectations of de-escalation in the Iran conflict took the geopolitical premium out of the barrel during the week, and the tanker fires around the Gulf mean the supply risk has not disappeared—a sentence written before the Guards raised their tally to three this morning, and the first thing Monday’s open will reprice.

The one session the world did hold on Sunday was seventy minutes long and festive. India’s exchanges opened for the Diwali Muhurat session—pre-open at 2:05 p.m. in Mumbai, continuous trading from 2:20 to 3:30 p.m., 0350 to 0500 ET—marking Laxmi Pujan and the start of Samvat 2083, the Hindu financial new year. The session closed up: the Sensex rose 400 points to 81,406 and the Nifty crossed 25,100, with Tata Steel and Sun Pharma among the leading gainers, in the session’s account filed below. Regular Indian trading resumes Monday and closes again Tuesday for Diwali-Balipratipada. It is a ceremonial hour and the desk files it as one; its direction, on the day Poland mourned and the strait burned in claims, was up. The rest of the markets’ week is a calendar: Monday’s full reopening, Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi and counting deadlines in two American states, and an oil price that ended Friday below a hundred dollars with a war premium half in and half out.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Kraków, the triangle has three sides: the wounded at 15 in the square accounts and 16 in the prosecutors’; the suspect at 24 in the prosecutors’ and police accounts and 25 in others; his sister at 20 in the morning’s prosecutors’ account and 21 in the accounts the overnight edition filed. The desk publishes all three triangles and chooses in none of them; the settled facts are the investigation, the classification, and the nine dead. On Hormuz, the Guards say three tankers; no name, flag, crew, or independent confirmation attaches to any of the three, and the confirmed rescue and the explained disabling beside them are separate reports that no authority has joined. On Shizuoka, the injured stand between 15 and 24 by the hour of the count, and the magnitude stands at 5.7 by the agency that owns the scale and 5.5 by the American survey. On the count, the margins are unchanged and the figures in circulation are dated Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday; read with their dates, they do not conflict. On oil, the settlements agree and the weekly percentages do not, because their baselines do not. On Jerusalem, the mandate has changed hands and no government has been formed; both halves of that sentence are the news. On Asunción, the detention is a fact and the charges are allegations, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at noon with the case opened, the mandate running, the table enlarged, the count standing, and everything of consequence in this file—the Abu Dhabi talks, the counting deadlines, the markets’ reopening—falling on the same Tuesday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

Subjective
European Interest — the prosecutor’s office launches its investigation into the Kraków attack

Spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption announced the start of an investigation into the Kraków attack, and Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek emphasised that the division handles cases related to terrorist crimes. The Saturday attack was carried out by a 24-year-old man who drove into the Main Market Square and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 16, including two police officers; the prosecutor’s investigation, classified under terrorist offences, covers the murder of the six and the attempted murder of others including officers on duty, and a second act, the murder of three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Both injured officers have regained consciousness; the three at home—a father of 53, a mother of 52, and a sister of 20—had bullet wounds, Sub-Inspector Andrzej Fijołek said, so it is likely they died of gunshot wounds; both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment; and the suspect has not yet been formally arrested because of his medical condition, though he remains under constant surveillance.

Subjective
Augerton, carrying ABC News — Polish prosecutors open a formal terrorism investigation

Updated at 6:56 a.m. ET on November 8: Polish prosecutors opened an investigation Sunday into Saturday’s Kraków shooting and intend to treat it as a terrorist act, Prosecutor Tomasz Waszczuk told ABC News; they are preparing six murder charges, potentially rising to nine if investigators establish the gunman was responsible for the deaths of his parents and sister, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk said were found dead at home. Six people were killed in the attack and more than a dozen wounded, including two police officers; authorities said the attack was likely inspired by far-right ideology; police shot and arrested the suspected gunman, identified in this account as a 25-year-old Polish citizen; and Poland declared two days of mourning.

Subjective
Energy Radio — the Kraków shooting, the running account through Sunday morning

The running account, last updated at 9:40 a.m. UK time on Sunday: six people killed and fifteen injured after a gunman opened fire from a car in and around the Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon; at 9:30 a.m. UK time prosecutors in Kraków said Saturday’s attack will be classified as a terrorist offence, with spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk telling Polish television a formal investigation will be opened on Sunday; the 24-year-old suspect is still in hospital under constant guard and cannot yet be questioned or charged, which prosecutors say may not be possible for hours or days, and he could face life imprisonment; early findings suggest he held a firearms licence, and the investigation will look at how he obtained it, his background, his personal connections, and the events leading up to the attack; Waszczuk has confirmed the detained man is 24-year-old Michał O., according to Polish media, with prosecutors investigating alongside the Internal Security Agency and examining ideological and personal motives; two of Kraków’s carriage drivers are among the most seriously injured; hospitals have appealed for blood donors; bomb disposal experts found no explosives in the suspect’s car; and a Mass for the victims is set for 4 p.m. local time Sunday at St. Mary’s Basilica.

Subjective
Le Monde — Poland in shock after the Kraków mass shooting

Poland woke up on Sunday, November 8, as if thrust into a new era: on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Kraków a man opened fire with an automatic weapon from his car, killing six people and wounding 15 others around the market square in the historic centre, and was arrested a few streets away after a shootout of about 20 minutes. Police identified him as Michał O., a 24-year-old Polish national with no criminal record, from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, 140 kilometres northeast of Kraków; that evening police found the bodies of his parents and sister in the family apartment. Initial findings did not clarify his motives but revealed a young man with radical ideas, in Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s account; the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime joined the investigation to examine media and social-media reports of possible links to radical groups; on Sunday morning prosecutors announced an investigation into an act of terrorism; two officers were wounded, one seriously; and two days of national mourning, Sunday and Monday, run with flags at half-staff, the first political answer expected at the November 11 national holiday.

Subjective
News Central — Poland mourns six killed in the Kraków shooting

Poland began a two-day national mourning period after the shooting in Kraków left six people dead and 15 injured; the Main Market Square remained cordoned off on Sunday as residents laid candles for the victims. Police confirmed a British national was among those killed, with citizens of Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal, and Russia among the injured, according to the PAP agency. Three bodies found at the suspect’s residence in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres northeast of Kraków, were identified as his parents and sister—a 53-year-old man and two women aged 52 and 21. The suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish national, was shot and wounded by police and remains in critical condition in hospital. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident as terrorism, although police had not established a motive. Police appealed for blood donations for the officer identified as Jakub Kulik, whom they commended for confronting the armed suspect without hesitation, and investigators quoted by Polish media said the suspect had no previous criminal record.

Subjective
The Levant Files — the Sunday live file: the mandate, the strait, and Riyadh

The live file for Sunday, November 8, updated at 5:34 p.m. Cyprus time: at 5:07 p.m. Cyprus time it heads an entry ‘Herzog Hands Eisenkot the Mandate to Form Israel’s Next Government’; at 2:39 p.m. Cyprus time it reported that the Revolutionary Guards Navy’s tally had risen to three tanker fires in the Strait of Hormuz, the third incident unverified, the ships’ identities unknown, and the United Arab Emirates’ rescue of 22 crew members from a burning cargo ship not yet linked to the tally, with a tanker fire reported off Khasab, Oman, likewise unlinked; the Guards’ spokesman Hossein Mohebbi dismissed Washington’s new Iron Gate task force and said Iran had taken steps to strengthen ties with its neighbours; on Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Qatar condemned the Houthi attacks citing two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh and called for an immediate halt, Doha reaffirming support for Saudi measures, while the Saudi-led coalition’s Sunday-morning tally stood at five interceptions, the Energy Ministry reported limited debris damage to an Aramco office building and no casualties, and the authorities in Sanaa reported at least 33 killed in Saturday’s strikes near the capital.

Subjective
The Jewish Weekly — Eisenkot asked to form a government by Herzog

President Isaac Herzog’s decision to ask Gadi Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government marks a significant setback for Benjamin Netanyahu, whose existing alliance with Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich cannot simply resume governing on its previous terms, though the result is not yet a settled transfer of power, Israel having produced a parliamentary deadlock. Herzog announced that Eisenkot would receive the mandate on Sunday, November 8, following consultations in which 67 members recommended the Yashar leader against 46 backing Netanyahu, with United Torah Judaism’s seven recommending neither. Once formally entrusted, Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a government, with a discretionary extension of up to 14; failure does not automatically return Israel to elections, since the president can give another member a further 28 days, and a 21-day parliamentary stage can follow. Eisenkot’s four-party change bloc holds 48 seats; the additional 19 recommendations came from the Arab-led parties.

Subjective
The American Quorum — Herzog chooses Eisenkot to try to form Israel’s next government

Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday that Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s principal rival, would receive the first opportunity to form a government after an election that left both blocs short of a majority; the formal handover was scheduled for Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. in Jerusalem, after which Eisenkot has 28 days to negotiate, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, and Netanyahu remains prime minister while the process proceeds. Herzog’s November 5 statement recorded recommendations for Eisenkot from factions representing 67 lawmakers against 46 for Netanyahu. A recommendation identifies the politician a faction wants to negotiate first; it is not a completed bargain over ministers, policy, or parliamentary support. The October 27 election gave Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and the parties aligned against him, excluding the Arab lists, 48. Israel’s Basic Law establishes the 28-day period and permits extensions totalling no more than 14 days; receiving the mandate is an opportunity to negotiate, not an appointment as prime minister.

Subjective
IANS — Netanyahu faces a major setback as Herzog tasks Eisenkot with forming the government

Jerusalem, November 8: President Isaac Herzog has tasked opposition leader and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, dealing a significant setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to retain power after the October 27 election. Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, secured the backing of 67 lawmakers in consultations, compared with 46 who recommended Netanyahu; the formal handover was scheduled for Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. local time at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem, and Eisenkot will have 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Sixty-one seats are required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. In this account’s breakdown, Eisenkot received support from 48 lawmakers of the Change Bloc, seven from the Arab party Ra’am, and 12 from the Joint List.

Subjective
India International Times — the Emirates rescue all 22 aboard a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman

The United Arab Emirates Coast Guard rescued all 22 crew members from a cargo ship that caught fire in the Gulf of Oman, the UAE National Guard said Sunday; rescuers answered the crew’s distress call, evacuated everyone aboard, administered first aid, and handed the crew to the authorities, all 22 in stable condition, the vessel unidentified and the fire’s cause unstated. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said Sunday it had received a report that a tanker caught fire on Saturday about eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, and that its crew had been evacuated. In its statement on Saturday’s operation, United States Central Command identified its target as the St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said early Sunday that one oil tanker had struck mines east of the strait and a second had hit mines while crossing it, both with navigation and positioning systems switched off and both burning after the explosions; the navy named neither tanker, and its account could not be independently verified.

Subjective
Nation Press — 22 rescued as a cargo ship burns in the Sea of Oman

A cargo ship caught fire in the Sea of Oman on November 8 and the United Arab Emirates Coast Guard brought all 22 crew members to safety, the crew all of Arab nationality and in stable condition after first aid, according to the UAE National Guard, which did not disclose the fire’s cause or the damage. The navy of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said early Sunday that two oil tankers attempting an unauthorised route in the Strait of Hormuz caught fire after striking naval mines, one east of the strait and one crossing it, both with navigation and GPS systems off and both burning, and warned that any vessel cooperating with the American army and entering the unauthorised region would definitely hit naval mines, as reported by Xinhua. United States Central Command said its forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, a military aircraft firing precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The identities of the two tankers in the Guards’ account and their flags have not been officially confirmed.

Subjective
Press TV — the Guards warn they will hit harder if the United States attacks Iran’s vessels

November 8: the Revolutionary Guards warned the United States against attacking Iranian vessels in regional waters, vowing a harsher response to any such move. Spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi said on Sunday that the war between Iran and the enemy continues on military and economic fronts; reacting to the American military’s newly announced plan to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routes under its Iron Gate campaign, he said Washington can never achieve the type of economic blockade it is seeking, whatever form it takes. Central Command, which Iran has designated a terrorist organisation, announced on Saturday a new task force to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials; Admiral Brad Cooper said it would reinforce what he described as the success of the American naval blockade of Iran, the task force based in Tampa, Florida, coordinating with other agencies to block Iran’s land borders and Caspian Sea routes. On Sunday, three oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran’s maritime traffic regulations, in the same account.

Subjective
Crisis Zone — Task Force Iron Gate: Central Command targets Iran’s border routes

Published November 8 at 10:43 a.m.: United States Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, November 7—a team of about 20 civilian and military personnel at headquarters in Tampa, Florida, whose formation Admiral Brad Cooper directed. A Central Command graphic, quoted by Türkiye Today, says the task force will monitor, detect, and disrupt any illicit movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s borders and the Caspian Sea, the graphic highlighting the borders with Türkiye, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, and Pakistan. Central Command named no crossings, methods, or legal authorities, so its early reach may run through sanctions, banks, and neighbouring capitals. On Sunday, Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Fars agency that the Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, Reuters reported. Türkiye Today reported that Iran demands an end to the blockade before it reopens the Strait of Hormuz; no report links Iron Gate to the talks.

Subjective
