The same settlement produced warrantless wiretapping under the President’s Surveillance Program, disclosed in 2005; the torture program documented in the Senate Intelligence Committee’s 2014 summary; Guantánamo; and the 2001 military-force authorization’s two-decade career across four presidents. The largest documented domestic-surveillance expansion of the last fifty years was built before, and inherited by, the current administration; it is the standing baseline of standard operating procedure for state power at home.

Baseline three is the deportation record itself, from the department’s own yearbook, and the current regime’s distinguishing features are not its removal totals. On the department’s Yearbook Table 39—a removal being a compulsory movement under a removal order, a return a confirmed departure without one, an expulsion the Title 42 category of 2020 to 2023, and all broad totals counts of events, not of unique people—the Obama administration’s fiscal 2009–2016 totals are 3,062,466 removals and 2,186,427 returns, a combined 5,248,893; the label applied to that record was coined by an advocate, Janet Murguía of the National Council of La Raza, on March 4, 2014: “this president has been the deporter-in-chief.” The first Trump administration’s removals and returns sum to about 1,795,000, about 2,002,000 with fiscal 2020’s Title 42 expulsions. The Biden administration’s fiscal 2021–2024 totals are 2,032,300 removals and returns plus 2,754,120 expulsions, about 4,786,000 on the broadest count; the Migration Policy Institute’s characterization is “nearly 4.4 million repatriations” through February 2024. For the current term, the Institute estimated about 980,000 deportations from January 20, 2025 through July 31, 2026—a pace below the Obama-era removal peak on the order-based measure, with the detention population and the death counts at records. The distinguishing features of the current regime in the documented record are the abolition of the enforcement-priority tiers that had structured ICE since 2014, by Executive Order 14159 of January 20, 2025—with the nuance that ICE’s fiscal 2026 budget justification reintroduced priority language nearly identical to the rescinded 2021 memo, on the Heritage Foundation’s analysis—; the scale of third-country removals, 27,943 from January 20, 2025 to August 5, 2026 on ICE data obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, as filed in Special Report No. 2; interior enforcement at a visibility not seen in the earlier regimes; and the detention-death series filed above. Behind the window stand the deep-history anchors, also filed in No. 2: the Palmer Raids of 1919–1920, which deported 556 people after mass arrests; the Mexican Repatriation of the 1930s, which removed hundreds of thousands, up to 60 percent of them United States citizens on the standard scholarly estimate; and Operation Wetback, whose official figure above one million is contradicted by the scholarly consensus of about 300,000. Mass expulsion with weak process is a recurring American practice across a century, under presidents of both parties and none. That is the baseline fact any departure claim must clear.

Filed together, the three baselines run under administrations of both parties, and the file states the continuity without drawing from it. The covert-action baseline is a bureau program of 1956–1971, exposed in 1976. The surveillance baseline was built after 2001 and continued by presidents of both parties, its founding emergency declaration renewed annually by Obama, Biden, and Trump alike. The deportation baseline’s largest combined total in the window belongs to a Democratic administration, its second-largest broad count to another, and the Republican administrations in the series sit below both on the order-based measure—while the current administration’s detention population and custody deaths stand at records on the same government’s figures. A reader running the first section’s frameworks against this record has both parties’ administrations on the page, in the government’s own numbers. The desk files the continuity and draws no conclusion from it.

January 6: The Same Instrument, Applied to the Other Famous Count

The January 6 death ledger is complete only when it carries every side and separates the day from its aftermath. The District of Columbia medical examiner supplied the causes for the deaths of the day. Attendee, officer, and defendant in the table are positions in the event and its prosecution, not findings about any death.

NameSideDateOfficial causeMannerTiming
Ashli BabbittAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Gunshot wound, left shoulderHomicideOf the day
Kevin GreesonAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseaseNaturalOf the day
Benjamin PhillipsAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseaseNaturalOf the day
Rosanne BoylandAttendeeJan. 6, 2021Acute amphetamine intoxicationAccidentOf the day
Brian SicknickOfficerJan. 7, 2021Acute brainstem and cerebellar infarcts due to acute basilar artery thrombosisNaturalNext day
Howard LiebengoodOfficerJan. 9, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Jeffrey SmithOfficerJan. 15, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Kyle DeFreytagOfficerJuly 10, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Gunther HashidaOfficerJuly 29, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Christopher StantonDefendantJan. 9, 2021SuicideSuicideAfter
Matthew PernaDefendantFeb. 25, 2022SuicideSuicideAfter
Nejourde MeachamDefendantAug. 28, 2021Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter
Mark AungstDefendantJuly 2022Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter
David HomolDefendantApr. 17, 2024Suicide, reportedSuicide, reportedAfter

The only homicide on January 6 was Babbitt’s, and the official reviews cleared the officer who fired. Capitol Police Lt. Michael Byrd shot Babbitt as she climbed through the broken window of the Speaker’s Lobby door. The Justice Department declined charges after finding no evidence that Byrd did not reasonably believe deadly force necessary in self-defense or defense of Congress; the Capitol Police found the shooting lawful and within department policy. Boyland’s examiner ruling also has a printed dispute beside it: a pathologist retained by her family concluded compressional asphyxia, while District police internal affairs cleared an officer whose baton strikes near Boyland became part of the family’s use-of-force claim. No court has adjudicated Boyland’s cause.

Sicknick’s record contains two statements by the same examiner, and both are required. Chief Medical Examiner Francisco Diaz ruled the manner natural and told the Washington Post that the autopsy found no evidence of an allergic reaction to chemical irritants and no evidence of internal or external injuries. Diaz also said Sicknick had engaged the rioters and that “all that transpired played a role in his condition.” No one was charged with killing him; two men were charged with assaulting him with chemical spray. The District’s Police and Firefighters’ Retirement and Relief Board separately found Jeffrey Smith’s January 6 injuries the sole and direct cause of his later suicide—the one formal causal adjudication attached to an aftermath death in the ledger.

The phrasing in public argument and the examiner’s record are different objects. Attorney General Merrick Garland’s January 2025 formulation referred to “the five officers who lost their lives in the line of duty”—Sicknick and the four later suicides. The examiner recorded no officer homicide and no officer death on January 6 itself. Line-of-duty recognition by the Capitol Police, the Justice Department, and benefit boards is an institutional determination printed in the research record; it is not a medical-examiner finding that rioters killed five officers. Any total drawn from the table must say whether it is counting deaths of the day, the next day, or the aftermath.

No corresponding national ledger exists for civil unrest as a whole. No federal body publishes deaths and injuries from riots by side or in total; the FBI’s LEOKA series counts officers feloniously killed in all circumstances—73 in 2021 and 64 in 2024, for example—without a riot subset for killings. Protester-side totals exist only as constructions: Forbes and Associated Press reporting counted about 19 deaths in the opening weeks of the 2020 unrest; the Guardian and ACLED counted at least 25 across 2020; an academic dataset counted 31 associated homicides; and an open-compiled multi-year list reaches 42, each under a different inclusion standard. The absence of a common instrument is part of the fifty-year record.

The Frameworks Applied: Where the Authors Land

This section does the only application work an objective file may do: it records where the frameworks’ own authors and other named scholars land, and the documented facts each side cites. It renders no measurement of its own. Under Paxton’s framework, per Paxton, the label applies, on the ground he names: open encouragement of civic violence to overturn an election. The facts his side cites: January 6, 2021; the 2020 election-overturn effort, documented in the January 6 committee record and the Georgia indictment record; the mass pardons and commutations of January 20, 2025, about 1,500 January 6 defendants, including men convicted of assaulting police; and the president’s “poisoning the blood” rhetoric of late 2023 and after, in his own words. The facts the other side cites within the same framework: Paxton’s stage model requires elite collaboration abandoning democratic liberties and redemptive violence without legal restraint as governing practice; the 2026 midterms proceeded and removed the president’s party from Congress; and the courts operate against him, as filed above. Under Griffin’s framework, per Griffin, the label does not apply: no coherent revolutionary ideology, no new-man project, no party militia, no project to replace the constitutional order. The facts his side cites: the movement’s program is restorative—“again”—rather than futural-revolutionary; its economic core is deregulatory; its organization is a personalist electoral coalition inside an existing party. The facts the other side cites: Griffin himself calls the MAGA slogan palingenetic in form, and critics inside fascism studies argue the rebirth myth need not be coherent to function, since Griffin’s framework runs on mythic core. Under Stanley’s pillars, Stanley applies all ten to the current United States in his own writing; his framework expressly contemplates fascist politics inside a still-functioning democracy, so the institutional record filed above does not, within his framework, refute the application. His critics, Griffin and Payne among them, argue the pillars describe illiberal populism generally and thereby dilute the category.

The comparative floor under the whole argument is a matter of record, and both sides of the argument stand on it. The reference regimes’ documented record includes, for Nazi Germany, the industrialized murder of approximately six million Jews and millions of others, a world war killing tens of millions, and the abolition of elections, parties, unions, and courts as independent bodies within months of taking power; and for Fascist Italy, the abolition of parliament, the murder of Giacomo Matteotti, the racial laws, and wars of conquest. No sourced element of the 2025–2026 United States record assembled in this file is of that category or scale, and the abolition list stands unexecuted in the institutional record filed above. That floor underlies two different uses, and the file prints both and takes neither: the argument that the label, applied to the present, fails by orders of magnitude; and the position of the scholars recorded above that the label, applied now, describes a politics and a trajectory—in Paxton’s terms, the territory of his first three stages—not a completed regime, which none of the four framework authors in this file claims.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The first side is the definition itself: the field’s frameworks disagree about the threshold, and their authors, applying their own instruments to the same man, reach opposite conclusions—Paxton and Stanley apply the label, Griffin and Payne withhold it, and Eco’s list, by its author’s design, cannot settle the question it is most often used to settle. No agreed metric exists, and the democracy indices that moved sharply this year measure a different quantity than the one in this report’s headline. The second side is the compliance record: the fifty-year baseline contains no judicial finding of presidential defiance, and the 2025–2026 record contains such findings in writing from multiple judges, an appellate reversal of the largest contempt proceeding, compliance in the flagship case after 83 days, and compliance with the Supreme Court’s two largest merits rulings—and no official scorekeeper exists by whom that record could be summed into a rate. The third side is the deaths record: the custody list is the government’s own and its current fiscal year is its highest, and the operations category beside it has no official list at all, so the one total the public argument most wants does not exist in any source and is not manufactured here. Around those three open points, the bearings that are single-valued are these: the midterms were held on schedule four days ago and the opposition won both chambers on the Associated Press’s calls, uncertified as this report files; no opposition party is banned and no news organization has been shuttered by the government in the record; the detained population and the custody death count stand at records on the government’s own figures while removal totals sit inside the historical range on the same government’s yearbook; and Christian nationalism measures at one American in ten. The log proceeds.

The Companion Essay

The argument this file does not make is published by this paper’s publisher on his own program, The Chris Abraham Show, in his own voice, as “The Worst Hitler Ever.” The essay takes the position the record above is most often argued from: that the president is the worst fascist ever—that he cannot do the thing the label names, that the villainy is performed rather than executed, and not jackbooting enough to register on the frameworks’ own scales. This paper prints no part of it and adopts none of it; the link stands so the reader can follow the argument the desk declined to carry, from the record above to the case the record supports in another man’s telling.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty-two items.

Subjective
Robert O. Paxton — The Anatomy of Fascism, Knopf, 2004

The field’s standard behavioral definition, quoted in the report above from page 218, with the five stages of fascism from movement to radicalization or entropy, and the finding that only Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany passed through all five. The framework against which its author later measured an American president.

Subjective
Robert O. Paxton — “I’ve Hesitated to Call Donald Trump a Fascist. Until Now,” Newsweek, January 11, 2021; and The New York Times Magazine, October 23, 2024

Paxton’s own application of his framework: the January 6 attack removes his objection, the label “now seems not just acceptable but necessary,” the historical circumstances remain profoundly different from interwar Europe; in 2024 he confirms the diagnosis and says in the same interview that the word generates more heat than light.

Subjective
Roger Griffin — The Nature of Fascism, 1991

The “fascist minimum”: a palingenetic form of populist ultranationalism. Griffin’s published commentary on the present case, as carried in scholarly surveys of it, withholds the label—an “ochlocrat” practicing illiberal populism, rebirth rhetoric without the revolutionary ideology his definition requires.

Subjective
Umberto Eco — “Ur-Fascism,” The New York Review of Books, June 22, 1995

The fourteen features, from the cult of tradition to Newspeak, with the author’s own caveat printed in the same essay: the features cannot be organized into a system, many contradict each other, and one suffices for fascism to coagulate around it. The desk files the list and the caveat together.

Subjective
Jason Stanley — How Fascism Works: The Politics of Us and Them, 2018

The ten pillars of fascist politics, defined by their author as tactics a still-democratic polity can exhibit, and applied by him in full to the current United States in his books and interviews from 2018 forward. His framework expressly does not require a fascist state.

Subjective
Stanley G. Payne — A History of Fascism, 1914–1945, 1995

The typology that distinguishes fascism from other authoritarianisms by anti-liberalism, anti-conservatism, and selective anti-capitalism, a party militia, and the totalitarian new man. Payne’s position in scholarly discussion, as carried in surveys of it: authoritarian populism, not fascism, and a warning that overuse of the term undermines precision.

Subjective
The New York Times — John Kelly’s recorded interviews, October 22, 2024

The president’s longest-serving chief of staff reads a general definition aloud and answers it: the former president “certainly falls into the general definition of fascist, for sure,” “certainly prefers the dictator approach to government.” The definition is the general one Kelly read, not a scholarly framework; the Trump campaign at the time called his accounts fabricated.

Subjective
Bob Woodward — War, 2024

Gen. Mark Milley, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs, as quoted in Woodward’s reporting: Trump is “fascist to the core” and “the most dangerous person to this country.” A secondhand quotation in a journalist’s book, filed as attributed.

Subjective
Federal Judicial Center — the history of executive enforcement of judicial orders

The judiciary’s own institutional history: substantial compliance as the historical norm, defiance on rare occasions, the Worcester non-enforcement, Merryman, and the Jackson enforcement line marked as apocryphal. The baseline document for the report’s compliance section.

Subjective
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — Detainee Death Reporting

The agency’s statutory public list of deaths in its custody, by fiscal year, kept under the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act of 2018. The spine of this report’s deaths section: fiscal 2026 stands at 36 listed deaths on the page, with two more announced in the agency’s own releases.

Subjective
Basu et al. — “Mortality in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement Detention,” JAMA, April 16, 2026

The full series assembled from ICE’s own sources: 272 deaths in custody from fiscal 2004 through partial fiscal 2026, and the rate series—13.0 per 100,000 person-years in fiscal 2023, 47.5 in fiscal 2025, 88.9 in partial fiscal 2026, the highest since fiscal 2004.

Subjective
Human Rights Watch — the detention mortality measurement, June 25, 2026

The organization’s measurement of the custody death rate against the detained population: the rate up about 138 to 140 percent year over year on a 77 percent rise in the population—deaths rising faster than the number detained, on its figures.

Subjective
Senate Select Committee — Final Report, the Church Committee, April 26, 1976

The government’s own investigation of its intelligence agencies, 2,702 pages: COINTELPRO’s disruption and neutralization campaigns against lawful political activity, the informant-labeling and spouse-letter tactics, the campaign against Dr. King, and the finding that the targets ranged far beyond enemies of freedom.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security, Office of Homeland Security Statistics — Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 39

The department’s own removal, return, and expulsion series by fiscal year, from which the report’s administration-by-administration totals are summed: Obama 5,248,893 removals and returns combined; the broadest full-term Biden count about 4.79 million with expulsions; the first Trump administration about 2.0 million on the same construction. Event counts, not unique people.

Subjective
Freedom House — Freedom in the World 2026

The index’s United States score: 81 of 100, down 3 points, its lowest on the current scale, down 12 since 2005—and the rating unchanged: Free. An expert-coded assessment of democracy, printed in this report under that label.

Subjective
V-Dem Institute — Democracy Report 2026

The index’s United States movement: Liberal Democracy Index 0.75 to 0.57 in one year, rank 20th to 51st of 179, and reclassification from liberal democracy to electoral democracy for the first time in over fifty years—with its analysts’ own note that the electoral mechanics remain fundamentally intact.

Subjective
Economist Intelligence Unit — Democracy Index 2025; Pew Research Center, 2026

The EIU’s United States score, 7.65 of 10, a flawed democracy as classified since 2016 and the lowest United States score in the index’s history; and Pew’s side-by-side republication of the Freedom House, V-Dem, and EIU series from 2005 to 2025, the cleanest single exhibit of the trend lines.

Subjective
Public Religion Research Institute — American Values Atlas, 2025 (reported February 17, 2026)

The Christian nationalism battery on more than 22,000 interviews: Adherents 11 percent, Sympathizers 21 percent, Skeptics 37 percent, Rejecters 27 percent; supporters a majority of Republicans at 56 percent; the shares stable since measurement began in late 2022.

Subjective
Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry — Taking America Back for God, Oxford University Press, 2020

The field’s standard sociological treatment: the definition quoted in the report, the six-item Baylor Religion Survey scale, and the four-way sort from Rejecters to Ambassadors, with the authors’ own discussion of how the middle categories are cut.

Subjective
Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — “Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2024,” April 2025

The denominator of the hegemon question: United States military expenditure $997 billion, 37 percent of the world total, 3.2 times the second spender, 66 percent of NATO spending.

Subjective
Just Security — Litigation Tracker; CNN — the judicial-criticism analysis, 2026

The trackers behind the report’s litigation volume: roughly 700 to 800 challenges filed or active, one mid-2026 snapshot at 262 rulings for plaintiffs to 126 for the government; and CNN’s count of at least 77 orders containing sharp judicial criticism, from 69 judges, 11 of them Trump appointees. Method-dependent figures, filed as their makers’ counts.

Subjective
Brennan Center — the election-administration decisions catalog, 2026; Associated Press — midterm race calls, November 3–7, 2026

The catalog of at least 34 district-court decisions halting administration election-administration efforts, 8 of them by Trump appointees; and the AP calls on which this report’s midterm record rests—both chambers to the opposition, seven Senate flips, five governorships—uncertified as filed.

item.title: Explosions Again on Qeshm, a President Removed in Asunción, and the Count Still Waits
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The midday file for Saturday, November 7, 2026: Paraguay's former president Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General's Office on Saturday morning to face prosecutors a day after his removal over the Ueno Bank collapse, Qatar's prime minister said mediation between Washington and Tehran continues with significant progress made and a good agreement the aim, the Senate count did not move — Mississippi's margin reported between about 2,500 and 2,734 votes depending on the tally and Alaska's at 637 — and the markets' week stood settled with Brent at $98.32, down 13.3 percent, while Berkshire Hathaway reported operating earnings down 5.8 percent. Collected at 1200.
item.content:encoded:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Peña Before the Prosecutors, the Count Unmoved, and Oil Down Thirteen Percent on the Week

The news at midday on a closed-market Saturday: the week’s one completed presidency ended the morning in a prosecutor’s office in Asunción, the mediator in Doha said the talks live and progress has been made, the count in Mississippi and Alaska did not move and its published figures do not agree with each other, and the markets’ week stood settled—stocks down for a fourth week, oil down thirteen percent—under the one report of the day, Berkshire Hathaway’s softer quarter and record cash.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 14, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the midday figures differ from the morning’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Saturday at noon is a short file, and the desk files it short. The morning produced one completed act, in Asunción, where former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office to appear before prosecutors, a day after the Senate removed him over the collapse of Ueno Bank and authorities placed him under house arrest. It produced one official statement of consequence, in Doha, where Qatar’s prime minister said the mediation continues, progress has been made, and the aim is a good agreement rather than a perfect one. The count produced nothing: no new totals were reported from Mississippi or Alaska by noon, and the figures in circulation disagree with each other by several hundred votes in Mississippi, which the desk states plainly below. The markets produced a reading rather than a session: the exchanges are closed, the week stands settled at the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent and Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week, and the one scheduled report of the day, Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, arrived at 0800 with operating earnings down 5.8 percent and a cash position at a record. The desk files the day in that order.

Asunción at Midday: The Former President Before the Prosecutors

The removal is complete, and the case has begun. Reuters’ Asunción file, filed below, reports that former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office on Saturday to appear before prosecutors, a day after he was impeached and placed under house arrest in the crisis triggered by the collapse of the digital lender Ueno. Prosecutors said on Friday that the charges against Peña were still being determined but could include influence peddling. A second account puts the appointment at 11 a.m. before the Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office, with Prosecutor Silvia González confirming that Peña spent Friday night detained at his Asunción residence; after his statement is received, or his refusal to give one is recorded, prosecutors must file formal charges and request precautionary measures from the duty court. The accusations in the impeachment itself are on the record from Friday: conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña has denied wrongdoing. Those are allegations, stated as allegations; no court has ruled on any of them.

The government that replaced him is at work, and its first subject is the depositors. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in on Friday to complete the term through August 2028. The figures of the collapse stand as filed overnight: Ueno served about three million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adults, and held as much as $850 million in public money; regulators seized it on November 3 after its solvency fell below half the required level; the deposit guarantee covers up to about $38,000 per depositor, and preliminary central bank estimates place 97 percent of account holders fully within that ceiling, with payment required within 15 days under banking law. Alliana told compatriots affected by the collapse that they would be fully compensated, in the account filed below. What the new government has not yet put on the record by noon is the machinery: which office pays, on what schedule, and from what fund. That is the next fact in this file, and it has not arrived.

Qeshm and Doha: No Confirmation From Washington, a Statement From the Mediator

The war’s midday state is the night’s state, with one addition from the mediator. Reuters’ Saturday file on the mediation reports that Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani said the country’s mediation efforts between the United States and Iran were continuing to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control; that the American administration remained willing to find a solution even after the midterm elections; that significant progress had been made; and that he expressed confidence a settlement could be reached. His sentence, as carried, is: “We cannot wait to reach a perfect agreement; we hope to reach a good agreement.” The same file records the other side of the morning: Tasnim said initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island with no official information on possible damage, and the United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran. The explosions reported from Qeshm in the night remain unconfirmed as to origin and damage; Iran’s claims of American drones destroyed over the island remain unconfirmed by Washington; and the mediation, by the mediator’s own statement, remains open.

Qatar’s International Media Office added the correction the morning required. Circulating reports that the prime minister had said the two sides had failed to reach an agreement are, in the office’s words, “false and misleading,” and his remarks were “deliberately distorted.” The office stated that both sides continue to work towards a deal and that Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with Washington and Tehran. The fuller statement is filed below. A claim of failure circulated, the office running the talks denied it by name, and the prime minister then said progress had been made. No agreement has been announced by any side. The larger American decision the week has waited on since Thursday—whether to resume the war in full—has not been announced by noon either.

The Count at 1200: No New Totals, and the Tallies Disagree

Mississippi has not moved, and the desk corrects its own morning figures to the range the tallies actually support. The overnight edition carried the wire’s Friday-evening margin: Scott Colom, the Democrat, ahead of Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, by 2,574 votes. The accounts the desk took in by noon do not agree on that number. One account puts the separation at nearly 2,500 votes on Friday, with an estimate of about 30,000 ballots outstanding—an estimate revised down from about 44,000 on Friday morning. A second records the Decision Desk HQ tally at 2,734 votes on Friday afternoon. A results page carrying the wire’s data shows 953,314 votes counted with 96.9 percent of the expected vote in and about 31,000 remaining, and calculates that Hyde-Smith would need 53.2 percent of the remaining vote to overtake Colom. The cocked hat on Mississippi at noon is therefore a range, not a point: Colom leads by somewhere between roughly 2,500 and 2,734 votes, with roughly 30,000 ballots estimated outstanding. The settled facts around the range are these: 9,242 affidavit ballots had been processed by Friday, mail ballots postmarked by Election Day may arrive through November 10, voters may resolve identification issues through November 10, counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount procedure.

Alaska has not moved either, and its next movement is dated. Mary Peltola, the Democrat, leads Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by 637 first-choice votes, the figure that has stood since Wednesday, with about three-quarters of ballots counted. The Saturday account of the two races files the legal position: in Alaska the skirmishing began before the voting, the Justice Department sued to block certification should the incumbent lose, and on Friday Peltola’s campaign sued the Division of Elections for records identifying rejected absentee ballots and the reasons for each rejection—records the state calls confidential preliminary data, in the suit’s own account filed below. Absentee ballots may arrive through November 18, the day the ranked-choice tabulation is expected, since no candidate has cleared 50 percent; the state is not required to report more votes before November 10. A fourth candidate, a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan, holds about 3,600 votes, more than five times the margin, and how his voters ranked the two leaders is the open arithmetic of the race. At noon, neither Senate race has been called, for the fourth day.

The Markets’ Reading: A Closed Exchange, a Settled Week, One Report

There is no session to report on a Saturday, so the desk reports the week the session left behind. The closing account stands as filed Friday: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.3 percent on the day and down 2.7 percent on the week; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.42, up 1.1 percent on the day and down 3.4 percent on the week; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73, down 0.5 percent on the day and 0.9 percent on the week—the worst week for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq since June, in the week’s recap filed below. Oil’s week is the larger figure. Brent settled at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week, its steepest weekly fall since April 2020, and West Texas Intermediate closed at $90.83, down 12.8 percent, in the strait’s daily brief and the market accounts filed below; both benchmarks had peaked on October 30, Brent at $113.43, before hopes of an American-Iranian agreement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz pulled the premium out. The brief records the strait itself as closed in its own accounting, with two transits recorded on October 25 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, and 132 vessels holding position away from berth at 1200 UTC. Monday’s open, by every account the desk read, hinges on the weekend’s Iran headlines—which is to say, on the file in the section above this one.

The day’s one scheduled report arrived at 0800 and was softer at the top and larger at the bottom. Berkshire Hathaway’s release reports third-quarter operating earnings of $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier, on weaker insurance results; net earnings of $22.112 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share, down from $30.796 billion; investment gains of $9.407 billion against $17.311 billion a year earlier; and share repurchases of about $9.6 billion in the quarter, bringing the nine-month total to about $14.4 billion. The fuller account adds that operating earnings per Class A share, at $8,907, came in above the $8,821.84 average forecast of four analysts surveyed by FactSet; that underwriting profit fell 42.9 percent, with each of the three insurance groups earning less from underwriting than a year earlier; and that the cash position reached $377.4 billion at the end of September, a record. It was the third quarter under Chief Executive Greg Abel. Berkshire’s own instruction in the release is the desk’s: the summary is not adequate for an informed judgment, and the quarterly filing is the document.

Shenzhen Stands: No New Word by Noon

The week’s largest diplomatic fact received no new word on Saturday, and the desk files it standing. Beijing’s confirmation, first made on Wednesday, that China is in communication with Washington and Moscow about a meeting of Presidents Xi, Trump, and Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19 remains the position at noon, in the account filed below. The Kremlin said work is under way to arrange it. The White House has not confirmed it. The three leaders have never held formal talks together. What each capital wants differs on the record: Washington, nuclear weapons; Moscow, Ukraine discussed without Kyiv at the table; Beijing, Ukraine held to be a European conflict and not the meeting’s subject. No final decision has been announced. Eleven days remain.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Mississippi, the tallies in circulation at noon put Colom’s lead between roughly 2,500 and 2,734 votes; the desk publishes the range and does not choose inside it. On Qeshm, the reported explosions, the claimed drones, and the confirmed Friday strike are three separate facts that the files do not join, and the desk does not join them. On the mediation, the mediator says progress; no other party has announced an agreement, a date, or a text. On Asunción, the removal and the appearance are complete; the charges are not yet filed and the allegations are not findings. On the markets, the week is settled and Monday is not. The edition closes at noon with the count unmoved, the war undecided, and one presidency ended and answering questions.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 17 items.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — Paraguay’s ex-president faces prosecutors after impeachment and house arrest

Asunción, November 7: former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office on Saturday to appear before prosecutors, a day after he was impeached and placed under house arrest amid a political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of digital lender Ueno; prosecutors said on Friday that charges against Peña were still being determined but could include influence peddling; his removal brought Vice President Pedro Alliana to power to complete the term through August 2028; and lawmakers who backed the impeachment accused Peña of conflicts of interest, manipulating regulatory oversight and participating in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

Subjective
Sociedad Media — Peña detained at home, due before prosecutors Saturday

Asunción, November 7: Santiago Peña spent Friday night in custody at his residence after the Senate removed him as president over the collapse of Ueno Bank, the Senate voting unanimously among the 44 senators present with one absent; the Public Ministry said its agents detained Peña and former central bank president Carlos Carvallo Spalding for the alleged commission of breach of trust and other offenses; Prosecutor Silvia González confirmed Peña would appear Saturday, November 7, at 11 a.m. before the Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office; after his statement, prosecutors must file formal charges and request precautionary measures; and the probe covers alleged irregularities in the supervision of Ueno, possible conflicts of interest tied to Peña’s links to Grupo Vázquez, and the placement of public funds in the bank, including pension and health fund money.

Subjective
The Daily Caller — Paraguayan president removed from office after bank collapse

Asunción, November 6: Paraguay’s Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office on Friday, an hour before authorities placed him under house arrest, with not one of the 44 senators in attendance opposed and the removal resting on misconduct in office; Peña is the second Paraguayan president forced out by impeachment since 1989; Vice President Pedro Alliana took the oath soon afterward and will finish a term closing in August 2028; prosecutors cited suspected breach of trust in the arrest order, which also covered Carlos Carvallo, whom Peña had installed as central bank chief, with charges undetermined and possibly extending to influence peddling; regulators seized the digital lender Ueno on November 3 after its solvency fell under half the required level; the bank served roughly three million customers, about 60 percent of the country’s adults, and held as much as $850 million in public money; the deposit guarantee covers up to about $38,000 per depositor, with preliminary estimates placing 97 percent of account holders fully within that ceiling and payment required within 15 days; Peña held shares in Ueno’s holding company until last year and Carvallo had run the lender until 2023; and Peña tried to resign on Thursday but Congress refused, the lower house having already voted 78 to 0 to impeach him.

Subjective
Press TV — Paraguay impeaches and detains President Peña over the banking scandal

November 7: Paraguay’s former president Santiago Peña has been impeached, placed under house arrest, and replaced by Vice President Pedro Alliana following a banking scandal that locked almost three million people out of their accounts; the Senate voted on Friday to remove Peña over alleged misconduct linked to the collapse of Ueno Bank, a rapidly expanding digital lender with close ties to his administration; prosecutors placed the former president under house arrest on suspicion of breach of trust and other offenses; Peña is accused of using his political influence to channel hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into the lender while turning a blind eye to serious financial irregularities; Peña, who has denied wrongdoing, announced his resignation on Thursday amid public protests in the capital, Asunción; he did not appear at Friday’s Senate hearing after lawmakers rejected his request for an additional 72 hours to prepare his defense; and regulators seized control of Ueno Bank earlier in the week over solvency problems, freezing the accounts of nearly three million customers, the lender having accumulated more than $800 million in public deposits including pension funds.

Subjective
Reuters — Qatar says its mediation efforts between the US and Iran continue

November 7: Qatar’s prime minister said the country’s mediation efforts between the United States and Iran were continuing to prevent the situation in the region from spiralling out of control; the American administration remained willing to find a solution even after the midterm elections, signalling that Washington’s interest in reaching an agreement had not changed; significant progress had been made and the prime minister expressed confidence that a settlement could be reached; “We cannot wait to reach a perfect agreement; we hope to reach a good agreement,” he said; Iran has been proposing its own seven-day plan since September, so far rejected by the American president; Tasnim said on Saturday that initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage; and the United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — two missiles strike Qeshm Island, Tasnim says

Cairo, November 7: Tasnim said on Saturday that initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage and further details to follow once relevant authorities confirmed the incident; IRNA had earlier reported that local witnesses said two projectiles struck the Suza area after the sound of an aircraft was heard over the island; and Qatar’s International Media Office denied circulating reports that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement to end their war, describing the allegations as false and misleading.

Subjective
The Insight International — Iranian media report explosions on Qeshm Island

Tehran, November 7: Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf, with local witnesses describing two projectiles striking the Suza area after aircraft were heard overhead; state television said two explosions were heard in the Souza area late Friday and that there were no casualties; Fars reported explosions in Qeshm and in the port city of Bandar Khamir, saying they might be linked to warning shots toward the Strait of Hormuz; none of the accounts has been independently confirmed, and there was no immediate American confirmation of a new strike; and the reports are distinct from an earlier claim that the Revolutionary Guards electronically downed an American drone near Qeshm.

Subjective
Devdiscourse, carrying ANI — Qatar says the prime minister’s remarks on the talks were distorted online

Doha, November 7: Qatar’s International Media Office said reports circulating online claiming that Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani stated that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement are false and misleading, and that his remarks were deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability, with many of the claims spread by fake accounts; the prime minister stated that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal; Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations; and Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at brokering a new ceasefire and resuming stalled nuclear discussions, Axios reported.

Subjective
USA Today — Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still undecided as legal fights loom

November 7: two Senate races remain undecided days after the election, with legal battles looming in both; in Alaska, Mary Peltola led Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 votes with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted, according to the wire’s latest tally; the legal skirmishing there began long before anyone voted, a fourth candidate is a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan, the Justice Department sued to block certification should the incumbent lose, and on November 6 Peltola’s campaign opened a legal front of its own; Alaska’s final answer is more than a week away, with absentee ballots accepted through November 18, the same day the state expects to run its ranked-choice tabulation since no candidate has cleared 50 percent, that count to redistribute the votes of trailing candidates including the other Dan Sullivan; and in Mississippi the count continues under its own deadlines.

Subjective
AmeriLedger — Mississippi U.S. Senate midterm election 2026 live results

November 7: the Mississippi Senate results page, carrying data provided by the Associated Press with projections by the NBC News Decision Desk, shows Scott Colom at 49.1 percent, Cindy Hyde-Smith at 48.8 percent, and Ty Pinkins at 2.1 percent, with 953,314 votes counted and 96.9 percent of the expected vote in and an estimated 31,000 votes remaining; Hyde-Smith would need to win 53.2 percent of the remaining vote to catch or overtake Colom; as of Friday, 9,242 affidavit ballots had been processed and 3,139 mail ballots were still outstanding, according to the secretary of state, though more affidavit ballots are possible since voter identification issues can be resolved up to November 10; the page’s last update is stamped 8:43 a.m. ET; and the race has shifted 23.16 points toward the Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election.

Subjective
JournalArta — Mississippi Senate race too close to call as ballots are counted

November 7: Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith remained separated by nearly 2,500 votes as counting continued in Mississippi, leaving the contest too close to call, with an estimate putting about 30,000 votes outstanding; the remaining ballots matter in a race that could determine the size of the Democrats’ majority in the Senate; Mississippi’s decentralized counting process has left the number of ballots yet to be counted uncertain, the state having 82 counties and no central system for reporting vote totals; absentee ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and received by November 10 to count; the secretary of state said Thursday that about 7,000 provisional ballots had been processed with about 80 percent accepted, and counties must report provisional results with their certified results on November 13; the estimate for outstanding ballots stood at around 44,000 on Friday morning before being revised to closer to 30,000 by 4:45 p.m. Eastern; and Mississippi has no automatic recount law.

Subjective
Political.org — Peltola campaign sues Alaska elections division for records on rejected absentee ballots

November 6: the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola sued Alaska election officials on Friday, seeking the immediate release of records identifying absentee ballots rejected in the November 3 election and the reasons for each rejection; the state says the records are confidential preliminary data; the campaign says it requested the records on October 27 and again on November 4 under Alaska’s Public Records Act, received no response, and was later denied immediate access; as of results posted Wednesday afternoon, a 637-vote difference separated Peltola, at 102,962 votes, from Sullivan, at 102,325; the state will accept ballots up to November 18; a preliminary ranked-choice analysis by FairVote noted that Sullivan has the most first-choice support in the tranche of ballots in the cast vote record it analyzed, even though he trails in the division’s reported first-choice results, an analysis that does not match the official tallies one-to-one; and the suit is the first major legal skirmish in a contest that remains unresolved.

Subjective
Oninvest — the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq rose on Friday but ended the week in the red

November 6: the S&P 500 rose 0.3 percent and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1 percent at Friday’s close as technology stocks rebounded, partially recovering from the previous day’s record-volume sell-off; both indices still ended the week in the red, the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent and the Nasdaq Composite down 3.4 percent, their worst weekly performance since June, and both have now fallen for four consecutive weeks; and the Dow Jones index was the only one of the three to decline on Friday, by 0.5 percent, while losing the least over the five trading days.

Subjective
Straits — Strait of Hormuz daily brief, November 7, 2026

November 7: the daily brief records the Strait of Hormuz as closed, with Brent crude settled at $98.32, up 0.03 percent in the last session before the close; the navy of Iran claims a tanker caught fire after striking a sea mine east of the strait, per IRNA, with no maritime authority confirming it; Iran says the strait will stay closed until the United States accepts its terms, while a maritime authority reported a tanker transiting near Khasab, indicating some movement continues despite the declared closure; one seafarer was killed in a suspected missile attack on an oil products tanker in the Gulf, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT Velos Sapphire identified as the struck vessel, sailing unladen toward Bahrain; a claim that the strait is reopening and the closure declaration remain unreconciled; IMF PortWatch recorded two transits on October 25 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day; and as of 1200 UTC, 132 AIS-visible vessels were holding position away from berth in the strait and Gulf watch box.

Subjective
Business Wire — Berkshire Hathaway Inc. news release, third quarter 2026

November 7: Berkshire Hathaway’s release summarizes earnings for the third quarter and first nine months of 2026 and 2025, stated after tax; net earnings attributable to Berkshire shareholders were $22.112 billion for the quarter against $30.796 billion a year earlier, and $57.885 billion for the nine months against $47.769 billion; operating earnings were $12.705 billion for the quarter against $13.485 billion, and $37.034 billion for the nine months against $34.286 billion; investment gains were $9.407 billion in the quarter; net earnings per average equivalent Class A share were $15,502 against $21,413; Berkshire acquired approximately $9.6 billion in treasury shares during the third quarter, bringing the nine-month total to about $14.4 billion, with 1,418,900 Class A equivalent shares outstanding on September 30, 2026; and the release urges investors and reporters to read the quarterly filing posted on the company’s site, stating that the limited information in the release is not adequate for making an informed investment judgment.

Subjective
SourceFirst News — Berkshire Q3 operating profit falls 5.8 percent; buybacks $9.6 billion

November 7: Berkshire Hathaway bought back about $9.6 billion of its own stock during the third quarter, its quarterly report showed Saturday, even as operating earnings slipped 5.8 percent to $12.705 billion on weaker insurance results; it was Greg Abel’s third quarter as chief executive; net earnings fell to $22.112 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share, from $30.796 billion a year earlier, the company advising investors to look past quarterly investment swings; operating earnings came to $8,907 per Class A share, against an average forecast of $8,821.84 from four analysts surveyed by FactSet; after-tax underwriting profit fell 42.9 percent, with each of the three insurance groups earning less from underwriting than a year earlier; the loss ratio at Geico, the share of earned premiums consumed by claims and claim-handling costs, rose 5.1 percentage points to 76.6 percent; and insurance investment income fell 14.1 percent to $2.734 billion after tax.

Subjective
Political.org — China confirms talks under way on a possible Xi-Trump-Putin meeting at Shenzhen

November 6: Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin; Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China is in communication with relevant parties about a possible three-way meeting, which could take place on the sidelines of this month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, scheduled for November 18 and 19, with no final decision announced; the American president is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet Xi for the third time this year, with a fragile American-Chinese trade truce set to expire in January; Trump has said he would like to discuss nuclear arms control, while Putin is focused on the war in Ukraine, without Kyiv at the table; Putin is said to have proposed the trilateral format to Trump in a phone call on October 9, aiming at an agreement on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia; and analysts say the gathering may be mostly a photo opportunity, with little prospect of substantive agreements.

item.title: The Interview and the Edit: What the Record Shows About a 60 Minutes Segment
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.category: Special Report No. 2 — Filed Outside the Watches
item.description: A 60 Minutes segment on third-country deportations, the interview it cut from, the allegation it left out, and the standards the network states for itself. The whole record, attributed.
item.content:encoded:
Special Report

The Media File — A Broadcast and Its Record

Objective

The Interview and the Edit: What the Record Shows About a 60 Minutes Segment

On October 25, CBS aired thirteen minutes on third-country deportations. Within two weeks the segment had produced a fraud allegation the broadcast never mentioned, a longer interview released the next day, a standards file six decades deep, and a newsroom dispute reported in three outlets. The desk files the record whole: the segment, the policy underneath it, the dispute, and what could not be verified. Every claim is attributed.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0905 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026.

The File in Brief

The segment is documented. The dispute about it is documented. The completeness of the record CBS released is not. The facts the desk can file with confidence are these. On Sunday, October 25, 2026, 60 Minutes aired “Destination: Nowhere,” reported by contributor Gianna Toboni, on the administration’s practice of deporting people to countries not their own. It reported about 25,000 such deportations, and it profiled Moussa Diawara, a Malian man of 57 with no criminal record, whom an immigration judge in 2012 ordered removed from the United States but protected from return to Mali. The broadcast said Ghana, which received him on July 31, forced him to Mali within five days. On the night of the broadcast, the Department of Homeland Security’s general counsel, James Percival, who had sat for the program’s interview, posted that the program had selectively edited him and that Diawara’s original asylum application had claimed persecution for his homosexuality, a fact the broadcast omitted. Fox News reported that DHS had emailed CBS about the claim on October 6, nineteen days before the broadcast. CBS News declined to comment. On October 26, CBS posted a 43-minute “Extended Interview” with Percival. Whether those 43 minutes are the whole interview is not established: Percival said the interview ran nearly an hour, and CBS has published no transcript and given no reason for the release. The policy underneath the segment is real and litigated: by the count of Human Rights Watch, from Immigration and Customs Enforcement data, 27,943 people were deported to third countries between January 20, 2025, and August 5, 2026, and the Supreme Court hears the governing case on December 9. What no source in the file establishes is the segment’s intent, the completeness of the released interview, and any adjudicated finding on the allegation at the dispute’s center. The report files the record in that order.

The Segment: What Was Broadcast

The program reported a practice, a flight, and a man. “Destination: Nowhere” opened with the scale of the second Trump administration’s removals: “Nearly one million people were deported from the U.S. during the first year and a half of President Trump’s second term… About 25,000, though, were sent somewhere else… They’re called third countries.” The broadcast said deportations of this kind “can be legal and past administrations have carried them out, but not at this scale,” and that receiving countries get “millions of dollars in aid or other benefits from the U.S.” in return. Its five-month investigation, it said, “uncovered cases in which people ended up in places where U.S. immigration judges said they would likely be persecuted or tortured.” The program obtained the names of all 63 people on the flight that left Texas on July 30, 2026, and reached 19 of those sent to Ghana; 17 of the 19 said Ghana quickly transported them against their will to countries that judges had ruled they should not be returned to. It aired video it described, through an eyewitness, as Ghanaian officials dragging a woman, Rabbiatu Kuyateh, described as a nurse who had lived in the United States for 30 years, to a flight home to a country where she held protection from return. An immigration attorney, Meredyth Yoon, said on camera that the United States had been warned of Ghana’s conduct in a lawsuit the prior year and sent ten more flights afterward. Ghana’s government declined to comment to the program. The segment’s own count of the 63 people on the flight found 19 percent had a criminal charge or conviction, for theft, assault, drugs, or weapons offenses; the rest had traffic violations or none.

The case at the segment’s center was Diawara’s, and the broadcast told it in full except for one part of his file. The program said he entered the United States 25 years earlier, overstayed a tourist visa, and “applied for refugee protection, arguing he would be persecuted if he were returned to Mali”; that in 2012 a judge ruled he could be deported but not to Mali, after which he held a work permit; that ICE agents waited at his Houston-suburb home after his Uber night shift on July 11, 2026; that after three weeks in detention in Texas, without speaking to his lawyer or a judge, he was flown out and landed in Ghana on July 31. There, he said, he and others were held in a hotel by armed guards and not allowed calls. “Within five days, Diawara says, Ghanaian officials forced him onto a flight to… Mali.” In Mali he was, in the broadcast’s words, “homeless and in hiding”; part of the reason he did not feel safe, he told the program, is that he had converted to Christianity, in a Muslim-majority nation with an Islamist insurgency. He said he was dropped with no money or identification, and that after three weeks, with the help of local truckers, he escaped to another African country he asked the program not to name. He showed a DHS medication document and baggage tags listing the destination as Mali; Percival, shown them on camera, answered, “Well, he wasn’t flown to Mali. He was flown to Ghana, but I can’t speak to why that piece of paper says that.” After the interview, DHS told the program the tags were made by contractors not involved in determining destinations and the medication form was a “clerical error”. The broadcast said his attorney had asked a federal judge in Washington to order his return. His wife Barbara and his children, Corey, 16, and Chloe, 12, appeared. The broadcast made no mention of any sexuality-based claim in his asylum history. It did say, in narration immediately before an interview clip: “DHS also questioned the credibility of Diawara’s arguments for fearing persecution in Mali.” The episode drew 5.64 million viewers.

The Interview: What Aired, What Did Not

In the broadcast, Percival defended the policy and declined its central number. His interview material is intercut through the thirteen-minute segment, in five short passages among field reporting and family scenes. He said: “I absolutely believe with all of my heart that these third country removals have stopped crimes from happening and kept Americans safer. And that is our fundamental obligation of the Department of Homeland Security.” He explained the practice’s two uses: a serious criminal whose country “just won’t take them back,” and a person granted country-specific relief, ordered to leave but not to the home country. Asked about Ghana sending deportees onward, he said, “I’m not aware of any such cases,” and offered that deportees might have consented or that the foreign government had applied its own procedures consistent with international law. Asked what percentage of the detained and deported are violent offenders, he said, “I don’t have that figure off the top of my head.” The broadcast’s closing narration carried his position that the administration is “following the law that Congress has passed.”

The longer interview CBS posted the next day contains four exchanges the broadcast did not carry. First, a challenge on the onward returns: Percival asked, “Are you suggesting that when these people went back to their home countries that they were persecuted or tortured?” Toboni cited the judges’ standard and said some deportees had faced violence, but that actual persecution was “not her claim”; Percival answered that the ultimate question is whether anyone is being sent somewhere they will actually be persecuted or tortured, “and it doesn’t sound like you are making that claim.” Second, a statistics exchange: Toboni cited an internal DHS document under which, in the administration’s first year, 0.5 percent of the deported were accused or convicted of homicide and 1.4 percent of sexual assault. Percival answered: “Isn’t it wonderful that we are getting those people out of the country, should that be the limit of who has to follow the law? Just rapist and murderers have to follow the law?” Third, on compassion for nonviolent people separated from families, he said the people he has “the most compassion for is the American victims who we’re protecting,” and that “justice is about doing things that might be unpleasant to protect people”. Fourth, asked again for the violent-offender percentage, he gave the explanation the broadcast omitted: “there’s a very specific reason why this population is disproportionately criminal. Literally two reasons. Number one, when countries refuse to accept their nationals back, they disproportionately do that for violent criminals. People don’t really want to take their violent criminals back.” His second reason concerned withholding of removal, the country-specific protection Diawara held. In the circulated clips of that exchange, he cited no agency figure, and repeated that he did not have the percentage.

The release itself is part of the record, and its most repeated description is wrong. CBS titled the October 26 posting an “Extended Interview” and published it under its 60 Minutes Overtime brand, on CBS.com and YouTube; the podcast listing runs 43 minutes 12 seconds. CBS did not call it full, raw, or unedited in any text the desk found. The words “FULL, uncut” are the Department of Homeland Security’s, from its October 26 post: “WATCH WHAT @60Minutes DIDN’T SHOW YOU. Here’s the FULL, uncut interview.” Percival, on the night of the broadcast, had said of CBS that “they did promise they would publish the entire interview, so I look forward to my comments being posted in full this week,” and that he had spoken with the program for “nearly an hour.” His own excerpt clips followed on October 27, after the posting. No statement by CBS giving a reason for the release was found in any source. Whether the 43 minutes are the complete interview cannot be confirmed from the public record, and no transcript of the extended interview has been published.

The Omission: What Each Side Has Put on the Record

The administration’s allegation was made in public, on the night of the broadcast. Percival posted on October 25 that CBS had made Diawara the “poster child for what it claims are wrongful deportations,” and added: “His claimed reason for fearing Mali was that he is ‘gay’, just in case you’re wondering how bad the immigration fraud problem is.” DHS posted that Diawara “claimed on an asylum application that he would be persecuted for his homosexuality if he was returned to his home country, despite being married to a woman he has two children with,” and that 60 Minutes “left this absurd bit of fraud out of their ‘Texas dad’ segment”. ICE posted on October 26: “Fake & Gay!” Fox News reported on October 26 and 29 that it had obtained Diawara’s asylum application, filed in 2009, in which he wrote that he had “experienced extreme punishment and persecution based on the ground of my sexual orientation”. Some secondary accounts give the application’s year as 2012; 2012 is the year of the removal order and the grant of protection against return to Mali, which DHS’s own posts date to February 2, 2012. No adjudicated finding that the application was fraudulent appears in any source the desk reviewed. Asylum applications are confidential under federal regulation, 8 C.F.R. §208.6; an immigration-law commentary flagged that the application’s disclosure itself raises a confidentiality question. No statement by Diawara or his counsel responding to the allegation was found.

The warning, on the reported evidence, was an email dated October 6. A DHS spokesperson told the New York Post on October 27 that CBS had been informed “two weeks before” the segment aired. Fox News and the Post reported that they obtained a DHS email to CBS dated October 6, 2026, nineteen days before the broadcast, stating that Diawara, “who is married to a woman he shares two children with, oddly claimed he would be persecuted for homosexuality if returned home to Mali”. A network source told the Post the email did not explicitly allege fraud. CBS has neither confirmed nor denied receiving it; the network declined to comment to Fox News on October 29 and to the Post on October 30. The only defense of the broadcast on the record is anonymous: a “60 Minutes insider” told Fox News Digital that the broadcast had acknowledged DHS questioning the credibility of Diawara’s fear of persecution, which the transcript confirms it did, in the narration quoted above.

Why the material was omitted is the subject of two attributed accounts that do not fully agree. The Post reported on October 30 that, according to its sources, the segment intentionally left out the claim “to protect him”; that producer Andy Court had made an agreement with Diawara’s lawyer not to mention it and had not briefed 60 Minutes executive producer Nick Bilton or CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, who “went ballistic” on learning of it; that Bilton met with Toboni and Court on October 29; and that the network was weighing disciplinary action against Court, up to firing. Status News reported on November 6 that Toboni’s team made a deliberate decision to exclude the claim, fearing that publicizing it could expose Diawara to further persecution in Mali, where homosexuality is criminalized, and that Bilton and a senior lieutenant were at least partially informed, which partly contradicts the Post’s account; Status also reported staff accusing network leadership of throwing its journalists “under the bus”. CBS declined to comment for both stories. At the Information’s WTF Summit on October 29, Weiss asked critics, per the Post, to “judge us by our journalism.” No on-the-record statement by Weiss about this segment was found.

The Policy Underneath: Third Countries, in the Record

The practice rests on a statute, two guidance documents, and a case the Supreme Court hears in December. The Immigration and Nationality Act, §241(b), codified at 8 U.S.C. §1231(b), permits removal to a country that will accept the person where removal to the designated country is impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible; withholding of removal and protection under the Convention Against Torture bar removal to the specified country and do not by their terms bar removal to a third country. ICE guidance of February 18, 2025, directed review of withholding and torture-protection cases to determine the viability of third-country removal. Secretary Kristi Noem’s guidance of March 30, 2025, reaffirmed July 9, 2025, provides that where the receiving country has given diplomatic assurances, judged credible by the State Department, that removed people will not be persecuted or tortured, the person “may be removed without the need for further procedures”; otherwise the government must give notice of the country and, if the person states a fear, screen the claim as to that country.

The documented scale exceeds the broadcast’s figure, and most of it is not Africa. Human Rights Watch, analyzing ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project under the Freedom of Information Act, counted 27,943 third-country deportations from January 20, 2025, to August 5, 2026, against 8,563 in the comparable prior period, and 46,563 third-country removal orders through August 31, 2026. A tracker count put roughly 22,000 people sent to at least 26 countries since January 2025, about 19,000 of them to Mexico. The documented receiving countries include Panama, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Rwanda, Uganda, Liberia, Cabo Verde, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, and Sierra Leone. El Salvador’s CECOT arrangement of March 2025 proceeded under the Alien Enemies Act proclamation, a distinct authority from §241(b). In Africa: South Sudan received a first cohort of eight men in July 2025; Eswatini had received about 30 people by mid-2026 under a deal whose cap and payment figures conflict between sources; Rwanda agreed to take up to 250 people for $7.5 million, the first seven arriving in August 2025. Ghana’s agreement, announced by President John Mahama on September 10–11, 2025, accepted West African nationals only, under the ECOWAS free-movement protocol; Mahama said the first 14 arrivals, mostly Nigerians and one Gambian, were facilitated onward, the Nigerians by bus to Nigeria, and that no money was exchanged. Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa defended the arrangement as humanitarian and pan-African; the parliamentary minority argued it required ratification under Article 75 of Ghana’s constitution. Human Rights Watch reported that Ghana later returned several of the September 2025 group to their home countries. For the July 2026 flight at the segment’s center, Ghana’s government declined to comment, and no Ghanaian statement about it was found.

The courts have ruled in both directions, and the last word is scheduled. In D.V.D. v. DHS, Judge Brian Murphy of the District of Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction on April 18, 2025, requiring written notice in a language the person understands, a meaningful opportunity to raise a fear claim, and, if no reasonable fear is found, a minimum of 15 days to move to reopen, before any third-country removal; he found in May 2025 that the department had violated the injunction in an attempted removal to South Sudan on about 24 hours’ notice. The Supreme Court stayed the injunction on June 23, 2025, over a dissent by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson, allowing the removals to proceed while the case continued. On September 18, 2026, the First Circuit affirmed in large part a judgment requiring the government to seek removal first to designated or home countries, to give effective notice of the specified third country, and to allow a meaningful opportunity to contest on reasonable-fear grounds, and vacating the guidance; the Supreme Court stayed that judgment as well and granted review in DHS v. D.V.D., No. 26-426, with argument set for December 9, 2026. The broadcast’s summary of this posture, that an appeals court had found the policy unlawful and the Supreme Court had allowed the deportations to continue until it hears the case in December, is consistent with the record.

The Argument: Who Said What, and When

The administration’s case against the segment was made by its principals, in sequence. Percival’s posts of October 25–27 charged selective editing and the omitted asylum claim, and promoted the exchanges in §2 above: “You can kind of see why @60Minutes left stuff like this on the cutting room floor.” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told the Daily Caller on October 27 that the program had engaged in “selective editing” and “failed to include key information about how third country removals are essential to the safety of the American people”; that “these removals allow us to remove some of the most barbaric criminals, including child rapists and murderers whose home countries refuse to take them back”; and that the program chose to “peddle false sob stories of illegal aliens.” Larry O’Connor, on his Townhall program on October 28, played the omitted disproportionately-criminal explanation, called it “clear, concise, cohesive,” and argued the program cut it because it was a logical defense of the policy. The Federation for American Immigration Reform argued on October 28 that the segment minimized the deportees’ criminal records, noted the broadcast’s own 19 percent figure, and asserted that every person on the flights had been offered the chance to self-deport, with payment, to a country of their own choosing, and declined. Rich Lowry of National Review published a video analysis on November 2, “What 60 Minutes Didn’t Tell Viewers About Trump’s Deportations,” examining the full interview and the Diawara case; its description says Lowry questions whether CBS gave viewers the complete story. No transcript of the video was retrievable, and the desk asserts nothing of Lowry’s spoken argument beyond its published description and chapter titles.

The calls for consequences, and the defenses, are both thinner than the volume suggests. No public call by a named official or major outlet to cancel or end 60 Minutes over this segment was found. The documented prescriptions are these. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, said on Fox News on December 23, 2025, of the producers of the earlier, shelved CECOT segment: “Every one of those producers at ‘60 Minutes’ engaged in this revolt, fire them. Clean house.” The Post reported the network weighing discipline or firing for the Diawara segment’s producer. Aaron Ackerman, writing October 29, prescribed process: “Release the interviews. Explain consequential edits. Correct errors prominently.” Two process rules from earlier disputes are already in force at the network: release of transcripts of interviews with presidential candidates, adopted in the 2025 settlement described below, and the live or live-to-tape-only rule Face the Nation adopted in September 2025. On the other side, no named press critic was found on the record calling this segment sound journalism in full, and none calling for its retraction; the documented defense is the anonymous insider’s point that the broadcast acknowledged the credibility challenge, the safety rationale in the Post and Status accounts, and Sharyn Alfonsi’s December 2025 defense of her own segment, in an internal email, as a vetted story that should not be held for government non-participation.

The Standards: The Yardsticks on the Record

CBS has stated its editing standard twice in two years, in its own defense. On October 20, 2024, answering the charge that it had deceitfully edited an interview with Vice President Kamala Harris, 60 Minutes said the accusation “is false”: “Same question. Same answer. But a different portion of the response… When we edit any interview, whether a politician, an athlete, or movie star, we strive to be clear, accurate and on point.” On February 5, 2025, publishing the Harris transcripts and video it had given the Federal Communications Commission, it said the material showed the broadcast “was not doctored or deceitful. In reporting the news, journalists regularly edit interviews, for time, space, or clarity. In making these edits, 60 Minutes is always guided by the truth and what we believe will be most informative to the viewing public.” CBS News has maintained written standards since they were first compiled under Richard Salant in 1976; the 1999 edition’s introduction states that most of them “come down to two essential principles: accuracy and fairness.” The current handbook is not published. In September 2025, after Secretary Noem accused CBS of editing her Face the Nation interview, the network first said the edit “met all CBS News standards,” then, on September 5, changed the program’s policy to live or live-to-tape interviews only, citing audience feedback and “greater transparency in our interviews.”

The profession’s codes state the compression rule in one sentence each. The Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics, revised September 6, 2014, instructs journalists to “provide context”, to “take special care not to misrepresent or oversimplify in promoting, previewing or summarizing a story,” and to “never deliberately distort facts or context, including visual information”; the code states of itself that it is not legally enforceable. The Radio Television Digital News Association’s code holds that journalism “verifies, provides relevant context, tells the rest of the story and acknowledges the absence of important additional information,” and that responsible reporting “is clear about what it omits, as well as what it includes”.
