PBS’s editorial standards, a comparator broadcast standard, state that “editing should never alter the meaning of a person’s remarks,” permit condensing that fairly and accurately represents the remarks and their context, and prohibit placing a question next to a different answer. Joe Peyronnin, a television news executive of forty years at CBS, Fox, and Telemundo, stated the practitioner’s test on November 17, 2025: “whatever you edit has to fairly and accurately represent what she said, the point she was making”, and an editor may not join material in a way that can “change the meaning, or potentially change the meaning, or mislead the viewer.”

The adjudicated precedents cut in more than one direction. In the Harris matter, the Center for American Rights filed an FCC news-distortion complaint on October 16, 2024. Chair Jessica Rosenworcel dismissed it on January 16, 2025, as failing to allege intentional falsification as against protected editorial judgment; Chair Brendan Carr reinstated it on January 22, 2025, demanded the full unedited transcript and camera feeds, and the FCC published them on February 5, 2025. The full record showed that both aired excerpts came from the same single answer, the first half in a preview and the second half on the broadcast; no words were fabricated. No FCC finding of news distortion against CBS was issued. President Trump’s civil suit over the interview was settled by Paramount on July 1–2, 2025, for $16 million, paid to his future presidential library and to fees and costs, with no apology, and with 60 Minutes agreeing to release transcripts of future interviews with presidential candidates. The FCC approved the Skydance–Paramount merger on July 24, 2025. In the network’s older precedent, the Benjamin Report of July 1982, CBS’s own internal review of the documentary “The Uncounted Enemy,” found violations of CBS News standards, including editing in which interviewees appeared to answer different questions than those asked, and concluded the execution was seriously flawed on fairness, accuracy, and balance; the related libel suit was withdrawn in 1985. In November 2025, Peyronnin distinguished the BBC’s splicing of two parts of a Trump speech recorded some fifty minutes apart, which he called misleading, from the CBS Harris edit, which he treated as within the fair-representation rule.

The Institution: What CBS and 60 Minutes Say They Are

The network’s stated mission is empowerment through understanding, under standards it says it pioneered. CBS News’s publishing principles state: “At CBS News and Stations, we are dedicated to providing the highest quality journalism under standards we pioneered and continue to set today. Our mission is to empower Americans across all ages and demographics to understand the stories and issues that shape the world around us.” On politics, the same page promises to “hold your elected officials accountable through fair, unbiased and fact-based reporting.” The CBS Evening News announced five principles of its own on January 2, 2026, including “We work for you… Not our advertisers. Not politicians. Not corporate interests, including the corporate owners of CBS News,” and “We report on the world as it is… We’ll admit when we get it wrong.” The two other networks state their missions in their own documents. Disney’s journalistic-integrity statement commits ABC News to independence of editorial decision-making from the company’s commercial and political interests, to fairness and integrity, and to approaching the work “with rigor, to question thoroughly and skeptically, to analyze deeply.” ABC News president Almin Karamehmedovic told his staff in March 2025, in a memo reported by Deadline: “our mission is simple: straightforward journalism.” No standalone public NBC News handbook was found; its president, Noah Oppenheim, told Poynter in 2022: “Our mission is to illuminate and not advocate.”

The program’s founding premise, in its founder’s words, was storytelling. Don Hewitt created 60 Minutes, which premiered on September 24, 1968, as a CBS News production; it remains one. Hewitt’s documented framing of the secret was four words: “Tell me a story.” His 2001 memoir carries the title. He sought a program that “packaged reality as attractively as Hollywood packages fiction,” a television version of Life magazine mixing hard and soft news: “We could look into Marilyn Monroe’s closet so long as we looked into Robert Oppenheimer’s laboratory, too.” The first episode framed it as “a kind of a magazine for television.” Jeff Fager, a later executive producer, described the format in 2018 as combining Murrow’s See It Now and Person to Person, “hard-hitting journalism and entertaining profiles”, adding: “You start with fairness.” Hewitt’s own pitch criteria, as summarized in reference works, required that stories tell the audience something new, have a national dimension, “run their course in thirteen minutes or less, and have an up-front punch to garner an emotional response.” CBS’s current boilerplate calls the program “the most successful television broadcast in history,” offering “hard-hitting investigative reports, interviews, feature segments and profiles of people in the news,” regularly in Nielsen’s Top 10. Its published awards count, from its 2019–20 boilerplate, is 150 Emmy Awards, 25 Peabody Awards, and 20 duPont-Columbia awards, the most won by any single news program; no updated official count was found. Retired correspondent Steve Kroft said in June 2026: “It’s the highest-rated news program on television, and it has been that way for more than 50 years.”

The tension between the two halves of that founding formula has a documented history inside the institution. In his 1998 Gannett Lecture, Hewitt criticized the imitator newsmagazines his program’s success had spawned: “60 Minutes showed [executives] that a television newsmagazine can be worthwhile and profitable at the same time. The trouble is, they ignored the first half of that equation and zeroed in on the second”; and: “News is news and entertainment is entertainment, and crossing the line between them is often dishonest and always bad broadcasting.” The Wigand episode is the documented case of commercial pressure on the program. In November 1995, CBS aired its tobacco segment without the key interview with Brown & Williamson research chief Jeffrey Wigand, citing lawyers’ fear of a multibillion-dollar suit for inducing breach of his confidentiality agreement, while CBS’s owner was completing the $5.4 billion sale of the network to Westinghouse. The full interview aired on February 4, 1996. Fager, in 2016, called the decision to withhold it “a low point in our history,” and the story “probably the most important story that was ever reported by ‘60 Minutes.’” The program’s sibling in format, CBS Sunday Morning, is likewise a CBS News production, a newsmagazine aired since January 28, 1979, and conceived, per its reference record, as a broadcast version of a Sunday newspaper magazine supplement.

The Earlier Episode: “Inside CECOT,” December 2025

Eleven months before the Diawara segment, the same newsroom pulled a deportation segment hours before air, and the dispute became public in the correspondent’s own email. Sharyn Alfonsi’s report on Venezuelan men deported to El Salvador’s CECOT prison, alleging torture and abuse, was scheduled for December 21, 2025. CBS announced some two to three hours before broadcast that it would air in a future broadcast. Weiss, editor-in-chief since October 2025, said the decision was hers; at the December 22 editorial call she said the story did not “advance the ball,” that the New York Times and others had done similar work, and that it lacked a sufficient on-camera administration response. Her statement: “Holding stories that aren’t ready for whatever reason, that they lack sufficient context, say, or that they are missing critical voices, happens every day in every newsroom. I look forward to airing this important piece when it’s ready.” Alfonsi’s internal email, which leaked, said the story “was screened five times and cleared by both CBS attorneys and Standards and Practices. It is factually correct”; that interview requests had gone to the White House, the State Department, and DHS; that “government silence is a statement, not a VETO”; and that pulling it after every internal check had been met “is not an editorial decision, it is a political one.” On December 22, the episode as fed to the Canadian broadcaster Global TV appeared online and spread; CBS issued takedown notices. The segment aired on January 18, 2026, with its body unchanged and a new introduction and conclusion by Alfonsi incorporating written White House and DHS statements; Los Angeles Times reporting put the added material at about three and a half minutes, with no new interviews. Alfonsi’s contract later expired and was not renewed, in May 2026. In May and June 2026, Weiss replaced executive producer Tanya Simon with Bilton, and CBS parted with correspondents including Scott Pelley, who told the New York Times in June that CBS had bent to Trump and that Weiss “must go”; retired correspondent Kroft told Variety the same month that of Weiss, “everything she’s touched has turned to s***,” and that “60 Minutes, as the audience has known it, no longer exists.”

The Family Question: What the Law and the Studies Show

One premise of the broadcast’s framing, that deportation separates this father from his family, was not examined by any participant in the segment, the interview, or the dispute, and the desk found no participant or commentator in the record who raised the alternative. The documented law is as follows. A removal order runs against the removed individual only; removal proceedings are civil, not criminal, under INS v. Lopez-Mendoza, 468 U.S. 1032 (1984). United States citizens cannot themselves be deported; if citizen family members travel with a removed parent, they are in law leaving voluntarily, and parents may instead arrange care for them in the United States. The department’s own stated position in 2025 citizen-child cases is the same choice framing: Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said ICE asks parents whether they want their children removed with them or placed with a person the parent designates. A citizen departs and enters on a valid United States passport under 8 U.S.C. §1185(b), a documentation rule; relocation abroad does not strip citizenship, and the right to return is unaffected. No provision of United States law barring Diawara’s wife or children from leaving, or from later returning, was found. The broadcast stated that his wife and children are United States citizens; secondary coverage names his wife as Barbara Johnson, a registered nurse. No court filing stating the wife’s citizenship was found.

The other side of the question is also documented, in scholarship, in advocacy, and in dissent. Scholars use the term “de facto deportation” for emigration to accompany a deported family member. Hamilton, Masferrer, and co-authors, in the Russell Sage Foundation Journal of the Social Sciences in November 2025, estimated from Mexican census data that more than 11,000 people were de facto deported from the United States to Mexico between 2015 and 2020, including more than 6,000 United States citizens, almost 90 percent of them children. In survey data from 2015 to 2019, of deported Mexican parents separated from minor children, 39 percent planned to remain separated, 20 percent planned to reunify in the United States, and 11 percent planned to reunify in Mexico. Texas Civil Rights Project attorney Daniel Hatoum described the choice as presented to families: “Either take them with you or we’re going to separate them quickly from you”. Columbia Law professor Elora Mukherjee called the use of separation threats “calculated cruelty,” in Reuters reporting of December 11, 2025. In the case law, every federal appellate court to decide the question has rejected the claim that removing a parent unconstitutionally deports the citizen child: Perdido v. INS (5th Cir. 1969); Acosta v. Gaffney (3d Cir. 1977), reversing a district court that had held the infant’s de facto deportation “repugnant to the Constitution”, and holding that the parents make “the real choice of family residence” and that removal “merely postpone[s]” the child’s residence here; Ayala-Flores v. INS (6th Cir. 1981); and Oforji v. Ashcroft (7th Cir. 2003). The contrary position survives in Judge Harry Pregerson’s dissent in Memije v. Gonzales (9th Cir. 2007), speaking of “de facto expulsion from their native land,” and in Judge Richard Posner’s concurrence in Oforji, calling the children’s options “unappetizing choices… more excruciating the longer they remain here.” Congress provided a statutory channel instead of a constitutional bar: cancellation of removal under INA §240A(b) for “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” to a citizen family member, under the standard of Matter of Monreal-Aguinaga (BIA 2001), which weighs schooling, health, and country conditions under both the stay and relocate scenarios, and holds adverse country conditions alone insufficient.

For this family, the destination’s documented record runs in two directions. Mali’s Act No. 04-058 of November 25, 2004, as summarized in Mali’s own report to the United Nations Human Rights Office, provides at Article 13 that a temporary residence permit must be issued automatically to a foreigner married at least three months to a Malian national, on production of the marriage certificate, and to a foreign child under 18, or a dependent, of a Malian national; a visa of up to one year, renewable, accompanies the authorization. On that text, Diawara’s wife and both minor children fall within the automatic-permit categories once in Mali. Against that text stand two documented facts of 2026. The State Department’s Mali advisory, issued July 2, 2026, is Level 4: “Do not travel to Mali for any reason. Due to safety risks, family members cannot join U.S. government employees who work in Mali.” And as of January 1, 2026, Mali suspended visa issuance to United States citizens, with limited exceptions, in reciprocity for United States restrictions on Malians; whether spouses and children of Malian nationals are within the exceptions is not documented in any source the desk reviewed, and whether the children hold or could claim Malian nationality by descent is likewise not documented. The advisory is a safety assessment, not a legal bar; Article 13 governs residence after entry, not entry itself. The file carries both, and no participant in the dispute addressed either.

The Numbers in Their Past: Deportation by Administration

The comparison most often drawn rests on three different counts, and the desk prints the counts separately. Under the Department of Homeland Security’s usage, a removal is a compulsory movement out of the country under an order of removal; a return is a confirmed departure without such an order; an expulsion is the separate Title 42 public-health category used from March 2020 to May 11, 2023. The broad totals in circulation are counts of events, not of unique people; repeat crossers are counted repeatedly, particularly under Title 42. On the department’s Yearbook Table 39, the Obama administration’s fiscal years 2009–2016 sum to 3,062,466 removals and 2,186,427 returns, a combined 5,248,893. The label applied to that record was coined by an advocate: Janet Murguía, president of the National Council of La Raza, said on March 4, 2014, “For us, this president has been the deporter-in-chief.” For the Biden administration, the Migration Policy Institute counted about 1.1 million removals and returns from fiscal 2021 through February 2024, plus most of roughly 3 million Title 42 expulsions, for “nearly 4.4 million” repatriations by early 2024; summing Table 39 across the full term, fiscal 2021–2024, gives 2,032,300 removals and returns plus 2,754,120 expulsions, about 4.79 million. For the first Trump administration, Table 39 sums to about 1,196,000 removals and 599,000 returns across fiscal 2017–2020, about 1.795 million, rising to about 2.0 million with fiscal 2020’s 206,770 Title 42 expulsions; the Migration Policy Institute’s like-for-like count was about 1.5 million, and Syracuse University’s TRAC put ICE deportations below 932,000. Three definitions produce three numbers, all documented. For the current term, the Institute estimated about 980,000 deportations, removals and returns, from January 20, 2025, to July 31, 2026, consistent with the broadcast’s “nearly one million,” and noted that levels remain well below those routinely observed in the early 2000s; the department’s higher public claims, of three million or more departures including claimed self-deportations, are not adopted by the Institute.

The earlier episodes of mass removal carry their own definitional warnings. The Palmer Raids of November 7, 1919, and January 2, 1920, produced arrest estimates from 3,000 to 10,000 by source; 556 resident aliens were ultimately deported, after Acting Labor Secretary Louis Post cancelled some 2,000 warrants. For the Mexican Repatriation of the 1930s, Balderrama and Rodríguez, in Decade of Betrayal, estimated about one million people of Mexican descent driven out and “approximately 60 percent of those leaving were legal American citizens”; no official count exists, estimates in the literature run to two million, and California apologized by statute in 2005. For Operation Wetback in 1954, the Immigration and Naturalization Service claimed 1.1 to 1.3 million departures; Britannica records the claimed 1,100,000 against most estimates of about 300,000; the claimed figure covered the entire fiscal year ending June 30, 1954, although the operation began on June 10, included repeat arrests, and consisted, at more than 97 percent, of returns without removal orders. The enforcement-priority question has its own dated record: Secretary Jeh Johnson’s memo of November 20, 2014, set three priority tiers; Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas’s memo of September 30, 2021, re-imposed priorities; Executive Order 14159 of January 20, 2025, revoked the Biden-era guidance and, per the Heritage Foundation’s analysis of November 21, 2025, “mandated enforcement against all inadmissible and removable aliens.” The same Heritage analysis notes that ICE’s fiscal 2026 budget justification reintroduces priority language nearly identical to the rescinded Mayorkas memo.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The first side of this file’s triangle is the completeness of the released interview: CBS calls its 43 minutes extended, the department calls the same material full and uncut, and the interviewee says the conversation ran nearly an hour; no transcript exists by which to close the gap. The second side is the reason for the omission at the dispute’s center: the Post’s sources describe a producer’s agreement with a lawyer and an editor-in-chief kept in the dark, Status’s sources describe a deliberate safety decision with leadership at least partly informed, and the network itself has said nothing; the two accounts agree that the omission was deliberate and divide on who knew. The third side is the ground of the 2012 protection: the application Fox News published rests on sexual orientation, one analysis describes the withholding as resting on his conversion to Christianity, and the immigration court’s decision is not public, so which ground the judge credited cannot be filed. Around those three open points, the bearings that are single-valued are these: the segment aired on October 25 and said what the transcript records; an email of October 6 exists in two outlets’ reporting and CBS has not denied it; the released interview is 43 minutes and shorter than the interviewee’s account of the interview; and no court has adjudicated the allegation the segment omitted. The log proceeds.

The Companion Essay

The argument this file does not make is published by this paper’s publisher on his own program, The Chris Abraham Show, in his own voice, as “This Isn’t a Prison Planet.” The essay makes the case the segment’s participants did not raise: that a removed father’s wife and children may lawfully go with him, that the separation shown on screen is a choice the law leaves to the family, and that deportation is not imprisonment. It is the publisher’s argument, in the publisher’s voice, on the publisher’s own site. This paper prints no part of it and adopts none of it; the link stands so the reader can follow the argument the desk declined to carry, from the record above to the case the record supports in another man’s telling.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Twenty items.

Subjective
The broadcast transcript — “Destination: Nowhere,” 60 Minutes, October 25, 2026

The full text of the segment as aired: the 25,000 figure, the 63-person flight, the 17 of 19 onward returns, Diawara’s account of Ghana and Mali, the medication form and baggage tags, the narration stating that DHS questioned the credibility of his fear arguments, and the intercut Percival passages. The desk’s account of the broadcast rests on this text and on the CBS transcript as republished by WGHN.

Subjective
CBS — “Extended Interview: Homeland Security’s James Percival on third-country deportations,” 60 Minutes Overtime, October 26, 2026

The network’s own posting of the longer interview, titled extended, under its Overtime brand, with the network’s boilerplate describing the program as the most successful television broadcast in history. The podcast listing of the same material runs 43 minutes 12 seconds.

Subjective
National Review — Rich Lowry, “What 60 Minutes Didn’t Tell Viewers About Trump’s Deportations,” November 2, 2026

A video examination of the segment and the full interview, in five chapters: the report, the Diawara case, what the full interview reveals, the legal reality of third-country deportations, and the missing piece of the asylum claim. The video’s description says Lowry questions whether CBS gave viewers the complete story. No transcript was retrievable; the desk files the description and chapters only.

Subjective
Daily Caller — CBS posted the interview; DHS calls the edit selective, October 27–28, 2026

The Caller’s account of the release sequence and of the exchanges the broadcast did not carry, including the persecution challenge and the statistics exchange, with the White House spokeswoman’s statement that the program engaged in selective editing and peddled false sob stories.

Subjective
Fox News — the 2009 application and the October 6 email, October 29, 2026

Fox’s report that it obtained Diawara’s asylum application quoting persecution on the ground of his sexual orientation, and that DHS emailed CBS about the claim on October 6, 2026, nineteen days before the broadcast; the same report records that CBS News declined to comment.

Subjective
New York Post — Weiss and Bilton “weren’t briefed,” October 30, 2026

The Post’s account, from its sources, of a deliberate omission made to protect the subject, a producer’s agreement with his lawyer, an editor-in-chief who went ballistic, a closed-door meeting on October 29, and discipline under consideration; the Post also records that the October 6 email did not, per a network source, explicitly allege fraud, and that CBS declined to comment.

Subjective
Status News — “The ‘60’ Blame Game,” November 6, 2026

Status’s account of a deliberate, safety-based omission by the reporting team, of leadership at least partially informed, and of staff accusing the brass of throwing its journalists under the bus. The article is paywalled; the desk’s account rests on attributed summaries of it.

Subjective
Human Rights Watch — the third-country count from ICE data, October 2026

The organization’s analysis of ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project: 27,943 third-country deportations from January 20, 2025, to August 5, 2026, against 8,563 in the comparable prior period, and 46,563 third-country removal orders through August 31, 2026.

Subjective
First Circuit — opinion in D.V.D. v. DHS, September 18, 2026

The appeals court’s opinion affirming in large part the judgment against the 2025 third-country guidance: removal first to designated or home countries, effective notice of the specified third country, and a meaningful opportunity to contest on reasonable-fear grounds. The case is now before the Supreme Court as DHS v. D.V.D., argued December 9, 2026.

Subjective
Supreme Court — stay order in D.V.D. v. DHS, June 23, 2025

The Court’s unsigned order staying the injunction against third-country removals, over the dissent of Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson, allowing the removals to proceed while the litigation continues.

Subjective
Immigration Policy Tracking Project — the guidance and the Ghana arrangement

The tracker’s file on the February and March 2025 guidance and on the receiving-country arrangements, including Ghana’s acceptance of West African nationals and the reports of onward returns from the September 2025 cohort.

Subjective
News Central TV — President Mahama on the Ghana arrangement, September 11, 2025

Ghana’s president’s own account: West African nationals only, under the ECOWAS free-movement protocol, the first fourteen facilitated onward, the Nigerians by bus, and no money exchanged.

Subjective
Society of Professional Journalists — Code of Ethics

The profession’s code, revised in 2014: provide context, take special care not to misrepresent or oversimplify, never deliberately distort facts or context, and be accountable and transparent; the code states of itself that it is not a set of rules and is not legally enforceable.

Subjective
Ethics and Journalism — Joe Peyronnin on what the BBC did wrong and CBS didn’t, November 17, 2025

A forty-year television news executive’s statement of the practitioner’s test: an edit must fairly and accurately represent what the subject said and the point she was making, and may not change or potentially change the meaning or mislead the viewer; the BBC’s splice of a Trump speech is his example of the line crossed, the CBS Harris edit his example of the line kept.

Subjective
Associated Press via the First Amendment Center — the Paramount settlement, July 2, 2025

The wire’s account of the $16 million settlement of the President’s suit over the Harris interview, paid to his future presidential library and fees, with no apology, and with the program’s agreement to release transcripts of future interviews with presidential candidates.

Subjective
Associated Press via the First Amendment Center — the Face the Nation policy change, September 8, 2025

The wire’s account of CBS’s sequence in the Noem matter: the edit said to have met all CBS News standards, then the program’s move to live or live-to-tape interviews only, for greater transparency, with full transcripts and unedited video posted online.

Subjective
CBS News — publishing principles

The network’s own statement of its mission, to empower Americans to understand the stories and issues that shape the world around us, under standards it says it pioneered, with fair, unbiased, and fact-based reporting and accountability for elected officials.

Subjective
Britannica — Don Hewitt

The reference account of the program’s founder: “Tell me a story”; reality packaged as attractively as Hollywood packages fiction; Marilyn Monroe’s closet and Robert Oppenheimer’s laboratory; and the founder’s criteria, thirteen minutes or less with an up-front punch to garner an emotional response.

Subjective
Russell Sage Foundation Journal — “de facto deportation,” November 2025

The scholars’ estimate, from Mexican census data, of more than 11,000 people de facto deported to Mexico from 2015 to 2020, more than 6,000 of them United States citizens, almost 90 percent of them children, with the survey record of how separated families planned to reunify.

Subjective
U.S. Department of State — Mali travel advisory

The department’s Level 4 advisory: do not travel to Mali for any reason; family members cannot join United States government employees who work in Mali; and, as of January 1, 2026, Mali’s suspension of visa issuance to United States citizens, with limited exceptions.

item.title: Lagos Holds the Week, Sydney Opens Its Museum, and Sunday Is Diwali
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The Saturday Culture Feature for November 7, 2026: Lagos held three culture events in one week — Lagos Fashion Week from October 28 to November 1, and ART X Lagos and CANEX WKND both from November 5 to 8 — Sydney opened Powerhouse Parramatta on November 7 with 18,000 square metres across seven levels and a 23-day festival, Jakarta closed its SEA Waves fashion programme on November 1, Mexico City prepares two November openings, Dublin's book festival runs to November 8, Alotau's Kenu and Kundu Festival runs November 6 to 8, and Diwali's main day is Sunday, November 8. Collected at 0410.
item.content:encoded:
Weekend Features — Saturday Culture

Objective

Lagos Holds the Week, Sydney Opens Its Museum, and Sunday Is Diwali

One city held the week. Lagos closed a fashion week on November 1 and opened an art fair and a creative-industries weekend on November 5, all three running on heritage as material and on the same unanswered question: what was sold, and what was financed. On the same Saturday, Sydney opened a $915 million museum in Parramatta, Dublin entered the last two days of its twentieth book festival, Alotau raced its canoes, and India entered the middle days of Diwali, whose main day is Sunday. Mexico City and Singapore hold the month's later openings. The desk files the week in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. The first Saturday Culture Feature of this paper, filed ahead of the day's watches under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. International by house rule: no country's framework is applied to another country's culture. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief

The week's cultural centre, measured by events in one place in one week, was Lagos. Lagos Fashion Week ran from October 28 to November 1 with more than 50 labels. ART X Lagos, in its 11th edition, and CANEX WKND both run from November 5 to 8, in the same city, in the same four days. No other city in the week's file holds three events of that scale at once. Sydney supplies the week's single largest opening: Powerhouse Parramatta, 18,000 square metres across seven levels, opens today, November 7, with a festival of more than 170 events to November 29. The calendar behind those two facts is full and dated: Dublin Book Festival, November 4 to 8, more than 120 events in its 20th year; the Kenu and Kundu Festival at Alotau, November 6 to 8; Diwali, November 6 to 11, main day Sunday, November 8; the Centre Pompidou exhibition at Mexico City's Palacio de Bellas Artes from November 12 or 13; the São Paulo Bienal's travelling exhibition at the Museo Tamayo from November 15; and More than Human at Singapore's ArtScience Museum from November 28. Jakarta's week is already complete: SEA Waves at Jakarta Fashion Week closed on November 1.

Lagos: A Fashion Week, an Art Fair, and a Deal Room in One City in Eleven Days

Lagos Fashion Week treated heritage as material, and its business programme treated that material as an industry. The week's theme was “CRAFTED: Heritage. Innovation. Circular Futures,” in the fullest recap filed below. Akwete, Aso Oke, Adire, Kente, barkcloth, cowrie details and raffia appeared across the collections, worked through deconstruction, sheer fabrics, hand-printing and textile manipulation; fringe appeared in nearly half of the collections on the second day, which carried 19 shows. A second account names the same materials in the collections of Hertunba, Khadiju, Kilentar and Eki Kere, and records Ghanaian label Christie Brown's return after eight years. The schedule was continental, not national: labels from Ghana, Morocco, Benin, Uganda, Angola and South Africa stood on it beside the Nigerian houses. Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu walked for designer Ugo Monye, in both accounts.

The business sessions named the same gaps in the same order, and the recap records them plainly. Panels across four days covered who benefits from artisans' knowledge, financing fitted to fashion, overproduction and the protection of original designs, and what a multi-brand retailer requires from a label: standardised line sheets, reliable and scalable production, and clearly defined wholesale margins. The founder's position, given during the week, is that African fashion has an infrastructure problem, not a creativity problem; the recap lists the recurring infrastructure topics as unreliable electricity, limited manufacturing capacity, workforce development and design protection. Lagos Fashion Week has published no buyer count and no sales figure for 2026. That absence is a fact of the record, and the desk files it as one.

ART X Lagos opened on November 5 for its 11th edition, and its centre is a potter who died in 1984. The fair, founded in 2016, brings 15 international galleries to the Federal Palace on Victoria Island under the banner “A New Chapter, A New Decade,” in the fair account filed below. Its ICON exhibition, Ladi Kwali: Beyond the Vessel, curated by Dr. Jareh Das, presents Kwali's ceramics from the National Museum, Onikan, with private loans, photographs and archival recordings. Kwali, whose image appeared on the 20 Naira banknote, joined the Pottery Training Centre at Suleja in 1954 as its first female student and combined Gwari hand-coiling with wheel-throwing and high-temperature stoneware firing; her work was shown in London and at the Smithsonian. The fair pairs the retrospective with a masterclass for ten emerging artists, three of whom will each receive a ₦1,500,000 grant for studio production, and with live music, cinema and talks running beside the gallery floor to November 8.

CANEX WKND, running in the same days across the city, is the week's third Lagos event and its stated purpose is conversion. It spans fashion, film, music, literature, visual arts, gastronomy and sport at the Wole Soyinka Centre, with a Deal Room from November 5 to 7 where creative projects pitch directly to financiers, a fashion show and awards night on November 6, and a marketplace open all four days. Afreximbank has committed $2 billion to Africa's creative industries for 2024 to 2027. Its 2024 edition in Algiers was reported as having facilitated and agreed more than $540 million in deals among nearly 4,000 participants from 81 countries; the recap that carries that figure states that it comes from the organiser's own results, that “deals” is not the same as cash, and that no sector breakdown has been published. The three Lagos events therefore stand in one file with one open measurement: the fashion week published looks and panels and no sales count, the art fair published its programme and its grants, and the deal weekend's Lagos results have not been announced. What Lagos produced this week is counted in events, labels, galleries and days. What it produced in orders will be known only if the organisers publish it.

Sydney: A Museum Opens in Parramatta, Not in the Centre

Powerhouse Parramatta opens today, and its address is the fact. The museum stands at 34 Phillip Street in Parramatta, in Western Sydney, on Burramattagal and Dharug Country, in the opening account filed below. It contains 18,000 square metres of public and exhibition space across seven levels on the river, built around a steel exoskeleton, with wall sections finished in render made from 600,000 locally sourced crushed oyster shells. Four of its five opening exhibitions are free; visitors under 16 enter all five free; and its opening festival runs 23 days, to November 29, with more than 170 performances, talks and workshops.

Its centrepiece looks up. Task Eternal, on aviation and space, carries four Leonardo da Vinci drawings travelled from Milan, loans from the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum including an Apollo command module test model, a Rolls-Royce engine that powered Qantas Boeing 747-338 aircraft, a boomerang collected near Parramatta in the early 19th century on loan from the British Museum, and James Turrell's Shangri La (Over The Hump). Es Devlin's The Turning, her first major Australian exhibition, runs in five installations; outside, her Come Home Again carries 244 hand-drawn depictions of vulnerable and endangered species from New South Wales. A further exhibition, Overflow, takes First Nations relationships with water and Country as its subject, and The Mall takes the shopping centre itself as a cultural institution, with material from the David Jones archives. The account records controversy over the museum's $915 million cost beside its description of the building, and files both.

Jakarta: Eleven Nations in One Weave

Jakarta Fashion Week closed on November 1, and its SEA Waves programme was built as regional diplomacy in cloth. Through SEA Waves, Indonesia connected eleven Southeast Asian nations through fashion, textiles and shared heritage, under the theme “City of New Lights,” in the ministry's account filed below. The Wave of Weave Installation at the National Museum of Indonesia, open to January 8, 2027, presents 20 textile pieces from ten nations and five kebaya sets from Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The SEA Fashion Parade on November 1 brought designers from six countries — Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Cambodia and Vietnam — to two runway shows at Pondok Indah Mall 3. The ministry's stated purpose, in its official's words, is that cultural heritage inspires contemporary creativity and strengthens Jakarta's appeal as a regional hub for fashion and culture.

Mexico City: Two Openings, One Week Apart

Mexico City holds the month's densest gallery calendar after Lagos. At the Palacio de Bellas Artes, “Las formas de la energía” brings works from the Centre Pompidou's collections under the single thread of energy — light, matter and illusions of movement — with Schöffer's Lux 1 from 1957, Fontana's Concetto spaziale from 1963 and Vasarely's Meh (2) from 1967–1968 among the announced works, presented as part of the bicentenary of Franco-Mexican diplomatic relations, in the exhibition account filed below. At the Museo Tamayo, the travelling exhibition of the 36th Bienal de São Paulo, Not All Travellers Walk Roads — Of Humanity as Practice, opens on November 14 and runs from November 15 to February 7, 2027, with works by 26 artists; it is the first time the Bienal's travelling programme has come to Mexico, and the last stop of this edition's tour, in the Bienal's own notice filed below. The city then closes the month's music calendar with Corona Capital at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez from November 20 to 22.

The Calendar Around Them: Alotau, Dublin, Diwali, Singapore

Alotau's festival is the week's oldest practice in its newest form. The Kenu and Kundu Festival runs from November 6 to 8 at Alotau, capital of Milne Bay Province, Papua New Guinea, with traditional songs, singsing dances, arts-and-craft displays, kundu drums and long kenu canoes raced across Milne Bay, built with knowledge passed down through generations; the festival itself was founded in 2003, in the November calendar filed below. The same calendar sets the weeks ahead: Pirates Week in the Cayman Islands from November 11 to 15, Vancouver's Eastside Culture Crawl, in its 30th year with over 500 artists opening studios, from November 19 to 22, and Strawberry Fields in New South Wales from November 20 to 22.

Dublin's book festival is in its last two days, and its programme is a census of Irish writing. Dublin Book Festival runs from November 4 to 8 in its 20th anniversary year, with more than 120 events across the city — talks, launches, walking tours, workshops and family events — and a line-up carrying Mary Robinson, Roddy Doyle, Marian Keyes, Anne Enright, Sebastian Barry, Louise Kennedy and Kevin Barry, in the festival account filed below. On Sunday, its closing day, Roddy Doyle and Anne Enright converse together, and Jodi Picoult appears on her new novel, Hollow Bones.

Diwali's main day is Sunday, and Saturday is its middle. The festival runs from November 6 to 11 — Dhanteras on Friday, Choti Diwali today, the main day on Sunday, November 8, Govardhan Puja on Monday or Tuesday by regional calendar, and Bhai Dooj on Wednesday or Tuesday — observed across Hindu, Jain, Sikh and some Buddhist communities, with homes illuminated by oil lamps and candles and sweets and gifts exchanged, in the festival guide filed below, whose dates were checked on November 4. It is the only item in this feature observed in homes in every time zone the paper reaches, and the only one whose venue is not a venue.

Singapore closes the month. More than Human: Making With the Living World opens at ArtScience Museum on November 28 and runs to May 16, 2027, in its Asian debut, with over 140 works by nearly 55 artists, designers, architects, researchers and communities; developed by the Design Museum, London, its Singapore edition adds 25 works foregrounding perspectives from Asia, in the exhibition account filed below. A London exhibition arriving in Singapore enlarged, a Paris collection arriving in Mexico City, a São Paulo biennial arriving at the Tamayo, and Milan drawings arriving in Parramatta: the month's pattern, stated once, is circulation — collections travelling to the cities, and the cities adding their own work to what arrives.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Mexico City's opening date: 12 November 2026 in one listing for the Centre Pompidou exhibition, 13 November in the Centre Pompidou's own listing — a one-day disagreement, printed in the clipping below, with confirmation advised before visiting. Second, Lagos's money: a $2 billion commitment over four years and a reported $540 million in deals at Algiers in 2024 on one bearing, both organiser-carried figures; no buyer count, no sales figure and no sector breakdown on the second; and no Lagos 2026 result of any kind yet on the third. The events are counted; the commerce is not, yet. Third, Diwali's later days: Govardhan Puja on November 9 or 10 and Bhai Dooj on November 11 or 10, varying by regional calendar in the guide's own statement — a variation of observance, not an error. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: Lagos Fashion Week ran October 28 to November 1 with more than 50 labels; ART X Lagos and CANEX WKND both run November 5 to 8; Powerhouse Parramatta opens today with 18,000 square metres and more than 170 festival events; Dublin Book Festival closes Sunday after more than 120 events; Diwali's main day is Sunday, November 8; and Mexico City and Singapore hold openings on November 12 or 13, November 15 and November 28. The log proceeds to Saturday's watches.

The Clippings Filed With This Feature

Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective — a source with a position, printed because it is useful — and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. Eleven items.

Subjective
Gazelle Africa — ART X Lagos enters its second decade

Lagos, November 7: ART X Lagos returns from November 5 to 8, 2026, for its 11th edition under the banner “A New Chapter, A New Decade,” at the Federal Palace on Victoria Island; founded in 2016 by Tokini Peterside-Schwebig, the fair brings 15 international galleries from across Africa and its diaspora; its ART X ICON exhibition, Ladi Kwali: Beyond the Vessel, curated by Dr. Jareh Das, presents the Nigerian potter's ceramics from the National Museum, Onikan, with private loans, historical photographs and archival recordings; a masterclass for ten emerging artists follows, with three grants of ₦1,500,000 each for studio production; and the programme carries ART X Live!, ART X Cinema and ART X Talks alongside the gallery floor.

Subjective
The Creative Brief Africa — Lagos Fashion Week, and what CANEX is built to do next

Lagos, November 3: Lagos Fashion Week ran from October 28 to November 1 under the theme “CRAFTED: Heritage. Innovation. Circular Futures,” with more than 50 labels announced by organisers Style House Files, 19 shows on its second day, and an offsite finale on November 1 with Lisa Folawiyo, Andrea Iyamah, Emmy Kasbit and IAMISIGO named on the line-up; Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu walked the runway for menswear designer Ugo Monye; CANEX WKND, the flagship weekend of Afreximbank's Creative Africa Nexus, runs from November 5 to 8 at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, spanning fashion, film, music, literature, visual arts, gastronomy and sport, with a Deal Room from November 5 to 7 and a fashion show and awards night on November 6; Afreximbank has committed $2 billion to Africa's creative industries for 2024 to 2027; the 2024 edition in Algiers was reported as having facilitated and agreed more than $540 million in deals, with nearly 4,000 participants from 81 countries; and Lagos Fashion Week has published no buyer or sales numbers for 2026 so far.

Subjective
YNaija — seven things that stood out at Lagos Fashion Week 2026

Lagos, November 2: Lagos Fashion Week's runway carried influencers and reality television personalities, including Hilda Baci and Temi Nkem in Lush's presentation; Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu returned to the runway for designer Ugo Monye, his second appearance after 2022; Sevon Dejana's collection drew widespread online attention; designers and labels including Hertunba, Khadiju, Kilentar and Eki Kere worked in raffia, cowries, aso-oke and adire; Heineken introduced an Innovation Studio on fashion and technology; Ghanaian label Christie Brown returned after an eight-year absence; and off-site presentations by Orange Culture, Sisiano and Andrea Iyamah moved shows beyond the main runway space.

Subjective
PR Newswire, carrying the Ministry of Tourism of the Republic of Indonesia — SEA Waves at Jakarta Fashion Week

Jakarta, November 2: SEA Waves at the 18th Jakarta Fashion Week, running from October 26 to November 1, 2026, under the theme “City of New Lights,” connects eleven Southeast Asian nations through fashion, textiles and shared heritage; its Wave of Weave Installation at the National Museum of Indonesia, open to January 8, 2027, presents 20 textile pieces from ten nations and five curated kebaya sets from Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, the kebaya described as UNESCO-recognised Intangible Cultural Heritage; and its SEA Fashion Parade on November 1 at Pondok Indah Mall 3 brought together designers from Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Cambodia and Vietnam in two runway shows.

Subjective
The AU Review — inside Powerhouse Parramatta, Sydney's $915 million museum

Sydney, November 6: Powerhouse Parramatta opens on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at 34 Phillip Street, Parramatta, with 18,000 square metres of public and exhibition space across seven levels on the Parramatta River, on Burramattagal and Dharug Country; its opening festival runs from November 7 to 29 with more than 170 events; four of its five opening exhibitions are free and visitors under 16 enter all five free; its centrepiece, Task Eternal, on aviation and space, carries four Leonardo da Vinci drawings travelled from Milan and loans from the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum including an Apollo command module test model, with James Turrell's Shangri La (Over The Hump) installed above; Es Devlin's The Turning is her first major Australian exhibition, in five installations, and her outdoor sculpture Come Home Again carries 244 hand-drawn depictions of vulnerable and endangered species from New South Wales; and sections of the building's walls are finished in render made from 600,000 locally sourced crushed oyster shells.

Subjective
Artprice News — the Centre Pompidou in Mexico City, November 2026

Mexico City, November 5: the Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes hosts “Las formas de la energía. Obras emblemáticas del Centre Pompidou” from November 2026, presented as part of the bicentenary of Franco-Mexican diplomatic relations; the exhibition uses energy as a common thread through 20th-century experiments in light, matter and illusions of movement, with announced works including Nicolas Schöffer's Lux 1 from 1957, Lucio Fontana's Concetto spaziale, La fine di Dio from 1963, and Victor Vasarely's Meh (2), also titled Abeille, from 1967–1968; the dates are given as 12 November 2026 to 28 February 2027 in one listing and 13 November 2026 to 27 February 2027 in the Centre Pompidou's listing, with confirmation advised before visiting; and the museum's regular hours are Tuesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed Mondays.

Subjective
Fundação Bienal de São Paulo — the 36th Bienal travelling exhibition reaches Mexico City

Mexico City: the final stage of the travelling exhibition programme for the 36th Bienal de São Paulo, Not All Travellers Walk Roads — Of Humanity as Practice, opens at the Museo Tamayo with an opening on November 14, 2026, and runs to the public from November 15, 2026, to February 7, 2027, curated by Anna Roberta Goetz; it is the first time the Bienal de São Paulo's travelling programme has come to Mexico and the final stop of this edition's travelling programme; and the exhibition brings together works by 26 artists, among them Akinbode Akinbiyi, Alberto Pitta, Aline Baiana, Behjat Sadr, Ernest Cole, Forensic Architecture/Forensis, Forugh Farrokhzad, Imran Mir, Korakrit Arunanondchai, Mohamed Melehi, Myrlande Constant and Sharon Hayes.

Subjective
American Express Essentials — the global calendar for November

November 3: the Kenu and Kundu Festival at Alotau, Papua New Guinea, runs from November 6 to 8, 2026, with live music, traditional dancing, arts-and-craft displays and dramatic performances, handcrafted kundu drums and kenu canoes raced across Milne Bay, the festival founded in 2003; Pirates Week Festival at Georgetown, Cayman Islands, runs from November 11 to 15 for the 49th time; Vancouver's Eastside Culture Crawl runs from November 19 to 22, its 30th anniversary, with over 500 artists, designers and craftspeople opening studios; Strawberry Fields at Tocumwal, New South Wales, runs from November 20 to 22; and Corona Capital at Mexico City's Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez runs from November 20 to 22, with Twenty One Pilots, Gorillaz, The Strokes, The Offspring and The xx named in the line-up.

Subjective
Couchsurfing Blog — six fall and winter festivals worth travelling for

November 4, dates checked November 4, 2026: Diwali, in India and cities worldwide, has its main day on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and runs from November 6 to 11 — Dhanteras on November 6, Choti Diwali on November 7, Govardhan Puja on November 9 or 10 depending on the regional calendar, and Bhai Dooj on November 11 or 10; Diwali is described as the Hindu festival of lights, celebrating the triumph of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance, observed over five days across Hindu, Jain, Sikh and some Buddhist communities, with homes illuminated by oil lamps and candles and sweets and gifts exchanged; Loy Krathong and Yi Peng in Thailand follow on November 24, with Chiang Mai's Yi Peng lantern events expected around November 24 to 25; and the list continues to Harbin, Sapporo, Lunar New Year and Rio Carnival in the new year.

Subjective
Totally Dublin — Dublin Book Festival returns for its 20th anniversary

Dublin: Dublin Book Festival marks its 20th anniversary from November 4 to 8, 2026, with more than 120 events — talks, performances, book launches, walking tours, workshops and family events across the city; the line-up includes Mary Robinson, Roddy Doyle, Marian Keyes, Anne Enright, Sebastian Barry, Louise Kennedy and Kevin Barry; the festival opens on November 4 with The Irish Times Women's Podcast Book Club; Roddy Doyle and Anne Enright, two of Ireland's Booker Prize winners, converse with Martin Doyle on November 8; and Marian Keyes discusses the politics of women's commercial fiction, while Jodi Picoult appears in conversation with Miriam O'Callaghan about her new novel, Hollow Bones.

Subjective
The New Age Parents — More than Human at ArtScience Museum, Singapore

Singapore, November 2: More than Human: Making With the Living World opens at ArtScience Museum on November 28, 2026, and runs to May 16, 2027, in its Asian debut; originally developed by the Design Museum, London, in collaboration with Future Observatory, the exhibition presents over 140 artworks, projects, immersive installations and interactive experiences by nearly 55 artists, designers, architects, researchers and communities; the Singapore edition has been expanded with 25 works co-curated by ArtScience Museum and supported by DesignSingapore Council, foregrounding perspectives from Asia, including regional cultural traditions and wisdom; and tickets have been on sale from October 28 at Marina Bay Sands box offices and online.

item.title: Explosions Again on Qeshm, a President Removed in Asunción, and the Count Still Waits
item.dc:creator: Eunice
item.description: The overnight file for Saturday, November 7, 2026: Iranian media reported two missiles striking Qeshm Island early Saturday and Tehran claimed a second American drone downed in two days while Central Command called the situation relatively calm and Qatar said the mediation had not failed, Paraguay's Senate removed President Peña over the Ueno Bank collapse and Vice President Alliana took the oath, Beijing's confirmation of talks on a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting at Shenzhen stood as the week's largest diplomatic fact, and the Senate count did not move — Mississippi at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637. Collected at 0400.
item.content:encoded:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Explosions Again on Qeshm, a President Removed in Asunción, and the Count Still Waits

The night file, while Washington slept: the war reported itself again from Qeshm Island — two projectiles in the Suza area, a drone claimed down, no American confirmation of the specific impacts and no damage assessment from Tehran — and the mediation reported itself intact from Doha, where Qatar said reports of its failure were false. South America supplied the night’s one completed act: Paraguay’s Senate removed its president and swore in his successor. The count in Mississippi and Alaska did not move. Saturday opens with the markets closed and one scheduled item, Berkshire Hathaway’s third-quarter report at 0800 ET.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Saturday, November 7, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 13, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the president’s confirmation of Friday evening’s limited strike. The reports filed here are the night’s reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Friday’s facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

Nothing the week left open was closed in the night, and one presidency was. The open file at midnight — the larger Iran decision, the two Senate races, the leadership questions — stands open at 0400 in the same figures. What the night added is a second round of reports from Qeshm Island, a Qatari statement that the mediation between Washington and Tehran has not failed, and the first full accounts of Friday’s completed act in Asunción, where Paraguay’s Senate removed President Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, placed him under house arrest, and swore in Vice President Pedro Alliana to finish the term to August 2028. Beijing’s confirmation that talks are under way on a three-way meeting of Presidents Xi, Trump, and Putin at Shenzhen on November 18 and 19 stands beside them. The president, in Florida, added a sentence of his own: Russia and Ukraine, he said, want to settle, for the first time. The desk files the night in that order.

Qeshm Again: Two Projectiles Reported, a Drone Claimed, No Confirmation of the Impacts

Iranian media reported a second night of explosions on Qeshm Island, and no government has confirmed what the explosions were. Reuters’ Cairo file, filed below, reports that Tasnim said early Saturday that initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage, and that IRNA had earlier reported local witnesses saying two projectiles struck the Suza area after the sound of an aircraft was heard. A second account adds that state television reported two explosions in the Souza area late Friday with no casualties, that Fars reported explosions in Qeshm and in Bandar Khamir, and that none of the accounts has been independently confirmed and there was no immediate American confirmation of a new strike. A third file records the American position in one sentence: the United States military has not commented on the report. The reports arrive twelve hours after the president confirmed Friday evening’s limited strike on the same island, and the fullest account states plainly that the precise relationship between the reported impacts and the confirmed operation has not been independently established. That sentence stands at 0400.

Tehran’s second claim of the night is a drone, and it is the second in two days. The Iranian Army announced that its integrated air defense network destroyed an American MQ-9 Reaper drone over Qeshm, in the army’s account as carried in Tehran’s file, timed 0052 GMT on Saturday. A second file pairs it with Friday’s claim, in which the Revolutionary Guards said their air defenses destroyed an American MQ-1 drone over the same island. The account of the president’s remarks carries the only American sentence in the drone file: Central Command said the situation was “relatively calm” and declined further comment. The United States has not confirmed either claim, and no wreckage or imagery allowing independent verification appears in any file the desk took in.

The Mediation: Qatar Says the Failure Reports Are False

The diplomatic track produced the night’s clearest official sentence, and it came from the mediator. Qatar’s International Media Office on Saturday denied circulating reports that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement to end their war, describing the allegations as false and misleading, in the Reuters file above and in the fuller statement carried in the Doha file. The statement’s own words are that the prime minister’s remarks “have been deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability in our region,” and that the prime minister “stated today that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal.” Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with Washington and Tehran, the statement adds. The prime minister said at Oxford on Friday that mediation remains active and the crisis “cannot be left unresolved,” per the war file, which also carries the mediators’ reported two-day bridge proposal — the same draft the desk filed on Thursday. No agreement was announced in the night, by any side. What changed is the record about the talks themselves: reports that they had failed are denied, by name, by the office running them.

Asunción: A President Removed, a Successor Sworn In

Paraguay completed in one day the removal the night’s other capitals only discussed. The Senate on Friday removed President Santiago Peña for misconduct in office and poor performance of his duties, and authorities placed him under house arrest an hour later, in the Associated Press account filed below. Vice President Pedro Alliana took the oath to finish a term closing in August 2028. The vote is carried as 44 to nothing among the senators in attendance in the wire’s account, and as 44 to 1 in the account carrying CNN’s reporting and in a second full account; the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat. The lower house had voted 78 to nothing to impeach on Thursday. Mr. Peña had offered his resignation on Thursday and Congress refused it; the impeachment, unlike a resignation, stripped his immunity and the lifetime Senate seat a former president would otherwise hold. He is the second Paraguayan president forced out by impeachment since 1989. He denies wrongdoing.

The cause on the record is a bank, and its figures are the file’s fixed points. Regulators seized the digital lender ueno on November 3 after its solvency fell under half the required level. The bank served roughly 3 million customers — about 60 percent of the country’s adults — and held as much as $850 million in public money, $380 million of it from the state pension and health fund. Mr. Peña held shares in ueno’s holding company until last year, and the central bank chief he installed, Carlos Carvallo, had run the lender until 2023; the arrest order covered Mr. Carvallo as well. Prosecutors cited suspected breach of trust, with charges undetermined and possibly extending to influence peddling; the attorney general has opened three criminal cases. Mr. Peña must report to prosecutors on Saturday morning. The deposit guarantee covers about $38,000 per depositor, 97 percent of holders are estimated fully within it, and banking law requires payment within 15 days — the figures by which the new government will first be measured, beginning today.

Shenzhen and Ukraine: A Three-Way Meeting Under Discussion, a Settlement Claimed Near

Beijing has confirmed, in its own words, that a meeting of the three heads of state is under discussion. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a briefing in Beijing this week that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” in the fullest account of the confirmation filed below — Beijing’s first public confirmation, with no final decision announced. The expected venue is the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. The idea is reported to have originated with Moscow: President Putin proposed a trilateral format to President Trump in a phone call on October 9, aimed at ending the war in Ukraine; Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on November 3 that work was under way to organise such a meeting, per the Ukraine war briefing. The three leaders have never held a joint meeting. The reported priorities do not describe the same meeting: Mr. Putin’s is Ukraine, without Kyiv at the table; the president’s, stated publicly, is nuclear arms control; and the analysts in both accounts expect the gathering to amount, in substance, to a photograph. Whether Mr. Putin attends has not been announced. The confirmation itself — discussions, in the open, eleven days before the summit — is the fact.

The president added his own bearing on Ukraine in the night, from Florida. Asked whether it feels different now, he said: “It does. They want to settle. Russia and Ukraine for the first time, I think, want to settle,” and “I think it’s going to be a very big settlement. I think it’s going to involve all of Europe,” in the transcript file filed below, which also records meetings by phone on Saturday and in person on Monday and Tuesday — the Abu Dhabi talks. The Reuters account of the same remarks records the limits beside the claim: substantial differences remain over territory and security guarantees. Europe’s answer arrived on Friday and stands: European leaders dismissed the drive for a new security agreement negotiated over Ukraine, and the European Union’s foreign policy chief said any agreement, to be implemented, will require the European Union to be part of it, per the Irish Times account in the Europe file. At 0400 the Ukraine file holds three positions, each in its owner’s words: Washington says both sides want to settle; Europe says no settlement architecture without Europe; and Moscow’s proposed room for the question is Shenzhen, with Kyiv not in it.

The Count at 0400: No Movement, One New Lawsuit

Neither Senate race moved in the night, and the wire’s figures at 0400 are Friday’s figures. In Mississippi the Associated Press file stands at 467,930 votes for the Democrat, Scott Colom, and 465,356 for the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith — a lead of 2,574, with all 1,736 precincts reporting, an estimated 96.92 percent of the vote in, and the race too early to call, per the wire’s Mississippi page. The ballots that can still move it are the ones the procedure names: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day arriving by Tuesday, November 10, affidavit ballots resolved by the same date, and county certification by November 13, in a state with no recount provision. In Alaska the file stands where it has stood since Wednesday: the Democrat, Mary Peltola, at 102,962 and the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, at 102,325 — a lead of 637 at 73.95 percent of precincts reporting, too early to call, per the wire’s Alaska page. The next count is expected Tuesday and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18.

The night’s one new count item is a filing, not a figure. Ms. Peltola’s campaign sued the Alaska Division of Elections on Friday, seeking the immediate release of records identifying absentee ballots rejected in the November 3 election and the reasons for each rejection, in the account of the suit filed below. The campaign says it requested the records on October 27 and again on November 4 under the Public Records Act, received no response, and was later denied immediate access; the state says the records are confidential preliminary data. It is the first major legal filing in the Alaska contest. Saturday is a counting day in neither state. The count speaks next on Tuesday, in both.

Saturday Opens: Closed Markets, Settled Oil, One Report Due

The markets are closed on Saturday, and the week’s last figures are the ones the Midnight Watch filed. Friday’s European closes stand final in the closing account filed below: Britain’s FTSE 100 down 1.01 percent at 10,673.94, France’s CAC 40 down 0.81 percent at 8,139.00, and Germany’s DAX down 1.92 percent at 25,820.36 — Europe down on the day New York’s technology shares rose, and still ahead on the year. Oil’s Friday settlement is carried at $98.32 for Brent in the Basrah file’s benchmark table and at $97.48, down 81 cents, in the Basrah closing account, which records Iraq’s own grades down more than 23 percent on the week even after Friday’s rebound; the disagreement is printed in the Cocked Hat. The morning brief for November 7 counts the week’s bears in a row: the Nikkei down 20 percent from its June peak, Taiwan’s index 20 percent below its October high, and the Kospi 44 percent below its June high, with the indexes carrying less AI exposure up single digits on the month. Saturday’s one scheduled corporate item is Berkshire Hathaway’s third-quarter report, posted at about 7:00 a.m. Central, 0800 ET, per the company’s own notice — the first quarterly test under Chief Executive Greg Abel, with analysts expecting about $5.88 to $5.91 a share and attention on insurance underwriting and the deployment of about $364.7 billion in cash and Treasury bills, per the preview filed below. It lands after this edition collects and belongs to the Midday Watch.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Asunción’s vote: 44 to nothing among the senators in attendance in the wire’s account, 44 to 1 in two other full accounts, and 44 of 45 members present in a fourth — the removal unanimous or nearly so in every file, the single dissent present in some and absent in others; the successor’s number varies with it, the 52nd president in one file and the 53rd in another. Second, Qeshm: the president’s confirmed strike of Friday evening on one bearing; Tasnim’s and IRNA’s two projectiles in the Suza area early Saturday on a second; and on a third, no American comment on the Saturday reports, no Iranian damage assessment, and the relationship between the impacts and the confirmed operation stated as not independently established. Third, Brent’s Friday settlement: $98.32 in one closing table, $97.48 in another — two readings within a dollar of one closed market. Fourth, the drone claims: an MQ-1 on Friday and an MQ-9 on Saturday in Tehran’s accounts, and no confirmation, denial, or wreckage in any American file. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts at 0400 are single-valued: Paraguay’s president was removed on Friday and his vice president holds the office to August 2028, and Mr. Peña reports to prosecutors this morning; Qatar states that the United States and Iran are continuing to work toward a deal and that reports of failure are false; Beijing states that a three-way meeting of the heads of state is under discussion for Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, with no final decision announced; the larger Iran decision was not announced in the night; Mississippi stands at 2,574 and Alaska at 637, both uncalled, both speaking next on Tuesday; and Berkshire Hathaway reports at 0800. The log proceeds to Saturday.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Thirty items.

Subjective
Reuters, via 98.5 The River — two missiles strike Qeshm Island, Tasnim says

Cairo, November 7: Tasnim said on Saturday that initial reports indicated two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage and further details to follow once authorities confirmed the incident; IRNA had earlier reported that local witnesses said two projectiles struck the Suza area after the sound of an aircraft was heard over the island; and Qatar’s International Media Office denied reports that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement, calling them false and misleading and saying both sides continue to work toward an agreement.

Subjective
The Insight International — explosions reported on Qeshm Island

Tehran, November 7: state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, with witnesses describing two projectiles striking the Suza area after aircraft were heard overhead; state television said two explosions were heard in the Souza area late Friday with no casualties; Fars reported explosions in Qeshm and in the port city of Bandar Khamir, possibly linked to warning shots toward the Strait of Hormuz; none of the accounts has been independently confirmed and there was no immediate American confirmation of a new strike; and Qatar denied reports that Washington and Tehran had failed to reach an agreement, saying mediation continues.

Subjective
The Insight International — the president says minor strikes were carried out near Qeshm

West Palm Beach, November 7: the president said American forces carried out what he called minor strikes on Iranian air defenses near Qeshm Island, speaking after Iranian media reported explosions on the island; “We do minor strikes,” he said, describing an anti-aircraft device knocked out in about 15 minutes, maybe five; the state broadcaster quoted the army as saying air defenses intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over Qeshm; and Central Command said the situation was “relatively calm” and declined further comment on the explosion reports.

Subjective
Press TV — air defense destroys an MQ-9 Reaper over Qeshm Island

November 7, 0052 GMT: the Army’s Public Relations Office announced that the integrated air defense network intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 Reaper drone over Qeshm Island, targeted by new air defense systems operated by the Army Air Defense Force under the unified network; the account describes the MQ-9 as an armed reconnaissance drone capable of 50,000 feet and carrying Hellfire missiles, at about $30 million a unit; and it places the claim in a history running from the RQ-4 downed over the strait in June 2019 to repeated interceptions during the war that began in February 2026.

Subjective
Nmkhabar — Iran claims an MQ-1 and an MQ-9 downed over Qeshm

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed on Friday that air defenses destroyed an American MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island, and Iranian reporting on Saturday claimed an MQ-9 downed over the same island; the United States has not provided immediate confirmation of either claim; the file also records that Qatar presented a draft peace plan to Iran on October 30 which a senior Iranian official rejected as unacceptable, and that Qatar stated on November 3 that both the United States and Iran were reviewing the mediators’ proposals.

Subjective
WarBrief Live — the Qeshm strikes, what is confirmed and what is reported

November 7: the president confirmed on November 6 that American forces carried out limited strikes against Iranian air defenses on Qeshm Island hours after Iranian media reported two projectiles hitting the Suza area; the file divides the record sharply — the American strike confirmed by the president himself, Iran’s claims of an MQ-1 downed on November 6 and an MQ-9 on November 7 reported only by Tehran and not confirmed by Washington; Central Command described the situation around Qeshm as relatively calm and late on November 6 offered up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear programme; Qatar dismissed reports that the talks have failed, and mediators are reported to have put forward a two-day bridge proposal; and Qatar’s prime minister said at Oxford on November 6 that the crisis cannot be left unresolved.

Subjective
Clash Report — the president confirms a new strike on Qeshm Island

November 7, 0248 GMT: the president confirmed a new limited strike against an Iranian air defense system near Qeshm Island, speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach on Friday evening and describing the operation as minor; Tasnim reported early Saturday that two missiles had struck the island and IRNA cited witnesses who heard an aircraft before two projectiles struck the Suza area; no official Iranian damage assessment and no confirmed casualty figures had been released; the precise relationship between the reported impacts and the American operation has not been independently established; and the incident follows the strikes of November 2, described by American officials as defensive.

Subjective
Stockbiz — missiles strike Qeshm Island

November 7: Tasnim reported that Qeshm Island had been struck by two missiles, with no official information about damage; IRNA, citing local witnesses, reported that two objects fell in the Suza area after aircraft were heard overhead; the American military has not commented on the report; and the attack came after Iran’s military said on November 6 that its air defense forces had shot down an American MQ-9 drone over the island — a claim the same file also dates to the Saturday reporting — with Qeshm identified as Iran’s largest island, in Hormozgan province near the northern approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.

Subjective
ANI, via Devdiscourse — Qatar says both sides are working towards a deal

Doha, November 7: Qatar’s International Media Office said the prime minister’s remarks were distorted online by fake accounts claiming the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement; the reports are “false and misleading,” the remarks “deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability,” and the prime minister stated that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal; and Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations.

Subjective
Daily Caller, carrying the Associated Press — Paraguay’s president removed after a bank collapse

Paraguay’s Senate removed President Santiago Peña on Friday and authorities placed him under house arrest an hour later; not one of the 44 senators in attendance opposed the removal, which rested on misconduct in office, making him the second president forced out by impeachment since 1989; Vice President Pedro Alliana took the oath to finish a term closing in August 2028; prosecutors cited suspected breach of trust in an arrest order also covering the central bank chief Mr. Peña installed, with charges undetermined and possibly extending to influence peddling; regulators seized the digital lender ueno on November 3 after its solvency fell under half the required level — about 3 million customers, as much as $850 million in public money, $380 million of it from the state pension and health fund; the deposit guarantee covers about $38,000 per depositor with 97 percent of holders estimated fully within it; Mr. Peña held shares in ueno’s holding company until last year and denied the accusations; and he must report to prosecutors on Saturday morning, the attorney general having opened three criminal cases.

Subjective
Indian Economic Observer, carrying ANI and CNN — the Senate votes to remove President Peña

Asunción, November 7: the Senate on Friday voted to impeach and remove President Peña, stripping him of his immunity amid a criminal investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, following a fast-tracked trial; the Senate voted 44 to 1, after the lower house’s impeachment vote; Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as head of state; the crisis was triggered when Ueno Bank, an institution with which the president had established business ties, was shuttered overnight in a solvency crisis that cut off millions of depositors from their savings; and the attorney general has opened three separate criminal cases against Mr. Peña and several former officials.

Subjective
World Pulse Wire — Paraguay’s president impeached and arrested in a bank scandal

November 7: President Peña was removed by the Senate on Friday and placed under house arrest hours after Ueno Bank’s collapse froze the savings of nearly three million people; the Senate voted 44 to 0 among those present in this account’s headline figures and its text records every one of the 44 senators in the chamber voting to remove, with one senator absent, the verdict read as guilty of poor performance in his duties; the removal also takes away his immunity and his lifetime Senate seat; Vice President Pedro Alliana, 52, was sworn in as the 53rd president to serve until August 2028; Mr. Peña resigned on Thursday, Congress refused the resignation, and he denies wrongdoing; and prosecutors are weighing breach of trust and influence peddling.

Subjective
Pollar News — the Senate removes Peña; Alliana sworn in
